articles.title: Retention enema with Chinese botanical drug decoctions as an adjunct to conventional treatment for gastrointestinal dysfunction in severe acute pancreatitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of adding retention enemas with Chinese botanical drug decoctions to conventional treatment for gastrointestinal dysfunction in severe acute pancreatitis (SAP), and to appraise how the preparations were reported. METHODS: Seven English and Chinese databases were searched to 21 January 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs). We assessed risk of bias (RoB 2), data integrity, preparation reporting (ConPhyMP) and certainty of evidence (GRADE), and performed random-effects meta-analyses with Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals. RESULTS: Twenty-five RCTs (1,963 participants), all from China, were included; one further report was a duplicate publication. Five trials that reproduced the data of earlier trials from other hospitals were excluded from the primary analysis (20 trials, 1,643 participants). No trial was blinded or registered, and none chemically characterised its preparation. The enema was associated with shorter times to first defecation (SMD -2.79, 95% CI -4.37 to -1.20; 7 trials), first flatus (SMD -2.00, -3.64 to -0.35; 6 trials) and recovery of bowel sounds (SMD -2.88, -5.70 to -0.06; 5 trials), and with a higher effectiveness rate (OR 4.29, 2.70 to 6.81; 14 trials), but heterogeneity was very high and prediction intervals included no effect for the recovery times, and small-study effects were evident for the effectiveness rate. Adverse events were reported in six trials (OR 0.64, 0.20-1.99). Certainty was very low for all outcomes except length of stay (low). No clear evidence of a difference between Chengqi-type and other formulas was found, but the subgroup analyses were underpowered and do not establish equivalence. CONCLUSION: Very low-certainty evidence suggests that botanical drug retention enemas may hasten the recovery of gastrointestinal function in SAP. Because the trials were small, unblinded, at high risk of bias and partly affected by duplicated data, and the preparations were heterogeneous and uncharacterised, the findings cannot be attributed to any specific preparation, and safety remains uncertain. Rigorous, registered trials using characterised preparations are needed. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261301311, Identifier, CRD420261301311.

articles.title: Renoprotective effects of salvianolic acid B in experimental diabetic kidney disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of efficacy, mechanisms, and translational robustness.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Salvia miltiorrhiza Bunge has a long history of use in traditional Chinese medicine, and salvianolic acid B (SalB) is one of its major water-soluble phenolic constituents. SalB and chemically defined related forms have shown potential renoprotective effects in experimental diabetic kidney disease (DKD), but the consistency and robustness of these effects across models, chemical forms, and outcomes remain unclear. AIM OF THE STUDY: To systematically evaluate the renoprotective efficacy, mechanistic evidence, and robustness of SalB and prespecified chemically defined related forms, including lithospermic acid B/lithospermate B and magnesium lithospermate B (MLB), in experimental DKD. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Animal studies of DKD were systematically identified. Risk of bias was assessed using the SYRCLE tool. Continuous outcomes were pooled as mean differences (MDs) or Hedges' g, as appropriate, using random-effects models with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation and Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Subgroup analyses, prediction intervals, leave-one-out analyses, and sensitivity analyses were used to assess heterogeneity and robustness. RESULTS: Sixteen reports representing 13 independent animal studies were included. All included animal experiments used male animals. SalB-related interventions reduced serum creatinine (SCr; MD = -13.52 μmol/L, 95% CI -23.09 to -3.95) and blood urea nitrogen (BUN; MD = -3.85 mmol/L, 95% CI -6.85 to -0.86). However, heterogeneity was very high for both outcomes (I2 = 91.7% and 96.0%, respectively), and both 95% prediction intervals crossed the null. The pooled SCr effect remained statistically significant in the sensitivity analyses, whereas the BUN effect became non-significant after exclusion of one study. UACR was reduced (Hedges' g = -1.01, 95% CI -1.82 to -0.20), although only three studies contributed to this analysis, whereas the primary analyses of 24-h UAE and 24-h UTP, each based on three studies, were not statistically significant. MDA showed the most consistent mechanistic signal (Hedges' g = -1.77, 95% CI -2.55 to -0.99; I2 = 18.2%), although this analysis included only five studies. Estimates based on these small evidence bases should therefore be interpreted cautiously. TNF-α and IL-1β findings were summarized narratively by molecular level because mRNA and protein measurements were not combined. CONCLUSION: Current preclinical evidence supports the renoprotective potential of SalB and related defined chemical forms in experimental DKD, but the effects are outcome-dependent rather than uniformly consistent across renal endpoints. The pooled SCr estimate remained statistically significant in the sensitivity analyses but was highly heterogeneous and model-dependent, whereas the BUN estimate was highly heterogeneous and sensitive to exclusion of an individual study. Therefore, neither pooled estimate should be interpreted as evidence of a uniform effect across experimental settings. Evidence was comparatively consistent for MDA and supportive for UACR, whereas other renal, inflammatory, and fibrotic outcomes were less stable. Several outcomes were based on only three to five studies or showed substantial-to-very-high heterogeneity, and the exclusive use of male animals further limited precision and generalizability. Overall, these findings indicate potential, but not definitive, renoprotective efficacy. Specific pathway-level conclusions remain tentative because most pathways were investigated in only one or a few studies, and some supporting observations were derived from complementary in vitro experiments rather than independently replicated in vivo evidence. Future studies should use standardized models, include both sexes, apply rigorous chemical characterization, evaluate dose-exposure-response relationships, and prioritize independent in vivo replication and causal mechanistic validation. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261433596, identifier CRD420261433596.

articles.title: Comparing the pharmacological effects of different ginsenosides in rodent models of heart failure: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate and compare the effects and potential advantages of different ginsenosides in animal models of heart failure (HF). METHODS: We systematically searched for and extracted data from studies of ginsenosides, including Rb1, Rg1, Rg3 and Rg5, and total ginsenosides in animal models of HF. Outcomes included left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), left ventricular fractional shortening (LVFS), left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP), maximum rate of left ventricular pressure rise (+dP/dtmax), serum brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) and the heart weight index. Random-effects network meta-analysis estimated effects relative to model controls, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and 95% prediction intervals (PrIs). All networks were star-shaped, sharing the model control as a common comparator, and lacked closed loops; statistical inconsistency testing was therefore not possible. Exploratory analyses examined effect modification by model type, animal species, administration route and treatment duration. Sensitivity analyses included stratification by model type, separate analyses of BNP and NT-proBNP, alternative effect scales for HW/BW, and networks restricted to individual ginsenosides. Study quality was assessed using the SYRCLE risk-of-bias tool. The study sought to compare the pharmacological profiles of individual ginsenosides and provide evidence to inform intervention selection for clinical trials in HF. RESULTS: We included 29 studies covering 10 ginsenoside interventions. Several ginsenosides significantly improved cardiac functional outcomes compared with HF model controls. For serum BNP reduction, Rg1 (SMD = -2.38, 95% CI -4.51 to -0.25), Rb1 (SMD = -2.60, 95% CI -3.80 to -1.40) and total ginsenosides (SMD = -1.94, 95% CI -3.07 to -0.82) showed significant effects. However, the Rg1 effect was no longer significant after mixture nodes were excluded. Significant increases in LVEF were observed with total ginsenosides (MD = 17.56, 95% CI 7.65-27.48), Re (MD = 17.31, 95% CI 2.16-32.46), Rg3 (MD = 16.09, 95% CI 6.03-26.14), Rb1 (MD = 12.09, 95% CI 6.71-17.46) and Rg1 (MD = 13.68, 95% CI 3.28-24.09). LVFS was significantly higher with Rg1 (MD = 11.72, 95% CI 4.92-18.52), Rg3 (MD = 9.90, 95% CI 5.50-14.29), total secondary ginsenosides (MD = 10.30, 95% CI 2.12-18.48), Rb1 (MD = 8.95, 95% CI 6.16-11.74),Re (MD = 8.29, 95% CI 0.24-16.34) and Rd (MD = 6.48, 95% CI 0.45-12.51). Total ginsenosides (MD = -3.97, 95% CI -4.39 to -3.55), Re (MD = -1.65, 95% CI -2.24 to -1.06), Rb1 (MD = -1.49, 95% CI -2.54 to -0.44) and Rb2 (MD = -1.40, 95% CI -2.48 to -0.32) significantly reduced LVEDP. Total ginsenosides (MD = 1374.00, 95% CI 425.00-2,323.00) and Rb1 (MD = 1200.74, 95% CI 718.89-1682.60) significantly increased +dP/dtmax. For the heart weight-to-body weight (HW/BW) ratio, none of the five nodes (Rh2, Rb1, Rg5, Re and Rg1) showed a significant effect (all P > 0.05). The available evidence was insufficient to determine the effects of ginsenosides on HW/BW. CONCLUSION: Some ginsenosides improve haemodynamic and cardiac functional outcomes in rodent models of HF. Given the methodological limitations of the included studies, these findings require confirmation in high-quality preclinical studies. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://osf.io/ye48s/; Identifier, YE48S.

articles.title: Effect of an esketamine-based opioid-sparing perioperative regimen on early postoperative anxiety in women undergoing total laparoscopic hysterectomy: a randomized participant- and outcome-assessor-blinded controlled trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative anxiety is common after hysterectomy and may impair recovery. We evaluated whether an esketamine-based opioid-sparing perioperative regimen could reduce early postoperative anxiety in women undergoing total laparoscopic hysterectomy. METHODS: In this single-center, randomized, participant- and outcome-assessor-blinded controlled trial, women aged 45-60 years were assigned 1:1 to Group K or Group C. Group K received an esketamine-based opioid-sparing perioperative regimen comprising esketamine during anesthesia induction and maintenance and esketamine-containing patient-controlled intravenous analgesia, together with lower protocol-specified sufentanil and remifentanil dosing. Group C received a conventional opioid-based perioperative regimen, with normal saline used as the study-drug control. The primary outcome was the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS) score on postoperative day 1 (POD 1). Secondary outcomes included POD three anxiety, quality of recovery, pain, sleep, postoperative nausea and vomiting, and neuropsychiatric adverse events. RESULTS: Of 170 randomized patients, 167 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (83 in Group C and 84 in Group K). POD 1 SAS scores assessed 24 h after surgery were lower in Group K than in Group C, whereas no significant between-group difference was observed at 72 h after surgery (POD 3), after completion of PCIA. Group K also had higher QoR-15 scores, lower POD 1 pain and insomnia scores, and longer device-estimated total and deep sleep duration. No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in the incidences of the recorded common adverse events. CONCLUSION: An esketamine-based opioid-sparing perioperative regimen was associated with lower SAS scores at 24 h after surgery during the early postoperative treatment period; however, this between-group difference was not maintained at 72 h after completion of PCIA. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: [https://www.chictr.org.cn/historyversionpub.html?regno=ChiCTR2300074484]: identifier [ChiCTR2300074484].

articles.title: The hidden impact of laxatives on drug absorption and efficacy: a clinical perspective.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Laxatives are among the most widely used pharmacological agents worldwide, taken both as prescribed therapy and as unsupervised over-the-counter self-medication. Despite this near-ubiquitous exposure, their capacity to alter the pharmacokinetics and, consequently, the clinical efficacy or safety of concomitantly administered drugs remains under-recognized in routine practice. This article reviews under a clinical perspective the principal mechanisms by which laxatives interfere with drug absorption -accelerated intestinal transit, luminal dilution by osmotic agents, mucosal permeability changes induced by stimulant and anthranoid compounds, and electrolyte-mediated pharmacodynamic amplification- and summarizes the clinical evidence available for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs. Populations at particular risk, including patients with inflammatory bowel disease, older adults on polypharmacy, and individuals with chronic or covert laxative use, are discussed. Practical recommendations are proposed for clinicians, and priority areas for future pharmacokinetic research are outlined. AREAS COVERED: The literature was identified through a search of Medline and Science Citation Index databases, supplemented by screening of relevant reference lists and clinical-trial information. EXPERT OPINION: The use of laxatives may interfere with the absorption of several drugs, but the literature data on this issue are still relatively scarce. The simultaneous prescription of laxatives when other drugs are used must be always carefully evaluated, especially in older subjects.

articles.title: Endoplasmic reticulum stress in multiple myeloma: adaptive mechanisms, therapy resistance, and emerging therapeutic opportunities.
articles.abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM), a hematological malignancy of antibody-producing plasma cells is one of the most common hematological malignancies alongside leukemia and lymphoma. Despite a significant number of therapeutic advances in immunotherapy, proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, monoclonal antibodies, bispecific antibodies, and CAR T Cell therapies, it remains incurable hematologic cancer, mostly due to acquired resistance during therapy. Disease relapse and therapeutic resistance continue to be major clinical challenges. High rate of immunoglobulin production in MM cells, imposes chronic endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and renders myeloma cells highly dependent on adaptive protein quality control mechanisms particularly, unfolded protein response (UPR). The three principal UPR signaling include inositol-requiring enzyme 1 (IRE1), protein kinase RNA-like ER kinase (PERK), and activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6) coordinate cellular adaptation by restoring proteostasis, promoting cell survival, and enabling resistance to therapeutic stress. Increasing evidence indicates that dysregulation of ER stress pathways is interconnected with several other cellular stress pathways such as oxidative stress, the integrated stress response (ISR), mitochondrial dysfunction autophagy, and metabolic reprogramming, collectively supporting myeloma cell survival and disease progression. In this review we highlighted the importance of ER stress-associated pathway and emerging novel molecular targets with translational potential in MM. Relevant literature was selected based on its focus on ER stress, drug resistance and their molecular mechanisms in myeloma, were critically reviewed and interpreted. A comprehensive understanding of these mechanisms is important for the development of innovative therapeutic strategies to combat drug resistance and improve patient outcomes in MM.

articles.title: Potential therapeutic strategies targeting ferroptosis in chronic diabetic wounds.
articles.abstract: Chronic diabetic wounds, most commonly presenting as diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs), represent one of the most devastating complications of diabetes mellitus. They affect a large proportion of diabetic patients worldwide and are associated with elevated risks of non-traumatic lower limb amputation, high mortality, and substantial socioeconomic burden. Many affected patients fail to achieve complete wound closure following standard-of-care treatment, highlighting a critical unmet need for novel mechanism-driven therapeutic targets. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death (RCD) driven by the lethal accumulation of lipid peroxides, has emerged in recent years as a key pathogenic mechanism underlying impaired diabetic wound repair. Ferroptosis is defined by glutathione depletion, intracellular iron overload, and unrestrained lipid peroxidation. This review synthesizes current evidence regarding the regulatory mechanisms of ferroptosis, with a particular focus on its detrimental effects on the four major wound-repair-associated cell populations involved in cutaneous wound healing. Furthermore, we delineate the pathological alterations in chronic diabetic wounds that sensitize cells to ferroptosis. Ferroptosis-related biomarkers that may have clinical utility for predicting wound healing prognosis and monitoring therapeutic responses were also evaluated. A central emphasis of this review is placed on emerging anti-ferroptotic therapeutic strategies for diabetic wounds, accompanied by a critical appraisal of their preclinical efficacy and translational potential. Finally, we discuss prevailing challenges in the field and propose future research directions to accelerate the clinical translation of ferroptosis-targeted therapies for chronic diabetic wounds.

articles.title: Atomoxetine-associated Raynaud's phenomenon in children: an under-recognized risk of non-stimulant ADHD therapy.
articles.abstract: Raynaud's phenomenon (RP) is an increasingly recognized yet still underreported adverse effect of ADHD pharmacotherapy. Whereas stimulant-associated RP is well documented, atomoxetine-related RP has surfaced only in isolated pediatric cases, leaving a gap in our understanding of non-stimulant toxicity. This narrative review reports the first Asian pediatric case identified in English- and regional-language literature and synthesizes the global evidence base, integrating five pediatric cases, targeted literature retrieval, and disproportionality analyses of FAERS and WHO VigiBase. Atomoxetine carries a consistent pharmacovigilance signal for RP. Beyond the elevation of synaptic cleft norepinephrine, the five cases point to suspected contributors: plasma drug concentration, CYP2D6-mediated metabolic variability-particularly relevant in East Asian populations-and individual susceptibility with superimposed triggers. Onset latency is highly variable (hours to years), and the course in reported cases is milder and fully reversible, without digital ulceration, features consistent with, though not determined by, the sustained, gradual peripheral noradrenergic elevation produced by selective norepinephrine transporter inhibition, in contrast to the rapid catecholamine surges typical of stimulants. These findings call for longitudinal vigilance beyond the titration phase, prompt exclusion of secondary causes, and systematic pharmacovigilance reporting.

articles.title: Transient receptor potential ion channels in dry eye disease: mechanisms, pharmacological targeting, and clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Dry eye disease (DED) is a multifactorial, symptomatic disease characterized by loss of homeostasis of the tear film and/or ocular surface, with tear film instability and hyperosmolarity, ocular surface inflammation and damage, and neurosensory abnormalities acting as etiological factors. Transient receptor potential (TRP) channels are nonselective cation channels that translate thermal, osmotic, mechanical, and chemical cues into Ca2+ signaling, neuronal activity, secretory reflexes, and inflammatory responses across the ocular surface. Among the TRP family members implicated in DED, TRPM8 has the most advanced translational evidence: it contributes to ocular surface cooling/wetness sensing and basal tearing, and the TRPM8 agonist acoltremon was approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration in 2025 for the signs and symptoms of DED in adults. TRPV1 links hyperosmotic stress to epithelial inflammatory signaling and nociception, but also participates in reparative neuroimmune responses after corneal injury. TRPA1 is strongly implicated in chemical nociception, neurogenic inflammation, and pain sensitization, whereas TRPV4 is better supported as a regulator of epithelial volume homeostasis and membrane-associated mucins. These channels therefore differ substantially in cellular context, disease-stage dependence, and clinical maturity. This review integrates current mechanistic, preclinical, and clinical evidence for TRPM8, TRPV1, TRPA1, and TRPV4, discusses emerging evidence for TRPP2, and proposes a phenotype-oriented framework for pharmacological targeting. Particular emphasis is placed on evidence hierarchy, unresolved controversies, long-term sensory safety, and biomarkers needed to advance precision TRP-directed therapy in DED.

articles.title: AI-Assisted Lipid Nanoparticle Design for In Vivo mRNA Delivery: A Multiscale Therapeutic-System Engineering Framework.
articles.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have rendered mRNA therapeutics clinically viable, yet their design remains impeded by tightly intertwined chemical, physical, biological, and manufacturing variables. This review argues that artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted LNP design should be approached as multiscale therapeutic-system engineering rather than reduced to isolated predictive tasks. We propose that AI models must holistically integrate ionizable lipid chemistry, supramolecular assembly, protein corona remodeling, endosomal escape, organ- and cell-specific tropism, cargo attributes, safety profiles, and process robustness into a cohesive framework. Current studies demonstrate that machine learning can prioritize ionizable lipids, predict formulation properties, guide tissue-selective delivery, and expedite the design-build-test-learn cycle. However, many models remain constrained by insufficient sample sizes, poor in vitro/in vivo translation, reliance on random-split validation, and narrow potency-centric endpoints. We propose and apply a claim-specific evidence hierarchy for AI-LNP studies and propose standardized multimodal datasets, mechanism-informed descriptors, scaffold-level holdout tests, and manufacturability-aware objective functions. We conclude that digital models of LNP delivery must be treated as emerging hypotheses until anchored by prospective and clinically relevant evidence.

articles.title: Plant-Derived Exosome-like Nanovesicles: Advances in Preparation, Characterization, Bioactivity, and Drug Delivery.
articles.abstract: Plant-derived exosome-like nanovesicles (PELNs) have emerged as a research hotspot in the field of biological nanocarriers owing to their unique advantages, including natural safety, favorable biocompatibility, and excellent bioactivity. Currently, as a highly promising new type of natural drug delivery carrier, PELNs have demonstrated broad application prospects. However, issues such as immature large-scale preparation processes, insufficient preparation stability, and incomplete in vivo safety evaluation systems restrict their industrialization and clinical implementation. To clarify the current research status and application potential of PELNs and facilitate their clinical translation and development, this study systematically integrates and sorts the biogenesis mechanisms and material component characteristics of PELNs, summarizes and compares the current mainstream preparation technologies and characterization methods, elaborates on their pharmacological activities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-tumor, skin repair, and neuroprotection, and the corresponding mechanisms of action, summarizes the research progress of their clinical application in skin diseases, brain diseases, and other fields, and proposes targeted prospects for future improvement directions, such as process optimization and targeted modification based on the existing bottlenecks. This study aims to provide theoretical support and conceptual references for in-depth research, clinical translation, and industrial development of PELNs.

articles.title: Hydrogel-Mediated Cancer Immunotherapy: Material Design, Immune Regulation and Translation.
articles.abstract: Durable responses to cancer immunotherapy remain difficult to achieve in many solid tumors, where rapid clearance and inadequate intratumoral exposure combine with immunosuppression and systemic toxicity to limit treatment benefit. Local hydrogel delivery offers a way to concentrate immunomodulatory signals at the lesion, although its performance varies with the formulation, payload, and tumor setting. Drawing on melanoma, breast cancer, and other solid-tumor models, this review relates hydrogel design to payload-mediated immune regulation, combination therapy, and preclinical translation. Injectable and in situ-forming systems have prolonged local exposure to immunogenic cell death inducers, adjuvants, cytokines, and checkpoint inhibitors, while also supporting adoptive cell delivery. Some multicomponent formulations release their payloads at different times, but the contribution of this sequence to efficacy remains unresolved. Selected syngeneic studies report improved local control and reduced recurrence or metastasis, with abscopal responses or rechallenge protection in some cases. Across these studies, retention and release kinetics, considered together with the payload, appear more informative than material class alone. Because most reports evaluate individual immune endpoints, coordinated regulation across the cancer-immunity cycle has yet to be demonstrated. Durable clinical benefit also remains unproven. We examine these findings in relation to matrix properties, release behavior, tumor heterogeneity, and model selection, separating demonstrated effects from design potential. Clinical development will require formulations suited to specific indications, standardized immune and safety assessment, and scalable manufacture, supported by clinical tests of defined mechanisms beyond general claims about the platform.

articles.title: Poly(ADP-ribose) Glycohydrolase (PARG) Inhibitors: Mechanisms of Action, Structural Optimization, and Combination Therapeutic Strategies in Cancer Therapy.
articles.abstract: In recent years, poly(ADP-ribose) glycohydrolase (PARG), a key enzyme in DNA damage repair pathways, has emerged as a major focus in anticancer drug discovery. PARG inhibitors exhibit broad-spectrum antitumor effects across diverse tumor types via multiple mechanisms, such as triggering sustained nuclear replication stress and mitotic catastrophe, as well as modulating the stability of cell cycle checkpoint proteins. This review systematically summarizes the mechanisms of action of PARG inhibitors, recent advances in their structural optimization, and their applications in combination with immunotherapy, ATR/CHK1 inhibitors, and natural products, aiming to highlight the unique value and clinical translation prospects of PARG inhibitors as a new generation of highly selective, multi-mechanism antitumor agents.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal Coordination of Photosensitizer Delivery and Irradiation Regimens in Cancer Photodynamic Therapy.
articles.abstract: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) depends on the spatial and temporal overlap of photoactive photosensitizer, light, and oxygen. Formulation improvements are therefore meaningful only when they change the exposure available during irradiation and improve an indication-relevant outcome. This narrative review links delivery and activation to drug-light interval selection, oxygen-dependent dosimetry, combination-treatment sequence, and clinical implementation. Representative comparisons support three conclusions. First, cellular uptake and total tumor concentration incompletely describe active exposure, and the preferred irradiation window depends on whether treatment targets vasculature, tumor cells, or light-triggered drug release. Second, temporal fractionation and oxygen-informed dose estimates can improve treatment interpretation within specific systems, but their thresholds are not transferable without validation. Third, programmed release and combination efficacy provide weaker evidence for an optimal sequence than comparisons that isolate treatment order; mathematical synergy also depends on the model and endpoint. Human studies establish the feasibility of multivariable monitoring more clearly than the clinical benefit of feedback-based treatment. We propose conditional priorities based on measured limitations in light coverage, active photosensitizer availability, oxygen supply, and systemic disease control, together with criteria for stopping unnecessary increases in formulation complexity. Translation requires reproducible potency, compatible devices, and comparative patient benefit across the complete treatment pathway.

articles.title: Hydrogel-Loaded Mesenchymal Stem Cell-Derived Extracellular Vesicles for Burn Injury: An Emerging Framework for Functional Skin Regeneration.
articles.abstract: Burn injuries compromise the structural, vascular, immunological, and barrier functions of the skin, creating a self-sustaining wound environment marked by persistent inflammation, oxidative stress, microvascular dysfunction, extracellular matrix degradation, and impaired cellular regeneration. Mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (MSC-EVs) have emerged as promising cell-free therapeutics because they deliver bioactive microRNAs, messenger RNAs, proteins, lipids, and other regulatory molecules to macrophages, endothelial cells, keratinocytes, and fibroblasts. Through these intercellular signals, MSC-EVs can promote inflammatory resolution, angiogenesis, cytoprotection, re-epithelialization, matrix remodeling, and scar modulation. However, the therapeutic potential of freely administered EVs is constrained by rapid clearance, enzymatic degradation, loss through wound exudate, and insufficient retention within injured tissue. Hydrogels address these limitations by providing hydrated, tissue-conforming matrices that preserve EV integrity, regulate local release, and prolong exposure at the burn site. Natural polymers, including hyaluronic acid, collagen, gelatin, chitosan, and alginate, offer biocompatibility and extracellular matrix-like interactions, whereas synthetic materials such as polyethylene glycol (PEG), poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA), and polyacrylamide allow more precise control over mechanical behavior, degradation, and molecular transport. Injectable, sprayable, and stimuli-responsive platforms further support conformal administration and pathology-responsive release. The available burn evidence derives mainly from thermal injury models, so this review distinguishes burn-specific findings from supportive evidence in other cutaneous wounds. A central premise of this review is that the regenerative activity of EV-hydrogel systems should not be understood as the additive effect of two independent components. Rather, therapeutic performance emerges from the coordinated interaction between vesicular cargo and hydrogel-governed pharmacokinetics. The hydrogel determines when, where, and for how long intact EVs remain available to recipient cells, while EV cargo directs the cellular programs required for tissue repair. This integrated perspective provides a framework for the rational co-design of EV composition, biomaterial properties, and release behavior. Preconditioning, cargo engineering, hybrid biomaterials, and three-dimensional bioprinting may further strengthen this functional integration. Despite substantial preclinical promise, clinical translation remains limited by EV heterogeneity, inconsistent reporting of EV doses and application schedules, limited evidence that vesicles remain intact after release, sparse data on release kinetics and storage stability, manufacturing variability, insufficient burn-specific evidence, and unresolved safety and regulatory requirements. This review critically examines the biological mechanisms, delivery technologies, engineering strategies, and translational barriers associated with hydrogel-loaded MSC-EVs, and advances an integrated design framework for restoring durable, vascularized, and functionally organized skin after burn injury. It also compiles reported EV doses and regimens, release kinetics, and storage conditions to support standardized reporting and product development.

articles.title: Fisetin Nanotherapeutics for Cancer Prevention and Treatment: Bioavailability, Preclinical Efficacy, and Translational Challenges.
articles.abstract: Fisetin, a polyphenolic compound derived from Venetian sumach (Rhus cotinus L.), exhibits notable antioxidant, neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory, and senolytic effects. The compound Fisetin is a secondary metabolite. Chemically, it is known as 2-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl)-3,7-dihydroxy-4H-1-benzopyran-4-one, 3,3',4',7-tetrahydroxyflavone, or 5-deoxy quercetin. Presently, it is obtained from various plants. This bioactive molecule is also reported to exhibit anticancer potential, and researchers have shown promising activity in the management of various cancers, including oral, breast, lung, and brain cancers, as well as other malignancies. Despite holding significant promise, as with other natural compounds, this molecule is associated with challenges such as poor aqueous solubility, compromised bioavailability, greater lipophilicity, and uneven pharmacokinetic distribution. This review highlights the research-based evidence for Fisetin in cancer treatment and emphasizes nanotechnology-based approaches employing this bioactive molecule across various cancers. Examining fisetin's clinical trials helps chart its evolution from a dietary supplement to a promising anticancer drug.

articles.title: Group 8 Bimetallic Complexes for Light-Driven Cancer Therapy.
articles.abstract: The incorporation of a second metal center with different biological targets and complementary physicochemical properties into metal-based compounds represents a promising strategy to enhance anticancer efficacy and overcome the limitations of conventional monometallic drugs. In recent years, increasing attention has been devoted to multitarget anticancer agents, including heterometallic complexes. This review provides an overview of recent advances in Group 8 bimetallic complexes containing iron, ruthenium, or osmium for light-driven cancer therapy. Particular emphasis is placed on their molecular design, photophysical and photochemical properties, mechanisms of action, and anticancer activity. The influence of the two metal centers on photoactivation, generation of reactive species, cellular targets, and therapeutic efficacy is discussed, together with emerging structure-activity relationships. Finally, current challenges and future perspectives for the development of these complexes as photoactivated anticancer agents are highlighted.

articles.title: Molecularly Aged Protein States as Targets for Drug Design and Delivery in Neurodegenerative Diseases.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative drug discovery usually represents a protein target by its gene, canonical sequence, and one or a few structures. That representation can miss the molecular history accumulated by proteins that persist in the brain. Spontaneous chemistry, incomplete repair, altered turnover, proteolysis, phase transitions, and assembly remodeling generate states that may differ from the canonical target in exposure, function, and therapeutic accessibility. We call compositionally resolved species age-generated proteoforms and use molecularly aged protein states when the exact composition remains uncertain. This Review develops a target-state framework for Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia, Huntington disease, and multiple sclerosis. It separates detection from age association, causality, brain exposure, proximal target engagement, and clinical evidence. Disease-specific analyses connect tau and amyloid-beta proteoforms, alpha-synuclein and lysosomal or mitochondrial assemblies, TDP-43 loss-of-function states, and persistent myelin or extracellular-matrix states to rational modalities and critical validation experiments. Repair, selective removal, stabilization, state-selective antibodies and small molecules, intrabodies, replacement, and synthesis control are evaluated together with blood-brain barrier transport, cellular and organelle access, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics. Each class of target state is mapped to the delivery constraint it imposes and the platform for which a precedent exists, and the exposure requirements that state selectivity implies are set out explicitly, including the fraction of a pool that must be engaged, the duration required to move a slowly accumulating state, and the consequences for dosing interval and pharmacodynamic biomarker choice. The aggregate-directed amyloid antibodies are analysed as the existing clinical test of the framework and of its limits. Machine learning remains central to proteoform identification, multimodal prioritization, structure modeling, and molecular design, provided that labels and prospective tests preserve target-state identity. Classical quantum chemistry can address bounded reaction and recognition problems. Quantum computing is treated as an exploratory implementation that requires matched classical baselines and explicit resources. The central requirement is not that an old protein be abnormal, but that a defined disease-relevant state can be selectively engaged while preserving the functional pool.

articles.title: Microneedle Patches as a Future Delivery System for Internal-Organ Diseases.
articles.abstract: Therapies for visceral diseases have advanced more rapidly than the routes used to deliver them. Oral dosing is limited by degradation and first-pass metabolism; repeated injections impose practical burdens; and surgery-based local delivery is restricted to perioperative settings. Microneedle patches provide a potential platform that can be deployed at two distinct interfaces: organ-surface delivery for local treatment and transdermal delivery through the skin for systemic exposure. Existing reviews have mainly focused on microneedle materials, dermatological applications, or individual organ systems. This review compares skin-applied and organ-surface microneedle delivery within one framework, with emphasis on release design, cargo constraints, microvascular targets, and translational requirements. Organ-surface patches have shown therapeutic efficacy in preclinical cardiac and hepatic models. Skin-applied patches have also produced remote organ effects in selected preclinical models, but most studies do not quantify target-organ exposure, and large-animal or human pharmacokinetic evidence remains limited. We therefore distinguish patch release, systemic absorption, target-organ exposure, and therapeutic efficacy as separate levels of evidence. We further discuss challenges related to peptide, protein, and extracellular-vesicle stability, dose capacity, scalable manufacturing, and regulation. Clarifying these gaps may help guide the development of microneedle patches for visceral diseases.

articles.title: Deep Eutectic Solvents for Dermal Delivery of Venoactive Natural Compounds: Current Evidence and Translational Challenges.
articles.abstract: Chronic venous disease is characterized by sustained venous hypertension, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, microvascular alterations, edema, and progressive tissue remodeling, providing a rationale for locally acting therapeutic strategies. Venoactive natural compounds, including escin, flavonoids, anthocyanins, and proanthocyanidins, possess pharmacologically relevant vascular, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory activities, but their pharmaceutical application is frequently constrained by poor aqueous solubility, chemical instability, unfavorable skin partitioning, and limited permeation. This review examines deep eutectic solvents (DESs) and natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESs) as multifunctional platforms connecting phytochemical extraction with primarily local dermal delivery and, where systemic absorption is intended, transdermal delivery. Particular emphasis is placed on the relationships between hydrogen-bond acceptor/donor composition, molar ratio, water content, polarity, viscosity, and solvation behavior and three interconnected functions: enhanced extraction and solubilization, stabilization of labile phytochemicals, and modulation of cutaneous transport. DESs/NADESs may enhance skin delivery through composition-dependent interactions with stratum-corneum lipids and keratin, hydration of the barrier, and modification in drug thermodynamic activity and vehicle-skin partitioning. These mechanisms are particularly relevant to flavonoids, for which hydroxylation, glycosylation, molecular size, and hydrophilic-lipophilic balance strongly influence skin penetration and retention. Emerging DES-based microemulsions, films, hydrogels, and related systems demonstrate promising improvements in solubility, stability, and skin delivery. However, direct evidence in venous disorders remains limited, and translation requires composition-specific safety assessment, human-skin permeation and retention studies, standardized characterization of multicomponent extracts, and clinically relevant efficacy studies. Overall, DESs/NADESs may link phytochemical extraction with dermal formulation, but their clinical value for venous disorders remains to be established.

articles.title: Sustainable Cyclodextrin-Integrated Nanocomposite Hydrogels: Molecular Engineering, Biological Interactions, and Biomedical Applications.
articles.abstract: Cyclodextrin (CD)-integrated nanocomposite hydrogels combine molecular recognition, a hydrated polymer network, and a nanoscale functional phase. However, improvements are often attributed to the complete formulation without distinguishing the contributions of its individual components. This critical review examines CD-containing hydrogels within a common framework, considering the role of CD, the function of the polymer matrix, the contribution of the nanophase, the quality of component-specific controls, and the relevance of the test model. It discusses carbon-based, metallic, catalytic, MXene, conductive-polymer, and cellulose-based systems in the contexts of drug delivery, wound management, tissue engineering, biosensing, and wearable bioelectronics. The review focuses on host-guest interactions, hydration-dependent mechanics, swelling and release, antimicrobial selectivity, nanoparticle retention, and the limitations of extrapolating laboratory findings to clinical applications. It distinguishes demonstrated effects from plausible mechanisms and identifies cases in which the available controls do not establish synergy. It also considers sustainability in relation to material sourcing, synthesis, energy and solvent use, purification, durability, and end-of-life management; the use of renewable feedstocks alone does not demonstrate environmental benefit. The central argument is that the added complexity of a CD-matrix-nanophase formulation is justified only when comparative testing demonstrates a reproducible, application-relevant advantage over simpler alternatives.

articles.title: Furocoumarin-Rich Medicinal Plants for Vitiligo: Phytochemistry, Melanogenic Mechanisms, and Nano-Encapsulation Strategies.
articles.abstract: Depigmentation disorders of the skin remain difficult to manage despite decades of pharmacological development, and current first-line options are constrained by relapse, incomplete response, or dependence on ultraviolet exposure. A family of structurally related plant compounds called furocoumarins, independently adopted by Egyptian, Unani, and Ayurvedic medical traditions centuries before any mechanistic understanding existed, offers a coherent but underexamined therapeutic framework built around a single paradox: the same compound class that causes severe light-induced skin injury at uncontrolled doses restores pigment at controlled, light-activated doses. This review compares seven species from this plant family across the pathogenesis, mechanism, formulation, safety, and clinical-trial literature rather than cataloging phytochemistry alone. Direct interrogation of the literature overturns several assumptions carried by prior reviews of this compound class: a widely assumed co-stimulatory compound within the best-studied species is shown instead to suppress pigment production through an unrelated pathway; one traditional lineage long treated as botanically distinct is shown to rely on the same source plant as another; and clinical evidence, assumed distributed across the family, is shown to be concentrated almost entirely in a single species-derived compound, leaving the most phytochemically documented species without any identified controlled human trial. A previously unexamined pharmacokinetic interaction between this compound class and a newly approved systemic treatment is identified through cross-study inference. Controlled-release formulation strategies are evaluated against what has and has not been directly demonstrated for this specific compound family, revealing that most proposed carrier types remain entirely untested. A three-arm clinical trial design is proposed as the field's most consequential unmet experiment. Together, these findings reframe furocoumarin phototoxicity as a solvable formulation problem rather than an inherent limit of the compound class, and identify a single, well-defined clinical trial as the most direct route to converting a centuries-old traditional therapy into an evidence-based, dose-controlled treatment option for a condition that current pharmacology has yet to fully resolve.

articles.title: Highways to the Brain: Nanoformulations for the Treatment of Central Nervous System Pathologies.
articles.abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) disorders remain difficult to treat because many pharmacologically active molecules do not achieve adequate exposure in the brain. The blood-brain barrier (BBB), blood-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) barrier, efflux transporters, extracellular matrix, and local clearance mechanisms impose different constraints according to the target compartment and administration route. Nanocarriers can protect unstable payloads, alter pharmacokinetics, and support receptor-mediated or local delivery, but the same properties that promote transport can also increase immune recognition, tissue retention, and neurotoxicity. This review critically examines how nanoparticles (NPs) size, surface charge, composition, degradability, ligand density, and release kinetics should be matched to intravenous, intranasal, intrathecal, intracranial, and oral administration. Rather than treating these routes as interchangeable, we compare the barriers encountered by each route, the payloads for which it is best suited, and the experimental conditions that limit interpretation of reported brain uptake. Particular attention is given to the weak correspondence between many rodent efficacy studies and human delivery constraints, including protein-corona formation after systemic dosing, species differences in BBB and nasal anatomy, limited parenchymal penetration from cerebrospinal fluid, and the procedural risks of direct administration. The resulting route-specific framework is intended to support application-driven formulation design and more informative preclinical evaluation of CNS nanomedicines.

articles.title: Local Drug Delivery for Chronic Venous Disease During Pregnancy and the Postpartum Period: Therapeutic Gaps and Opportunities for Biopolymer-Based and Hybrid Polymeric Formulations-A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Chronic venous disease (CVD) often appears or worsens during pregnancy, yet evidence on the efficacy, maternal systemic exposure, and fetal or infant safety of available treatments remains limited. This narrative review, addressed to pharmaceutical scientists, formulation researchers and clinicians, integrates the natural history of CVD in pregnancy and postpartum, clinical data on local and systemic therapies, maternal-fetal-lactational determinants of local delivery, and the status of biopolymer-based and hybrid polymeric formulations for cutaneous and mucosal use, mostly non-invasive. Compression relieves symptoms but did not prevent new varices in a small randomized prevention trial; oral venoactive drugs lack an adequate safety base. In the sources reviewed, in which non-English publications were not specifically sought, no randomized trial of a topical pharmacological agent for lower-limb CVD in pregnancy or the puerperium was identified, and no study measuring milk or infant exposure after topical use of a venous product was identified. Heparin permeates intact human epidermis poorly, and placental transfer favors small, lipophilic, unbound molecules. Hydrogels, nanocarrier reservoirs, minimally invasive microneedles, active textiles and mucoadhesive gels each address a different compartment, but their evidence is preclinical or limited to non-pregnant adults. A pregnancy-adapted target product profile is proposed, and the principal exposure-related evidence gaps are identified.

articles.title: Recent Advances in Aegle marmelos Fruit Polysaccharides for Pharmaceutical Applications: A Review with Prospectives.
articles.abstract: Nowadays, the pharmaceutical industry is turning to sustainable and biodegradable materials in place of synthetic or petroleum-based ones because of their low toxicity and biocompatibility. Bael fruit gum (BFG), a naturally occurring, water-soluble polysaccharide from Aegle marmelos (A. marmelos), has been widely explored as a carrier material because of its biodegradability, biocompatibility, and abundant, readily modifiable hydroxyl groups. This review differs from earlier reviews of A. marmelos, natural gums, and plant polysaccharides in that it treats the fruit gum itself as a pharmaceutical material and links extraction, composition and structure, modification chemistry, dosage-form performance, safety, and translational barriers. This review distinguishes gum, mucilage, polysaccharide, and extract-based materials; compares extraction routes and the techniques used to characterize BFG; explains how structure governs water retention, viscosity, gelation, mucoadhesion, and release; and differentiates chemical, physical, enzymatic, and nanoparticle-based modifications. Applications are discussed by dosage form hydrogels and wound dressings, matrix tablets, microspheres, nanocarriers, mucoadhesive systems, films, and scaffolds, with quantitative outcomes where reported, together with the available evidence on safety. Important gaps remain in natural variability between batches, limited control of swelling and release in gastrointestinal fluids (and susceptibility to enzymatic degradation, which may be exploited for colon targeting), the absence of genotoxicity, immunogenicity and large-scale production data, and the lack of clinical evidence. These gaps define priorities for future work on modification technology, sustainable extraction, safety assessment, and biomedical applications.

articles.title: The Pathological Microenvironment and Smart Nanotherapies for Diabetes-Associated Erectile Dysfunction: From Redox Regulation to Neurovascular Remodeling.
articles.abstract: Diabetes mellitus-associated erectile dysfunction (DMED) is characterized by impaired nitric oxide signaling, microvascular injury, neuropathy, metabolic dysfunction, and cavernosal remodeling. These abnormalities may limit responses to phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors and compromise regenerative treatment. This focused narrative review examines the potential of nanotherapeutic delivery and microenvironment modulation to address these pathological barriers. We discuss catalytic nanozymes, hypoxia/reactive oxygen species-responsive neurotrophic constructs, mitochondria-targeted piezoelectric systems, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 (FBP1) mRNA-loaded lipid nanoparticles, and extracellular vesicle-hydrogel composites. By distinguishing cell experiments, interventions in diabetic animals, human observational studies, and early clinical experience with related non-nanoparticle interventions, we compare representative platforms in terms of mechanism, administration route, functional endpoints, biodistribution, duration of effect, and safety. Human functional studies provide strong evidence for impaired nitric oxide signaling, whereas therapeutic strategies targeting lactate metabolism, lactylation, ferroptosis, and mitochondrial turnover remain predominantly at the preclinical stage. We further discuss the potential value of candidate clinical phenotypes and exploratory biomarkers for future patient stratification and examine key translational challenges, including local dosing feasibility, off-target exposure, repeated-dose immunogenicity, reproductive safety, and manufacturing consistency. Overall, current findings provide a mechanistic rationale and research direction for further development of DMED nanotherapies. Further preclinical validation and clinical studies are needed to establish their efficacy, safety, and potential advantages over standard treatment.

articles.title: First Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis on the Effect of Cyclodextrins on the Pharmacological Activity of Antihypertensive Drugs.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Despite the availability of numerous antihypertensive agents, achieving effective and sustained blood pressure control remains a challenge. Treatment-resistant hypertension, dose-limiting adverse effects, and poor oral bioavailability are among the major factors limiting the efficacy of conventional antihypertensive therapy. Cyclodextrins (CDs) are widely investigated as potential drug delivery systems for various therapeutic classes owing to their favorable safety profile, biocompatibility, chemical inertness, and structural diversity. Through the formation of inclusion complexes, CDs may improve the aqueous solubility, stability, and bioavailability of poorly water-soluble drugs, thereby enhancing their performance. We aimed to systematically evaluate the potential of cyclodextrins as drug delivery systems for enhancing the pharmaceutical properties of antihypertensive agents, providing the first systematic review and meta-analysis in this field. Methods: We applied the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines (PRISMA) to perform our research. Results: The synthesized literature reveals that most CD-antihypertensive complexes exhibit a 1:1 molecular stoichiometry, though 1:2 and 1:3 guest-to-host ratios also occur. This review establishes that CD complexation improves drug release kinetics, enhances stability, and increases aqueous solubility of the antihypertensive agents. In vivo studies confirm the low toxicity and robust therapeutic efficacy of these complexes. Finally, a meta-analysis of four quantitative studies corroborates the potency of CDs as effective delivery vehicles of compounds with antihypertensive effects. Conclusions: These findings underscore the potential of CDs in hypertension management and highlight the critical need for more in vivo studies and clinical trials to achieve a comprehensive therapeutic evaluation.

articles.title: Shape as an Independent Design Parameter for Blood-Brain Barrier Crossing: Anisotropic Nanoparticles in Neurodegenerative Diseases.
articles.abstract: Background: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) impose a growing burden, yet effective therapy remains limited because the blood-brain barrier (BBB) restricts CNS drug delivery. Existing reviews treat particle geometry as secondary to composition, size, and surface functionalization. Objectives: This review examines shape anisotropy as an independent design parameter for BBB crossing, arguing that non-spherical geometry qualitatively changes the logic of particle-barrier interaction. Methods: As a narrative review, it synthesizes studies comparing anisotropic and spherical particles of comparable size and surface chemistry, with emphasis on mechanistic evidence linking geometry to transport. Findings: Geometry governs adhesion under flow, membrane wrapping, endocytic route multiplicity, and intracellular trafficking. A barrier-crossing versus penetration-depth trade-off is identified: efficient transcytosis and deep parenchymal distribution are mutually exclusive. The same anisotropy that enhances BBB interaction also reduces its predictability-the "paradox of shape"-owing to the protein corona, endothelial heterogeneity, and disease-altered barrier status. Conclusions: Shape is not a universal "key to the BBB" but a controllable, context-dependent parameter, shifting the field from an optimal geometry toward disease-oriented, robustness-based design.

articles.title: Hydroxyapatite-Based Alendronate Coatings for Local Drug Delivery and Implant Osseointegration.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hydroxyapatite (HA) coatings offer an osteoconductive interface and a mineral reservoir for alendronate. Their pharmaceutical value depends on whether binding produces biologically available exposure without impairing healing. This review examines that relationship in HA-alendronate coatings on titanium. Methods: A structured critical narrative review used PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection, with reference-list screening. Screening identified 62 primary studies; contextual literature supported mechanistic and translational interpretation. Results: Adsorption, mineral incorporation, laser deposition and hybrid reservoirs produce different loading and release profiles. Cell and animal findings depend on formulation, dose, comparator and model. Mineral content, bone-to-implant contact and mechanical fixation provide complementary evidence and are not interchangeable outcomes. Human studies have mainly evaluated other bisphosphonates in fibrinogen coatings or alendronate applied as a gel around dental implants. Some reported less marginal bone loss, but improvements in implant stability were inconsistent. These results do not directly establish the efficacy of HA-alendronate coatings. Conclusions: Translation requires reproducible manufacture, measured active-drug availability, preserved physiological remodeling, durable coating adhesion and controlled trials for a defined implant indication. Strong mineral binding alone does not establish effective local therapy.

articles.title: Biomimetic Cell Membrane-Engineered Covalent Organic Frameworks for Smart Drug Delivery: Design Principles, Engineering Strategies, and Translational Challenges.
articles.abstract: Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) have attracted growing interest as drug delivery platforms owing to their ordered porosity, tunable pore architecture, and versatile chemical functionality. Favorable physicochemical characteristics alone, however, do not guarantee effective performance in vivo, and biomimetic membrane engineering has emerged as a strategy for modifying the biological interface of COF nanocarriers. This review develops a principle-based framework structured around five interconnected concepts: biological identity transfer, functional mimicry, homotypic targeting, biophysical compatibility, and programmable responsiveness. Rather than treating membrane coating as a universally beneficial modification, it examines how far these functions depend on membrane source, retained biomolecules, membrane orientation, coating quality, and the properties of the underlying framework. Ten primary membrane-engineered COF systems are compared quantitatively across framework chemistry, membrane source and coating method, particle characteristics, cargo loading, release behavior, biological model, pharmacokinetics, therapeutic outcomes, safety, and study limitations. Five membrane-engineering strategies are evaluated against defined fabrication, scalability, integrity, targeting, cost, and regulatory criteria, distinguishing throughout evidence obtained directly in COF systems from findings extrapolated from other nanocarriers. Translational barriers, including donor variability, membrane integrity, immunogenicity, sterility, framework degradation, batch reproducibility, and regulatory requirements, are examined. Current evidence supports preclinical feasibility but not established translational readiness.

articles.title: Ulinastatin-Loaded Erythrocyte Pharmacocytes as a Targeted Drug Delivery Platform for Acute Pancreatitis: A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Acute pancreatitis (AP) is a common inflammatory disorder associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare burden, particularly in patients with systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), pancreatic necrosis, and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS). Despite advances in intensive care management, nutritional support, and minimally invasive interventions, effective pharmacological therapies targeting the underlying inflammatory and enzymatic mechanisms remain limited. Protease activation, excessive inflammation, and immune dysregulation are key drivers of AP progression. Ulinastatin, a broad-spectrum serine protease inhibitor, exerts anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and organ-protective effects by modulating protease activity, NF-κB signaling, cytokine production, and inflammasome activation. However, conventional intravenous administration is limited by rapid systemic clearance, nonspecific distribution, and insufficient drug exposure at sites of pancreatic inflammation, necessitating repeated dosing. This narrative review aims to evaluate the scientific rationale and the therapeutic potential of ulinastatin-loaded erythrocyte-based drug delivery systems as an innovative strategy for improving the efficacy of acute pancreatitis therapy by optimizing the sustained anti-inflammatory effect of ulinastatin in foci of pancreatic inflammation. Methods: Qualitative narrative synthesis of relevant experimental and clinical literature on AP pathogenesis, ulinastatin pharmacology and therapy, protease inhibition, erythrocyte ghosts, erythrocyte pharmacocytes, and erythrocyte-based drug delivery systems was critically reviewed. The analysis focused on evidence relevant to pancreatic inflammation, drug-delivery performance, potential therapeutic benefits, and translational limitations. Results: Available evidence supports the pharmacological relevance of ulinastatin in inflammatory and protease-mediated conditions and identifies erythrocyte-derived carriers as a potential platform for drug encapsulation, prolonged circulation, and controlled drug release. Direct experimental studies investigating ulinastatin-loaded erythrocyte pharmacocytes in AP are currently lacking. Conclusions: By combining the pharmacological properties of ulinastatin with the physiological advantages of erythrocyte-mediated drug delivery, this approach may offer potential therapeutic benefits. However, these potential advantages remain hypothetical and require validation through dedicated pharmaceutical characterization, pharmacokinetic, biodistribution, and efficacy studies. Ulinastatin-loaded erythrocyte pharmacocytes represent a scientifically plausible but currently unvalidated drug delivery strategy for AP. This narrative review critically examines the therapeutic rationale for combining ulinastatin with erythrocyte-derived drug carriers as a potential targeted delivery strategy for acute pancreatitis. It synthesizes relevant evidence on ulinastatin pharmacology, erythrocyte-based drug delivery, inflammatory mechanisms, and the limitations of conventional systemic administration. Particular attention is given to the potential advantages, translational challenges, and key research gaps associated with this proposed approach. Further preclinical studies are warranted to comprehensively evaluate their pharmacokinetic properties, biological activity, safety, therapeutic efficacy, and potential for clinical translation.

articles.title: Targeting Nuclear Export in Multiple Myeloma: Selinexor, Emerging XPO1 Inhibitors, and Future Therapeutic Strategies.
articles.abstract: Background and Aim: Exportin 1 (XPO1) is the principal nuclear export receptor for numerous tumor-suppressor proteins, regulatory factors, and selected oncogenic mRNAs, and it has emerged as a therapeutically relevant vulnerability in multiple myeloma (MM). Selinexor, a first-in-class oral selective inhibitor of nuclear export (SINE), targets XPO1 and has demonstrated antimyeloma activity both as a doublet and in combination with established therapeutic agents. This review summarizes the biological rationale and molecular mechanisms of XPO1 inhibition, the pharmacological basis of dose and schedule optimization, the clinical evidence supporting selinexor-based therapy, the positioning of XPO1 inhibition relative to BCMA-directed and T-cell-redirecting therapies, mechanisms of resistance and candidate predictive biomarkers, emerging next-generation XPO1 inhibitors, and practical considerations regarding toxicity management. Materials and Methods: A narrative review of the published literature on XPO1 biology and selinexor in MM was performed, with emphasis on preclinical mechanistic studies, prospective clinical trials, and studies addressing resistance, biomarkers, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and treatment-related toxicity. Particular attention was given to pivotal and clinically relevant studies evaluating selinexor-based regimens, including Selinexor Treatment of Refractory Myeloma (STORM), BOSTON, and combination cohorts from the STOMP program, together with recent translational studies expanding the molecular framework of XPO1 inhibition. Results: XPO1 inhibition exerts pleiotropic antimyeloma effects through nuclear retention and reactivation of tumor-suppressor proteins, suppression of NF-κB-dependent signaling and oncogenic mRNA translation, enhancement of glucocorticoid signaling, and disruption of cellular protein homeostasis. More recent findings implicate treatment-induced XPO1 degradation through ubiquitin-regulatory mechanisms and suppression of lipid biosynthesis through the Lipin1-SREBP axis. Clinically, selinexor demonstrated activity in heavily pretreated triple-class refractory MM and subsequently showed improved efficacy when incorporated into once-weekly combination regimens, particularly with bortezomib and dexamethasone. Additional combinations with carfilzomib, pomalidomide, lenalidomide, and daratumumab have demonstrated clinically meaningful activity in selected relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) populations. The clinical pharmacology of selinexor-a short plasma half-life of 6-8 h, dose-proportional exposure, and pharmacodynamic effects that outlast plasma concentrations-provides the rationale for intermittent once-weekly dosing, and clinical development has progressively shifted from twice-weekly 80 mg schedules toward lower-dose once-weekly regimens (40-100 mg) supported by proactive toxicity management. In the current treatment landscape, selinexor-based regimens are unlikely to displace BCMA-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies or bispecific antibodies in eligible patients, but they retain a distinct role for patients who cannot access, are ineligible for, or progress after T-cell-redirecting therapy. However, prospective data in the post-BCMA setting are still lacking. Candidate determinants of response and resistance include XPO1 Cys528 alterations, hnRNPU, USP7-dependent regulation of XPO1 stability, and Lipin1-SREBP signaling; these differ substantially in the strength of the supporting evidence, and none is currently prospectively validated for patient selection. Beyond selinexor, second-generation and non-SINE XPO1 inhibitors such as eltanexor and SL-801 remain in early clinical development. Preclinical findings suggest that selinexor may favorably modulate T-cell and natural killer cell function, while limited clinical observations support further investigation of its use as holding or bridging therapy before CAR T-cell therapy. Preservation of T-cell fitness and improvement in subsequent clinical outcomes remain unproven. Treatment-related cytopenias, gastrointestinal toxicity, fatigue, and hyponatremia remain important but can frequently be addressed through proactive supportive care and dose optimization. Conclusions: XPO1 inhibition represents a mechanistically distinct therapeutic strategy in MM, and selinexor has established clinical activity across multiple relapsed/refractory settings. Increasing use of lower-dose, once-weekly combination strategies has improved its therapeutic feasibility, while emerging insights into XPO1 degradation, metabolic regulation, and molecular determinants of response are broadening the biological framework of this drug class. Within an increasingly crowded therapeutic landscape, the most plausible current role of selinexor-based therapy is as an oral, immediately available option for patients who are ineligible for, cannot access, or have progressed after BCMA-directed and T-cell-redirecting treatments. Prospective biomarker validation, randomized dose optimization, and clarification of treatment sequencing will be important for defining the future role of XPO1-directed therapy in MM.

articles.title: Brain Drug Delivery for Major Depressive Disorder and Treatment-Resistant Depression: From Brain Exposure to Clinical Translation.
articles.abstract: The treatment of major depressive disorder (MDD) and treatment-resistant depression (TRD) remains challenging because of delayed treatment onset, tolerability concerns, and the need for long-term management. Intranasal administration, molecular optimization, nanocarriers, blood-brain barrier (BBB)-targeted transport, and controlled drug release offer different approaches to improving antidepressant delivery. However, increased drug concentrations in the brain do not necessarily lead to better pharmacological effects; their value depends on whether the drug reaches its site of action and engages the relevant target. This review discusses the mechanisms, brain exposure, pharmacodynamic evidence, and clinical translation of different delivery strategies. Particular attention is given to the interpretive limitations of pharmacokinetic metrics and to the differences in evidence linking carrier distribution, functional cargo delivery, and antidepressant efficacy. Current clinical evidence is concentrated mainly on drugs that have entered clinical use, such as esketamine, whereas most novel targeted carriers and engineered extracellular vesicles remain at the preclinical stage. Their development requires identification of the specific drug-development bottleneck that each delivery system is intended to address, followed by validation of the relationships among effective brain exposure, pharmacological activity, safety, and formulation quality. An evaluation framework matched to the delivery mechanism may help determine whether delivery advantages observed experimentally can translate into meaningful therapeutic benefits.

articles.title: Nanocrystal-Based Hydrogels for Cutaneous Delivery: Advances from Fundamental Science to Translational Applications.
articles.abstract: Nanocrystal-loaded hydrogels (NbHs) have emerged as a promising formulation strategy for cutaneous delivery of poorly water-soluble drugs, synergistically integrating the solubilization and permeation-enhancing advantages of nanocrystals (NCs) with the favorable application properties of hydrogel matrices. This review provides a systematic and translational overview of recent advances in this emerging field. We first elucidate the fundamental mechanisms by which NbHs enhance skin delivery, including concentration gradient-driven diffusion, high drug loading, follicular targeting, and improved chemical stability. We then critically evaluate preparation strategies, covering top-down and bottom-up NC fabrication methods as well as two principal incorporation approaches: in situ gelation and blending incorporation. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive overview of therapeutic applications, ranging from arthritis and cosmetic formulations to the treatment of psoriasis, androgenetic alopecia, wound healing, atopic dermatitis, cutaneous malignancies, and fungal infections. Finally, we identify critical challenges and future directions, including stability issues, safety evaluation, scalable manufacturing, and the translational gap between pharmaceutical innovation and clinical application. This review aims to provide a "bench-to-bedside" perspective that bridges fundamental science and translational applications, offering valuable insights for the rational design and clinical development of NbHs.

articles.title: Pharmacokinetic Drug Interactions in Solid Organ Transplantation: From Molecular Mechanisms and Formulation Science to Therapeutic Drug Monitoring and Precision Dosing.
articles.abstract: Solid organ transplant (SOT) recipients are especially vulnerable to pharmacokinetic drug interactions because narrow-therapeutic-index immunosuppressants are used in the setting of polypharmacy, rapidly changing physiology, variable gastrointestinal function, and frequent anti-infective therapy. Interaction magnitude is rarely determined by the perpetrator drug alone; formulation, genotype, hematocrit, albumin, organ function, inflammation, and time after transplantation can materially change the observed exposure response. This narrative review integrates mechanistic and clinical evidence across desensitization, induction, maintenance immunosuppression, and rejection treatment. Particular attention is given to cytochrome P450 3A (CYP3A)- and transporter-mediated interactions, mycophenolic acid enterohepatic recirculation, formulation-dependent exposure, drug-drug-gene interactions, food and herbal products, physiological modifiers, interaction-informed therapeutic drug monitoring, and model-informed dosing. Quantitative transplant data are prioritized where available, with non-SOT evidence identified when it materially informs mechanism or management. A practical 6-D framework (Drug, Dose, Determinants, Drug interactions, Data, and Decision) is proposed to organize patient-specific assessment and move interaction management beyond binary alerts toward quantitative, concentration-guided precision dosing.

articles.title: Clinical Translation of Microneedles for Diabetes Drug Delivery and Metabolic Monitoring.
articles.abstract: Microneedles provide access to skin for peptide delivery and metabolic sensing, but insertion alone does not establish reliable treatment. This narrative review examines the evidence linking microneedle design to clinical claims in diabetes and identifies requirements for translation. Targeted literature retrieval distinguishes human delivery and sensing studies from animal and analytical experiments. Human hollow-microneedle studies show faster insulin absorption than subcutaneous administration, although improvement in primary glycemic outcomes is inconsistent. Responsive insulin and glucagon patches, incretin depots, and integrated sensing-delivery systems remain predominantly preclinical. Human sensing studies provide quantitative feasibility data, but accuracy depends on calibration, reference methods, population, and wear duration. We assess bioactive deposited dose separately from nominal loading, prospective decision accuracy separately from analytical agreement, and commanded delivery separately from verified exposure. Application mechanics, residual drug, local interference, manufacturing, and usability inform a proposed validation framework mapped to relevant standards and regulatory documents. This mapping is conceptual and does not constitute regulatory validation. The review identifies product-specific experiments needed to establish reproducible exposure, dependable measurements, and benefit against appropriate comparators. It does not infer human effectiveness from animal glucose lowering or assign one development pathway to all microneedle architectures.

articles.title: Food-Grade Lipid Nanocarriers and Intestinal Lymphatic Routing of Phytochemicals: Chylomicron Assembly as a Design Target.
articles.abstract: Oral exposure to lipophilic plant bioactives depends on lipid digestion and enterocyte handling. Long-chain fatty acids and monoacylglycerols can be re-esterified and assembled with apolipoprotein B48 into chylomicrons, creating a route through intestinal lymph that differs from portal delivery. Food-grade lipid nanocarriers may alter this pathway by changing lipid digestion, micellar solubilization, cellular uptake, and chylomicron secretion, yet evidence for lymphatic transport is often inferred from bioaccessibility or plasma exposure rather than measured directly. This review evaluates how triglyceride chain length, unsaturation, lipid physical state, emulsifier interfaces, food matrices, and processing shape the digestive transformation of nanoemulsions and lipid particles into mixed colloids and substrates for enterocyte lipid processing. It compares nanoemulsions, nanostructured lipid carriers, liposomes, and related systems, with attention to the distinction between intact-particle uptake and cargo incorporation into endogenous lipoproteins. Static and dynamic digestion, epithelial models, lymph-duct cannulation, chylomicron-associated analyte measurements, and human pharmacokinetics are considered as distinct evidence tiers. The synthesis identifies which design claims are supported by direct lymph measurements and which remain mechanistic hypotheses. A framework aligns lipid composition and cargo chemistry with the intended portal or lymphatic exposure pathway. By treating endogenous chylomicron assembly as a testable design target, this review distinguishes a route-specific mechanism from gains in solubilization, epithelial uptake, or plasma exposure alone.

articles.title: Starving the Aggressor: Recent Advances in Glucose Oxidase-Loaded Nanotherapeutics for Triple-Negative Breast Cancer.
articles.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive subtype characterized by progression, metastasis, and treatment resistance.
