Although options include immune checkpoint inhibitors, PARP inhibitors for selected patients, and antibody-drug conjugates, the absence of a single widely applicable molecular target and tumor heterogeneity remain challenges. Increased glycolytic activity in some TNBC tumors provides a rationale for metabolic intervention, although glucose dependence varies among tumors. Glucose oxidase (GOx) catalyzes the oxidation of accessible glucose in the presence of molecular oxygen, generating hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and gluconic acid. Depending on nanoplatform design and enzyme localization, glucose depletion may occur in the extracellular tumor microenvironment or intracellular compartments following cellular uptake and enzyme release. However, free GOx is limited by poor physiological stability, rapid inactivation, oxygen dependence, inadequate tumor accumulation, and systemic toxicity. Nanotechnology offers strategies to improve enzyme stability and tumor-selective delivery while integrating complementary therapies. Preclinical studies have investigated GOx-loaded nanoplatforms combining metabolic starvation with chemotherapy, chemodynamic therapy, ferroptosis induction, photodynamic and photothermal therapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy. Although these platforms demonstrate promising antitumor activity in experimental models, efficacy and proposed mechanisms vary across formulations and models. Pharmacological synergy should be claimed only when supported by quantitative analyses. Tumor heterogeneity, oxygen dependence, toxicity, manufacturing complexity, and regulatory challenges remain major translational barriers. Overall, current findings provide a strong preclinical rationale for further investigation of GOx-loaded nanotherapeutics, but do not establish clinical efficacy in human patients or permit predictions regarding future clinical adoption for TNBC.

articles.title: Phenoconversion in Thiopurine and Methotrexate Pharmacotherapy: A Systematic Framework for Integrating Germline Pharmacogenomics with Dynamic Phenotype Markers.
articles.abstract: Background: Pharmacogenomics (PGx) has improved thiopurine and methotrexate (MTX) safety by identifying inherited variants in drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters, including TPMT, NUDT15, and folate-pathway genes. Genotype-guided dosing is established for thiopurines, whereas MTX PGx evidence in immune-mediated disease remains weaker, without comparable consensus recommendations. Germline genotype alone cannot fully predict the expressed pharmacological phenotype, and phenoconversion-discordance between genotype-predicted and actual metabolic capacity-remains insufficiently addressed during inflammation, infection, hospitalization, and co-medication changes. Methods: This systematic review was conducted using prespecified eligibility and evidence-appraisal criteria and reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Results: Thiopurines and MTX were selected as contrasting evidence cases. Thiopurines have established TPMT/NUDT15-guided starting doses, routine safety monitoring, and erythrocyte 6-TGN/6-MMP measurements. In contrast, MTX pharmacogenetic associations remain inconsistent in immune-mediated disease; erythrocyte polyglutamate thresholds lack standardization, and concentration-guided interventions are established primarily in high-dose oncology. Across 45 core reports, the most reproducible dynamic modifiers included inflammation-mediated ADME suppression, drug-drug interactions, organ dysfunction, and exposure changes detectable through serial laboratory or metabolite measurements. Epigenetic, translational, post-translational, and microbiome mechanisms remain less clinically established. The operational thiopurine panel is therefore limited to TPMT/NUDT15 status, treatment context, CBC, liver/renal chemistry, disease-activity markers as reassessment triggers, and erythrocyte metabolites; DNA-TG and TPMT-locus methylation remain investigational. Conclusions: The Phenotype-Predictive Score is a theoretical, hypothesis-generating framework, not a validated clinical score, calculator, or dosing algorithm. Its equations and module weights require future drug-, indication-, endpoint-, and time-horizon-specific estimation in multicenter cohorts using penalized regression or dynamic pharmacokinetic models. PPS must not reassign TPMT/NUDT15 metabolizer phenotypes or guide treatment until external validation establishes calibration, transportability, safety, and clinical net benefit.

articles.title: Physicochemical Characterization, Manufacturing, and Stability of Liposomal Drug Delivery Systems: From Formulation Design to Pharmaceutical Translation.
articles.abstract: Liposomal drug delivery systems have evolved into clinically relevant platforms for delivering small molecules, biologics, and vaccines. Nevertheless, a persistent translational gap remains between promising laboratory-scale formulations and reproducible pharmaceutical products. This review provides a practical framework linking liposome formulation, physicochemical characterization, manufacturing, and stability to pharmaceutical translation. Particular emphasis is placed on relationships between critical process parameters and critical quality attributes, including vesicle size, polydispersity index, zeta potential, morphology, lamellarity, encapsulation efficiency, drug loading, and in vitro release behavior. Preparation and cargo-loading strategies are discussed across conventional research-scale methods and approaches with potential for scalable manufacturing. Microfluidic production of conventional liposomes is distinguished from the manufacture of structurally distinct RNA-loaded lipid nanoparticles. Purification strategies and analytical determination of encapsulation efficiency are examined, with attention to the distinction between separation techniques and quantitative analytical methods. Lamellarity is highlighted as a structural determinant of encapsulation capacity, membrane organization, and release behavior, with complementary assessment by cryo-TEM, 31P-NMR, and small-angle X-ray scattering. Quality-control challenges associated with aggregation, fusion, cargo leakage, phospholipid hydrolysis, oxidation, and sterilization are also considered. Dry-state stabilization through lyophilization and spray drying is discussed for its potential to improve long-term stability and reduce cold-chain dependence. Ligand-targeted liposomes introduce additional requirements for surface characterization and biological evaluation, while approved products and investigational formulations illustrate achievements and limitations in clinical translation. Overall, this review emphasizes the importance of establishing relationships between formulation composition, processing, structural organization, stability, and functional performance to support more reproducible development and informed pharmaceutical translation.

articles.title: Advances in the Research of Dual-Atom Nanozymes for Tumor Therapy.
articles.abstract: Dual-atom nanozymes (DAzymes) provide a new research strategy for regulating catalytic reaction pathways and redox homeostasis in tumor microenvironments (TMEs) by constructing adjacent metal active centers with specific coordination environments. Compared to traditional nanoparticle nanozymes and single-atom nanozymes (SAzymes), DAzymes have shown potential advantages in electronic structure regulation, multi-substrate activation, and multi-step catalysis. However, there is still a lack of systematic understanding of the structure-activity relationship between their catalytic performance and therapeutic effects. This review focuses on the research progress of DAzymes in tumor therapy. Firstly, its structural definition and classification boundaries are clarified, and the construction strategy, structural characterization, and dynamic evolution of diatomic active sites during the reaction process are systematically summarized. Subsequently, the focus of this study is on elucidating the effects of bimetallic electronic coupling, spatial coordination, defect regulation, and reaction selectivity on the generation and clearance of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and analyzing the applicability of catalytic performance under physiological substrate concentrations and in a complex TME. On this basis, the application of DAzymes in chemodynamic therapy (CDT), multimodal combination therapy, and tumor-targeted delivery is summarized, and the relationship between catalytic reactions and ferroptosis, cuproptosis, immunogenic cell death (ICD), and tumor metabolic response is further explored. In response to the insufficient evidence of diatomic structures, unclear attribution of catalytic synergy, and limited in vivo effectiveness evaluation in existing research, the focus is on analyzing the evidence correlation between structural authenticity, catalytic mechanisms, and biological effects, and discussing transformation challenges such as active site stability, metal release, catalytic persistence, and long-term biosafety. Finally, it is proposed to establish a verifiable, comparable, and transformative DAzyme research system through standardized structural characterization, physiologically relevant catalytic evaluation, mechanism causality verification, and interpretable data-driven design. This review aims to provide a theoretical reference for revealing the structure catalytic therapeutic effect relationship of diatomic sites and developing precise tumor catalytic therapy strategies.

articles.title: Beyond Glycemic Control: Periodontal, Salivary, and Oral Microbiome Effects of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists-A Scoping Review of Clinical and Preclinical Evidence.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are widely used to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity, yet their periodontal, peri-implant, salivary, and oral microbial effects remain incompletely characterized. This scoping review mapped the clinical and preclinical evidence on GLP-1RA-related oral effects, investigated mechanisms, and knowledge gaps. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception to 9 September 2026. Original human, animal in vivo, in vitro/ex vivo, and mixed-design studies were eligible when a GLP-1RA was a principal intervention or exposure and a relevant oral or orofacial outcome was reported. Two reviewers independently screened records. Study characteristics, interventions, outcomes, and findings were charted and synthesized descriptively. The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidance and was registered on the Open Science Framework after study selection but before completion of the methodological appraisal and manuscript. Results: Twenty-seven publications were included, 23 of which were wholly or partly preclinical. Four publications were exclusively human, and one mixed-design publication included an additional human observational component. Experimental findings suggested anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and osteogenic effects, but molecular responses were not consistently accompanied by structural benefits. Evidence concerning salivary function, oral microbial changes, and orofacial adverse events was limited and heterogeneous. Human findings were derived from non-randomized observational and descriptive designs. Conclusions: Evidence of potential oral effects is predominantly experimental, and human data are insufficient to establish clinical benefit or causality. Prospective controlled studies with standardized clinical outcomes are needed to determine whether experimental findings translate into meaningful oral-health benefits.

articles.title: Magnetic Liposomes for Theranostic Medicine: Advances in Construction, Medical Applications, and Limitations.
articles.abstract: Magnetic liposomes (MLs) integrate the drug-loading capacity of liposomes with the magnetic responsiveness of nanoparticles, providing a theranostic platform that combines magnetic targeting, MRI contrast, magnetically triggered release, and magnetic hyperthermia. Preclinical studies have demonstrated these functions, but clinical translation has lagged behind the volume of published work. This review focuses on translation-critical issues in MLs. Structural comparisons (core-shell, embedded, conjugated) are discussed with attention to whether buffer-based structure-property relationships hold in biological fluids. Synthesis methods are compared for size uniformity, encapsulation efficiency, and scalability. Surface modification is assessed with emphasis on ligand density and on the protein corona as a variable modulating ligand accessibility, biomimetic coating function, and magnetothermal heating. Applications are reviewed, including imaging, targeted delivery, controlled release, combination therapy, and gene editing, with attention to thermal dose heterogeneity and the temporal coupling between heating and drug release. Clinical barriers are framed as specific methodological gaps in magnetic field standardization, sterilization, and in vitro-in vivo correlation.

articles.title: Targeted Radiopharmaceuticals for Synovitis: Emerging Molecular Imaging and Theranostic Perspectives.
articles.abstract: The management of rheumatoid arthritis and related inflammatory arthropathies is evolving from late structural assessment toward early molecular phenotyping of synovitis. Target-specific radiopharmaceuticals for positron emission tomography (PET) and single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) now permit non-invasive detection of activated fibroblast-like synoviocytes, inflammatory macrophages, chemokine-driven immune-cell trafficking, angiogenesis, and mitochondrial stromal activation. This review analyzes the radiochemical basis of synovitis imaging, beginning with the radionuclide-dependent behavior of 11C, 68Ga, 64Cu, [Al18F]2+, and 99mTc, and then linking these properties to chelator selection, covalent radiolabeling, labeling conditions, and pharmacokinetics. The review further examines the development of radioligands targeting fibroblast activation protein (FAP), integrin αvβ3, folate receptor beta (β-FR), CXCR4, and the 18 kDa translocator protein (TSPO). It covers FAP-inhibitor scaffolds, RGD-based integrin probes, pteroyl-glutamate folate conjugates, CXCR4 antagonists, and TSPO heteroaromatic ligands. Clinical and translational datasets are discussed in relation to disease-activity evolution, treatment-response monitoring, and differentiation of stromal activation, macrophage infiltration, angiogenesis, and immune-cell recruitment. Finally, the review integrates kinetic modeling and dosimetric translation, emphasizing absorbed-dose estimation as a perspective on therapeutic optimization and safety constraints for emerging β-emitting and α-emitting synovial theranostics, 177Lu and 225Ac. Collectively, these developments define a bench-to-bedside framework for rheumatology precision medicine, in which radiopharmaceutical chemistry, molecular imaging, clinical trial evidence, and patient-specific dosimetry converge to guide diagnosis, therapeutic selection, and future targeted synovial micro-radioresection.

articles.title: Near-Infrared Fluorescent Probes and NIR-Responsive Nanomaterials for Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Advances in Imaging and Therapy.
articles.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract that requires accurate diagnosis, continuous disease monitoring, and effective treatment. Conventional approaches are often limited by invasiveness, insufficient sensitivity, and limited capacity for real-time disease monitoring. Near-infrared (NIR)-based theranostic technologies have emerged as a promising strategy for IBD management owing to their deep tissue penetration, low autofluorescence, high spatial resolution, and ability to integrate diagnosis and therapy on a single platform. This review summarizes the recent advances in NIR technologies for IBD diagnosis and treatment. It first introduces the fundamentals of NIR-I and NIR-II optical windows, the optical properties of intestinal tissues, and the design principles of NIR-responsive nanoplatforms. Recent advances in NIR fluorescence imaging for disease detection and monitoring, including small-molecule dyes, activatable probes, and nanoparticle-based imaging agents, are highlighted. NIR-responsive therapeutic systems, including photothermal therapy (PTT), photodynamic therapy (PDT), triggered drug delivery, and nanozyme-integrated catalytic therapy, are also reviewed in this article. In addition, multimodal imaging methods and imaging-guided therapeutic approaches are discussed, along with evolving combination therapies, including antioxidant nanozymes, immunomodulation, and microbiota-guided strategies. Finally, we outline the major challenges and future directions associated with clinical translation. Overall, NIR-based theranostic technologies hold considerable potential for precise diagnosis, real-time monitoring, and personalized treatment of IBD.

articles.title: Targeting α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptors in Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder: Mechanisms and Clinical Implications.
articles.abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a severe disorder that is characterized by intrusive thoughts, impaired mood and cognition, hyperarousal, and avoidance in the months and years following a traumatic event. PTSD is comorbid with depression, anxiety, substance abuse, and is challenging for the treatment with psycho- and pharmacotherapy. In light of novel neurobiological findings on the pathogenesis of the disease, innovative approaches to its treatment are investigated. Recently, targeting cholinergic signaling with an antagonist of α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChR), BNC-210, showed a significant promise in clinical trials. This opened up a novel therapeutic strategy that, considering its translational success, calls for a mechanistic understanding. In this review, we dissect the neurobiological role of α7 nAChR in regard of PTSD, and related depression and anxiety states. We discuss the synaptic role of the receptor in fear circuits, immune and endocrine role via the anti-inflammatory cholinergic pathway, and current evidence for the utility of pharmacological modulation of α7 nAChR.

articles.title: GLUT5 Targeted Drug Delivery in Cancer: A Critical Narrative Review of Transporter Specificity and Translational Design.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: GLUT5 (SLC2A5) is a fructose transporter investigated as a route for cancer drug delivery. This review examines whether the evidence supports transporter dependence, intracellular cargo delivery and therapeutic selectivity as distinct claims. METHODS: Fourteen representative empirical reports were mapped using six qualitative evidence domains. Europe PMC searches of PubMed-indexed title and abstract records, updated on 16 October 2026, retrieved 53 and 98 records, with 138 unique records after deduplication. Main texts were inspected for 12 reports; one additional appraisal used a scoped accepted manuscript extraction, and one remained abstract-based. CLINICALTRIALS: gov searches retrieved 48 unique records. RESULTS: GLUT5 structures support alternating access to a monosaccharide-binding cavity; passage of typical intact nanocarriers through this route is structurally implausible and unproven. Carrier studies instead show formulation-dependent cellular association, competition-sensitive uptake and, in selected systems, functional payload activity. Full-text appraisal credits the single-ligand and competition controls in dual-targeting liposomes and the competition and independent death measurements in porphyrin glycopolymers. These controls do not establish exclusive GLUT5 dependence. Target accessibility, physicochemical matching, inhibitor conditions, intracellular construct identity and genetic rescue remain recurrent limitations. No eligible GLUT5-targeted anticancer therapeutic delivery study was identified in the specified registry search. CONCLUSIONS: Fructose-associated uptake is a useful observation whose mechanism must be resolved for each construct. Genetic loss and rescue, chemical or physical confirmation of the delivered species, and efficacy linked to tolerated exposure should guide further development. The evidence map is representative rather than exhaustive, and access limits preclude absence-of-control judgments for the abstract-only report.

articles.title: From AKI to CKD: Biomimetic Nanomedicine Strategies for Kidney Diseases.
articles.abstract: Kidney diseases, including acute kidney injury (AKI), chronic kidney disease (CKD), and end-stage renal disease (ESRD), represent an interconnected clinical continuum characterized by complex etiologies, pathological heterogeneity, dispersed pathogenic cells, and limited therapeutic windows. Although current therapies can delay disease progression, they remain insufficient for precise renal lesion targeting, cell-specific intervention, and coordinated regulation of oxidative stress, inflammation, cell death, immune imbalance, microvascular injury, and fibrosis. Biomimetic nanomedicine has recently emerged as a promising preclinical strategy by mimicking natural biological structures, optimizing biointerfaces, and enhancing selective intrarenal delivery. Compared with conventional nanocarriers, biomimetic nanoplatforms based on cell membrane camouflage, engineered extracellular vesicles, extracellular matrix mimicry, ligand-guided delivery, and nanozyme catalysis can improve circulation stability, lesion recognition, and multipathway therapeutic regulation. In this review, we systematically summarize biomimetic nanomedicine strategies across AKI-, CKD-, and ESRD-related settings, focusing on cell membrane-coated nanoparticles, targeting ligand modification, biomimetic nanozymes, engineered extracellular vesicles, and extracellular matrix-inspired systems. We also discuss their expanded applications in dialysis membrane engineering, transplant monitoring, and regenerative medicine. Finally, we analyze key translational challenges, including long-term biosafety, interspecies differences, protein corona effects, manufacturing scale-up, quality control, and regulatory translation. Although still mainly at the preclinical stage, biomimetic nanomedicine offers important potential for improving renal delivery efficiency, enhancing cellular selectivity, and enabling synergistic intervention in kidney diseases.

articles.title: Bisphosphonate-Functionalized PLGA Nanocarriers for Doxorubicin Delivery to Primary Bone Tumors and Bone Metastases: From Mineral Affinity to Translational Evidence.
articles.abstract: Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), doxorubicin, and bisphosphonates combine a biodegradable drug reservoir, a cytotoxic payload, and a mineral-binding ligand with potential antiresorptive activity. Their integration into a single nanocarrier, however, requires evidence of lesion-specific drug delivery and an improved therapeutic index. This structured critical narrative review evaluates the development and translational potential of bisphosphonate-functionalized PLGA nanocarriers for doxorubicin delivery to primary bone tumors and bone metastases. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched to identify formulation, mechanistic, preclinical, and clinically relevant evidence. The analysis distinguishes hydroxyapatite binding from lesion localization, nanoparticle uptake from intracellular availability of pharmacologically active doxorubicin, and skeletal protection from direct antitumor activity. Preclinical studies support the feasibility of alendronate- and zoledronate-modified carriers, but substantial differences in ligand chemistry, payload, architecture, disease models, and outcome measures prevent generalization of therapeutic superiority. Clinical evidence with bisphosphonates, including the negative OS2006 osteosarcoma trial, further cautions against extrapolating preclinical skeletal activity to clinical antitumor benefit. A staged translational framework is proposed linking product identity, biological stability, mineral interaction, drug-resolved biodistribution, intracellular exposure, comparative efficacy, safety, and reproducible manufacture. Future development should prioritize clearly defined disease settings and demonstration of a measurable exposure advantage over established therapeutic comparators.

articles.title: Dissolving Microneedles for Psoriasis: An Intradermal Drug-Exposure Framework for Formulation Design and Clinical Translation.
articles.abstract: Despite increasing interest in dissolving microneedles (DMNs) for psoriasis therapy, current evaluations often emphasize device performance or therapeutic outcomes rather than drug exposure within target tissues. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease in which achieving sufficient and sustained local drug concentrations remains challenging because of pathological barrier alterations and limitations of conventional topical delivery. DMNs provide a promising minimally invasive approach by enabling direct deposition of therapeutic agents into skin compartments beyond the stratum corneum. This review proposes an exposure-guided framework for evaluating psoriasis-specific DMNs by integrating formulation design, device characteristics, intradermal drug exposure, and therapeutic response. The framework is based on three interconnected dimensions: amount, location, and residence time, which describe the quantity of drug delivered into skin, its spatial distribution within target compartments, and the persistence of local exposure. Current evidence regarding polymer selection, drug-loading strategies, microneedle geometry, and manufacturing processes is critically discussed according to their influence on these exposure-related parameters. Existing studies demonstrate that DMN design strategies can improve drug delivery and therapeutic outcomes; however, quantitative characterization of tissue-specific drug deposition, spatial distribution, and concentration-time profiles remains limited. The proposed framework provides a systematic approach to connect DMN formulation and device optimization with intradermal exposure, local pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) relationships, and clinical translation. Future development of psoriasis-oriented DMNs should incorporate standardized exposure assessment, mechanistic PK/PD evaluation, and human-relevant validation to support rational dose selection and clinical application.

articles.title: Citrus-Derived Bioactive Compounds in Anticancer Drug Discovery: Molecular Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential.
articles.abstract: Cancer therapy remains challenged by recurrence, metastasis, acquired drug resistance, and tumor heterogeneity, underscoring the need for safe multitarget agents and adjuvant strategies. Citrus fruits, widely used as medicinal and edible resources, provide abundant bioactive constituents in their peels, pulp, seeds, and processing by-products, including flavonoids, terpenoids, coumarins, polysaccharides, and pectin. Increasing preclinical evidence shows that Citrus-derived bioactive compounds modulate multiple processes involved in tumor initiation and progression. They inhibit proliferation; induce cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis, autophagy, and ferroptosis; suppress invasion, metastasis, and angiogenesis; attenuate oxidative stress and inflammation; reverse therapeutic resistance; and regulate the tumor immune microenvironment. These effects are associated with key signaling networks, including PI3K/Akt/mTOR, MAPK, NF-κB, STAT3, Wnt/β-catenin, Nrf2, PD-L1, and galectin-3. Owing to their pleiotropic mechanisms and generally favorable safety profiles, Citrus-derived compounds have potential as anticancer leads, therapeutic sensitizers, resistance modulators, and tumor-microenvironment regulators for integrated cancer therapy. However, translation is hindered by poorly defined active constituents in complex Citrus preparations and insufficiently characterized direct molecular targets, poor aqueous solubility, limited oral bioavailability, rapid metabolism, inconsistent quality control, weak pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic correlations, and insufficient clinical evidence. This review summarizes the chemical features, anticancer mechanisms, combination therapy potential, and translational barriers of citrus-derived bioactive compounds, providing guidance for candidate selection, formulation optimization, and anticancer drug development.

articles.title: Ligand-Engineered Nanoplatforms for Receptor-Mediated Drug Delivery Across the Blood-Brain Barrier: Design Principles and Translational Considerations.
articles.abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) excludes most therapeutic agents from the central nervous system and remains a major constraint in the treatment of glioblastoma, Alzheimer's disease, and other neurological disorders. Receptor-mediated transcytosis (RMT) offers a non-invasive route in which ligand-functionalized carriers engage receptors on brain endothelial cells and undergo vesicular transport across the BBB. This review examines transferrin (Tf), apolipoprotein E (ApoE), and receptor-binding peptides as the principal ligand classes used to engineer BBB-penetrating nanoplatforms, including polymeric nanoparticles, liposomes, micelles, lipid nanoparticles, and biomimetic carriers. Unlike reviews organized primarily by carrier type, administration route, or disease indication, we use a ligand-centered framework to connect receptor selection with affinity and avidity, surface density and orientation, intracellular trafficking, and carrier architecture. Particular attention is given to the progression from full-length natural proteins to compact peptides and stability-engineered ligands, including retro-inverso, stapled, and stimulus-cleavable designs. We also summarize representative within-study improvements in brain delivery and therapeutic outcome while emphasizing that effect sizes depend on the BBB model, disease model, dosing regimen, comparator, and analytical endpoint. Finally, we discuss species specificity, receptor-mediated safety liabilities, conjugation reproducibility, scale-up, and human-relevant BBB evaluation. These considerations position ligand engineering and pharmaceutical manufacturability as interdependent requirements for translating RMT nanoplatforms into clinically viable CNS drug-delivery systems.

articles.title: Hydrophilic Lubricants in Pharmaceutical Solid Dosage Forms: Mechanisms, Current Applications, and Future Perspectives.
articles.abstract: Lubricants are critical excipients in the production of solid pharmaceutical dosage forms, directly influencing powder flow, compaction behavior, and tablet quality. Magnesium stearate (MgSt) is widely used owing to its excellent lubrication efficiency. However, its hydrophobic surface coverage and sensitivity to shear conditions can severely reduce inter-particulate bonding. Consequently, this adversely affects tablet wetting, disintegration, and drug release, particularly under over-lubrication conditions. For this reason, hydrophilic, amphiphilic, and less hydrophobic alternative lubricant materials have gained increasing attention. In this review, these lubricants with hydrophilic, amphiphilic, or low-hydrophobicity properties are collectively referred to as "hydrophilic lubricants", and mainly include polyethylene glycol (PEG), sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS), poloxamers, and sodium stearyl fumarate (SSF). This narrative review summarizes the physicochemical characteristics, lubrication mechanisms, formulation applications, and effects on tablet mechanical properties, disintegration, and drug release of these alternative lubricants, and discusses the influence of lubricant properties, concentration, specific surface area, and incorporation method on lubrication performance. Furthermore, this review focuses on lubrication issues in continuous manufacturing and discusses the prospects of process analytical technology and predictive modeling. However, the available evidence remains predominantly derived from MgSt-based systems, and whether the relevant conclusions can be extrapolated to hydrophilic lubricants has not yet been validated. Nevertheless, these approaches hold promise for linking the distribution of hydrophilic lubricants and process conditions to tablet critical quality attributes, thereby providing a more rational control strategy for the lubrication process.

articles.title: From Empirical Correlation to Mechanistic Modeling: The Changing Landscape of IVIVC Approaches for Oral Modified-Release Drug Products.
articles.abstract: In vitro-in vivo correlation (IVIVC) is an important tool in the development, quality evaluation, and regulatory assessment of oral modified-release (MR) drug products. By establishing a quantitative relationship between in vitro dissolution and in vivo drug absorption, IVIVC provides a scientific basis for formulation optimization, bioequivalence evaluation, and the establishment of clinically relevant dissolution specifications. Conventional IVIVC approaches, which are primarily based on empirical correlations, have been widely applied in relatively simple MR systems. However, their predictive capability and extrapolation potential remain limited due to the lack of mechanistic understanding of drug release, absorption processes, and physiological factors. With the advancement of physiologically based biopharmaceutics modeling (PBBM), IVIVC is expanding from empirical correlation toward mechanistic modeling, providing a novel framework for evaluating the in vitro-in vivo relationship of oral MR drug products. This review summarizes the development and limitations of conventional IVIVC approaches, with particular emphasis on the principles, workflow, and recent applications of PBBM-driven mechanistic IVIVC in various oral MR formulations. Furthermore, commonly used modeling platforms and regulatory applications are discussed. Finally, current challenges and future perspectives of PBBM-IVIVC are highlighted. Unless otherwise specified, the term "modified-release (MR) drug products" in this review refers to oral modified-release drug products.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence, Microrobots/Nanorobots and Pharmaceutically Optimized Nanocarrier Systems for Precision Tumor Multitargeting.
articles.abstract: Precision oncology increasingly requires multi-target strategies addressing tumor heterogeneity, microenvironmental barriers, immune evasion, and drug resistance. This narrative review critically examines the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), microrobotic/nanorobotic systems, and pharmaceutically optimized nanocarriers for precision tumor multi-targeting. It highlights emerging intelligent nanomedicine strategies while distinguishing clinical evidence for selected nanocarrier products from preclinical and conceptual integration. This review explores AI-guided formulation design and patient stratification; microrobots and nano/micromotors for active delivery and intratumoral penetration; and optimized, stimuli-responsive nanocarriers for co-delivery of chemotherapeutics, immunomodulators, nucleic acids, and gene-editing agents. Tumor multi-targeting, microenvironment-responsive release, and synchronized drug delivery are critically assessed. AI-guided formulation studies include computational prediction and prospective laboratory validation, whereas active delivery platforms have predominantly been evaluated in vitro and in animal models. Preclinical and conceptual findings suggest that integrating AI-guided design, active navigation, and responsive nanocarriers may enhance spatial and temporal delivery control; reductions in systemic toxicity require system-specific validation. Study-specific quantitative matrices compare model validation, actuation conditions, payloads, release characteristics, and exposure measures, explicitly identifying missing data and non-comparable endpoints. Target prioritization incorporates biological validity, druggability, delivery feasibility, and clinical actionability. Investigational digital twins require longitudinal data quality control, calibrated uncertainty, drift surveillance, and clinician oversight. Although selected robotic-carrier combinations demonstrate preclinical benefits, fully integrated platforms enabling patient-specific adaptive treatment lack clinical validation. Translation requires indication-specific comparisons with simpler formulations, reproducible manufacturing, validated navigation, and prospective benefit-risk assessment. Future research should prioritize pharmaco-nanotechnologies, refined cancer molecular classification, and clinician-governed decision support before adaptive AI-assisted multi-target nanomedicine.

articles.title: Metal-Catalyzed Degradation of Polysorbates in Biopharmaceutical Formulations: Mechanisms, Analytical Approaches, and Mitigation Strategies.
articles.abstract: Polysorbate 20 and polysorbate 80 are the most widely used nonionic surfactants in biopharmaceutical formulations, and they serve as critical excipients protecting therapeutic proteins from interfacial damage and aggregation. Traditionally considered chemically inert, polysorbates are now known to undergo substantial degradation, compromising formulation stability. Polysorbate degradation proceeds via chemical hydrolysis, enzymatic hydrolysis, and oxidative pathways. In particular, trace transition metal ions initiate catalytic oxidation through Fenton and Haber-Weiss reactions to generate reactive oxygen species, triggering a self-amplifying cascade of polysorbate autoxidation and subsequent protein oxidative damage. Metal contaminants originate from raw materials, manufacturing equipment, and primary packaging, and degradation can be induced at trace concentrations, posing considerable challenges for contamination tracing and risk control. Despite the ubiquity of metal contaminants, the current literature lacks systematic and integrated mechanistic analyses of metal-catalyzed polysorbate degradation. This review comprehensively describes the structural characteristics, differential degradation profiles, metal-mediated oxidation mechanisms, and contamination sources of polysorbates before discussing the analytical methodologies and multi-barrier mitigation strategies used to address polysorbate use. The knowledge gaps identified and future research recommendations provided in this review offer mechanistic insights into quality optimization, risk management, and long-term stability control of biotherapeutic formulations.

articles.title: Targeted Degradation of the c-Myc Oncoprotein: Molecular Mechanisms, Technological Platforms, and Therapeutic Perspectives in Oncology.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: The c-Myc oncoprotein is a master regulator of cell cycle progression, cellular metabolism, and ribosome biogenesis, and its dysregulation occurs in more than 70% of human malignancies. Its intrinsically disordered structure and absence of deep hydrophobic binding pockets have historically limited direct pharmacological targeting, leading to its classification as an "undruggable" protein. Targeted protein degradation offers strategies to reduce c-Myc abundance by recruiting endogenous degradation machinery or introducing an exogenous protease. Methods/Results: This review evaluates recent strategies for reducing c-Myc abundance-classified into direct c-Myc degraders, indirect destabilization pathways, and proposed platform adaptations-encompassing established small-molecule modalities, including heterobifunctional proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) and molecular glues, oligonucleotide-based PROTACs, proteomimetic polymers, MIDN-dependent ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degraders, and orthogonal bacterial proteases. Adaptable platforms, including KRAS-directed TKD constructs and anti-c-Myc modular nanotransporters (MNTs), are discussed separately because c-Myc degradation has not yet been demonstrated for these adaptations. Conclusions: Collectively, these approaches broaden the potential of c-Myc-targeted degradation to address therapeutic resistance, influence the tumor immune microenvironment, and facilitate the clinical translation of intranuclear degraders.

articles.title: 3D-Printing Drug Delivery Systems for the Treatment of Infectious Diseases: Current Advances and Future Perspectives.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Infectious diseases remain a major burden on global public health, exacerbated by the serious threat of antimicrobial resistance and the limitations of conventional pharmaceutical formulations. This narrative review aims to analyze the current state of 3D printing technology in the development of drug delivery systems tailored to the treatment of infectious diseases, analyzing the main manufacturing techniques, the polymers used and the challenges associated with the design of customized or combined dosage forms, emphasizing its capabilities across various routes of administration, current challenges, and potential clinical prospects. Methods: A structured literature search was conducted in ScienceDirect, PubMed and Wiley for research articles published between 2020 and May 2026 using the terms "antibiotic" AND "3D printing" AND "drug delivery." Retrieved articles were selected, filtered, and categorized according to their route of administration. Results: Additive manufacturing enables the tailoring of dosage form geometry, drug loading and release kinetics, promoting the development of formulations for personalized treatments of infectious diseases. The most frequently used technique in the analyzed studies was semi-solid extrusion, probably due to its compatibility with various biomaterials and thermolabile active pharmaceutical ingredients. Topical applications represent the most studied area in the retrieved results of the search, integrating multifunctional properties such as stimuli response and wound healing. 3D printing has also expanded delivery platforms for vaginal, ocular, and oral routes, although the evidence for these routes remains largely preclinical. Conclusions: The studies analyzed suggest that pharmaceutical 3D printing is evolving from a manufacturing tool for personalized dosage forms to an advanced platform for designing multifunctional therapeutic systems. Overcoming current regulatory, clinical validation, and manufacturing challenges will be crucial for translating these innovations into clinical practice for the treatment of infectious diseases.

articles.title: Delivery Strategies Targeting Senescent Cells: From Precise Elimination to Functional Remodeling.
articles.abstract: The accumulation of senescent cells in tissues serves as a fundamental driver of aging and age-related pathologies, including chronic inflammation, tissue dysfunction, and organ degeneration. Conventional anti-aging interventions often suffer from limited specificity and off-target toxicity. Currently, developing therapeutic strategies capable of precisely targeting senescent cells is urgent. This review focuses on recent advances in delivery strategies designed to achieve either the selective elimination or functional modulation of senescent cells, with the goal of transitioning from broad-spectrum interventions to precision senotherapy. We systematically discuss the latest developments in senescence-targeting delivery platforms. To realize in vivo senescent-cell clearance, nanocarrier-based systems which are responsive to the senescent microenvironment and immune cell-based approaches are engineered. In parallel, we also reviewed emerging strategies for functional remodeling. Advanced delivery vehicles including lipid nanoparticles, extracellular vesicles, and engineered cell therapies are used to realize metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic modulation. The critical mechanisms of delivery systems in overcoming diverse barriers to improve specificity, bioavailability, and safety are highlighted. In this review, we aim to provide a preliminary framework that could serve as a useful reference for guiding the clinical translation of emerging senotherapies.

articles.title: MicroRNAs in Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease and Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease: From Pathogenic Networks and Disease Progression to Precision Biomarkers and Therapeutic Strategies.
articles.abstract: Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) arise from distinct etiological factors, but they share a broad spectrum of pathological features during disease progression, including steatosis, oxidative stress, autophagic dysfunction, inflammation, hepatocyte death, and fibrosis. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are considered important potential post-transcriptional regulators of these processes because of their capacity to coordinately modulate multiple target genes and signaling pathways across diverse hepatic cell populations. In this review, the involvement of miRNAs throughout the progression of ALD and MASLD is comparatively examined, with particular emphasis on their roles in lipid metabolic dysregulation, mitochondrial and oxidative stress, autophagic dysfunction, immune activation, hepatocyte death, and hepatic-stellate-cell-associated fibrogenesis. This review focuses on the role of miRNAs in intercellular communication between hepatocytes, macrophages, neutrophils, and hepatic stellate cells, emphasizing their cell-specific and context-dependent functions in coordinating liver disease progression. Apart from their mechanistic roles, circulating and extracellular-vesicle-associated miRNA signatures have shown great application potential as minimally invasive biomarkers for molecular stratification, disease progression, and precision medicine. Collectively, these findings suggest that miRNAs have broad translational relevance in liver disease. However, their clinical translation remains limited by challenges regarding stability, biodistribution, off-target effects, and cell-type-specific delivery, emphasizing the need for more precise liver-directed therapeutic strategies. These challenges highlight the importance of linking specific miRNA targets with disease stage, cellular source, and appropriate delivery approaches. In this context, the integration of disease etiology, pathological stage, cellular context, miRNA network architecture, biomarker signatures, and delivery technology is essential for evolving miRNAs from mechanistic regulators and biomarkers into precision therapeutic platforms for ALD and MASLD.

articles.title: Beyond Tumor Accumulation in Oncology Peptide Drug Conjugates: A Critical Narrative Review of Release-Competent Exposure and a Stage-Gated Translational Roadmap.
articles.abstract: Peptide-drug conjugates (PDCs) combine peptide-mediated targeting or transport with a pharmacologically active payload. This critical narrative review organizes oncology PDC development around release-competent exposure (RCE): the connection between conjugate integrity, formation of an identified active compound, delivery to its tumor compartment, pharmacodynamic effect, and therapeutic margin. Tumor uptake or accumulation is distinguished from the concentration-time profile of an identified active species in its relevant compartment. PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, and regulatory sources informed the review through 15 September 2026; the recorded retrieval procedures were re-executed and archived on 24 October 2026. We distinguish payload-releasing PDCs from enzyme-potentiated prodrugs and non-cleaving modalities, assemble established, adapted, and conceptual exposure measures, and integrate analytical requirements into a stage-gated development framework. Clinical examples include zelenectide pevedotin, PEN-221, zoptarelin doxorubicin, ANG1005, and melflufen. Five preclinical illustrations and a separate calculation from published tissue AUCs show how different observations inform the framework. ADC-derived principles are qualified by PDC-specific disposition, while sparse tissue sampling, imaging, and modeling are evaluated as translational strategies. Use of these exposure measures within RCE remains hypothesis-generating and requires construct-specific validation; established PK quantities are not thereby validated clinical surrogate endpoints.

articles.title: Hypoxia-Activated Small Molecules for Targeted Cancer Theranostics: Emerging Strategies for Precision Drug Delivery.
articles.abstract: Tumor hypoxia is a pervasive feature of solid tumors that promotes malignant progression, metastatic dissemination, and resistance to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy. At the same time, low oxygen tension creates a chemically exploitable vulnerability for selective drug activation. Hypoxia-activated prodrugs (HAPs) and activatable small-molecule theranostics are designed to remain comparatively inactive in oxygenated tissues and to undergo reductase-mediated conversion within hypoxic tumor regions, thereby releasing cytotoxic, targeted, immunomodulatory, or imaging-active species. In this Review, we organize recent advances according to the chemistry of the bioreductive trigger and the mechanism that links reduction to payload release or signal generation. We discuss nitroaromatic and nitroheterocyclic groups, azo linkages, N-oxides, quinones, azides, and redox-active transition-metal complexes, with emphasis on one-electron redox cycling, multielectron reduction, self-immolative fragmentation, and the influence of reduction potential and local oxygen concentration. Representative small-molecule systems are then used to illustrate how hypoxia activation can be integrated with fluorescence and multimodal imaging, phototherapy, immunomodulation, and targeted delivery. Finally, we examine the principal translational barriers including spatial and temporal heterogeneity of tumor oxygenation, reductase dependence, incomplete intratumoral activation, pharmacokinetic limitations, and the need for patient-selection biomarkers and outline design criteria for improving therapeutic index and clinical tractability. Together, these developments position hypoxia-responsive chemistry as a mechanistically tunable platform for precision drug delivery rather than simply a means of targeting oxygen-poor tumor regions.

articles.title: Sonosensitive Niosomes for Cancer Therapy: Design Principles, Current Evidence, and Future Directions.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Niosomes-vesicles formed through the self-assembly of non-ionic surfactants and cholesterol-have attracted attention as versatile, cost-effective, and chemically stable nanocarriers for delivering both hydrophilic and lipophilic anticancer drugs. Engineering these vesicles to respond to ultrasound (sonosensitivity) offers spatial and temporal control over drug release, potentially raising therapeutic concentrations at tumour sites while limiting systemic toxicity. This review compiles current evidence on the design principles of sonosensitive niosomes and situates them within the broader landscape of ultrasound-responsive vesicular carriers. Methods: In this narrative review, supported by a documented database search, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched in October 2026 without date or language limits, and 290 unique records were screened to establish whether any ultrasound-responsive niosomal formulation had been evaluated in a cancer model; background literature was identified from reference lists and citation searching. Results: Across the retrieved literature, surfactant and sonosensitizer selection, formulation and characterisation methods, and the acoustic mechanisms-primarily cavitation and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation-that drive ultrasound-induced cargo release are examined. None of the 290 screened records reported an ultrasound-responsive niosomal formulation evaluated in a cancer model, and only seven studies applied ultrasound to niosomes, all of which were outside oncology. Design principles are necessarily extrapolated from the mature literature on ultrasound-responsive liposomes, liposome-microbubble hybrids, and sonodynamic nanosensitizers. Persistent challenges in in vivo stability, targeting accuracy, and release-kinetics control, together with barriers to clinical translation such as scale-up, acoustic-parameter standardisation, and regulatory considerations, are highlighted. Conclusions: Sonosensitive niosomes are a promising but still-emerging platform. Their advancement depends less on further feasibility demonstrations than on formulation standardisation, targeted surface engineering, quantitative mapping of release to defined acoustic parameters, and rigorous in vivo validation, before integration with theranostic, multi-stimuli-responsive, immunotherapeutic, or gene-therapy strategies, which for niosomes remain prospective.

articles.title: Engineering Gold Nanocages for Precision Drug Delivery: From Structural Design and Stimuli-Responsive Release to Theranostic Applications.
articles.abstract: Gold nanocages (AuNCs) are hollow, porous plasmonic nanostructures featuring an internal cavity for cargo accommodation, a gold-rich surface amenable to functionalization, and tunable near-infrared (NIR) optical properties, enabling controlled delivery, photothermal activation, and imaging within a single platform. As AuNC research has evolved from galvanic-replacement synthesis and photothermal ablation toward stimuli-responsive and multifunctional systems, the central challenge has shifted from simply adding functions to achieving reproducible control of therapeutic exposure in space, time, and dose through coordinated structural and formulation engineering. This review examines the relationships among nanocage architecture, interfacial modification, cargo loading and retention, stimuli-responsive release, biological transport, therapeutic applications, and theranostic strategies ranging from imaging-enabled monitoring to imaging-guided intervention. Particular emphasis is placed on how particle size, wall thickness, porosity, cavity architecture, residual Au-Ag composition, surface state, and localized surface plasmon resonance influence loading capacity, release kinetics, optical energy deposition, cellular uptake, biodistribution, and biological fate. We further discuss how PEGylation, targeting ligands, responsive polymers, nucleic-acid gates, lipid layers, biomimetic coatings, and endogenous or exogenous stimuli can transform AuNCs from passive carriers into programmable delivery platforms. Across cancer, infection, inflammation, regeneration, and cardiovascular applications, precision delivery depends on coordinated control of localization, payload release, therapeutic exposure, and imaging-informed treatment decisions. Despite substantial progress, clinical translation remains constrained by challenges including reproducibility, residual silver, compositional heterogeneity, formulation stability, long-term gold retention, limited optical penetration, incomplete understanding of carrier and cargo fate, sterilization, manufacturing complexity, and scale-up. Future studies should prioritize quantitative structure-property-delivery relationships, formulation-level critical quality attributes, clinically relevant trigger thresholds and exposure ranges, and imaging-feedback workflows that demonstrate reproducible advantages over simpler delivery systems.

articles.title: Multimodal AI and Process Analytical Technology for Solid-Dosage Quality Inspection: A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Automated inspection is valuable when visual and process signals map to critical quality attributes (CQAs). This narrative review evaluates computer vision and complementary process analytical technology (PAT) for surface integrity, coating structure, chemical distribution, internal defects, and release-relevant quality. Methods: We synthesize selected literature on solid-dosage inspection, multimodal sensing, machine learning, and hybrid digital twins using a targeted narrative approach. Results: Visible imaging supports rapid surface inspection; optical coherence tomography and terahertz methods resolve coating and subsurface structure; Raman, near-infrared, and hyperspectral methods add chemical or spatial evidence. Task-specific pharmaceutical studies report promising performance, but rare defects, data leakage, domain shift, calibration, missing inputs, throughput, and lifecycle drift constrain generalization. CQA-driven fusion requires product-specific validation, calibrated uncertainty, human review, change control, and traceable data. Conclusions: Hybrid digital twins can support prospective scenario analysis and process understanding, but current evidence does not support autonomous batch release. Inspection outputs remain in-process evidence unless validated within a control strategy or surrogate relationship for the specified release attribute.

articles.title: Chitosan-Coated Liposomes: Advances in Synthesis, Modification and Biomedical Applications.
articles.abstract: Chitosan-coated liposomes (CLPs) have emerged as a multifunctional drug delivery platform that effectively overcomes the key limitations of conventional liposomes, including poor stability, rapid in vivo clearance, weak mucoadhesion, and insufficient targeting specificity. The natural cationic nature of chitosan enables stable coating onto negatively charged liposome surfaces via electrostatic interactions, forming a stable core-shell structure that significantly improves liposomal stability, prolongs circulation time, and enhances mucoadhesive ability. The abundant reactive groups on the chitosan backbone allow further conjugation of targeting ligands, polyethylene glycol chains, and stimuli-responsive moieties, thereby endowing the delivery system with active targeting, long-circulating, and smart drug release properties. Various coating strategies, such as electrostatic deposition, layer-by-layer self-assembly, ionic crosslinking, and microfluidic in-situ coating, provide flexibility and precise controllability for formulation design. These systems have demonstrated considerable therapeutic potential across multiple administration routes, as well as in anti-infective, tumor-targeted, and immunomodulatory applications, by improving drug retention, enabling controlled release, and enhancing bioavailability. Therefore, this review summarizes the synthesis methods, modification strategies, and biomedical applications of CLPs, with the aim of providing a reference for future development in this field.

articles.title: Hydrogel-Based Microneedles for Diabetic Wound Repair: Translational Requirements for Diabetic Foot Ulcer Therapy.
articles.abstract: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) arise from interacting neuropathic, biomechanical, vascular, and infectious processes that are incompletely reproduced by experimental diabetic wound models. Hydrogel-based microneedles (HBMNs) offer opportunities for localized therapeutic delivery, but their clinical value depends on whether tissue penetration provides advantages over appropriately formulated topical treatments. This critical narrative review examines HBMN architectures, therapeutic strategies, and barriers to clinical translation in DFU management. HBMN systems are distinguished by their hydration-dependent behavior, with direct therapeutic evidence limited to microneedle platforms containing a functional hydrogel component. Preclinical studies have explored approaches targeting infection and biofilms, persistent inflammation, oxidative stress, impaired oxygenation, and defective tissue regeneration. Recent developments include polymicrobial biofilm targeting, metabolic modulation, and extracellular-vesicle delivery. Preset release, stimulus-responsive delivery, and emerging feedback-informed approaches are discussed in relation to their distinct capabilities and limitations. Despite promising experimental findings, important uncertainties remain regarding the intended wound interface, delivered dose, cargo stability and potency, compatibility with offloading, and safety in ischemic or infected tissue. We propose a staged translational framework linking intended clinical indications to relevant disease models, appropriate comparators, reproducible product quality, and patient-important outcomes. HBMNs should be developed as adjuncts to multidisciplinary DFU care, with priority given to demonstrating clinically meaningful advantages over simpler delivery systems rather than increasing the functional complexity of experimental prototypes.

articles.title: From Passive Carriers to Niche Engineers: The Evolving Paradigm of Engineered Bacteria in Cancer Therapy.
articles.abstract: Engineered bacterial systems have been predominantly conceptualized as living drug-delivery vehicles, with their therapeutic value attributed primarily to tumor-homing capabilities and payload delivery. This framing, while productive in guiding early-stage research, may inadvertently constrain both the design space and the therapeutic ambition of bacterial therapeutics. An alternative perspective is emerging from recent advances in synthetic biology and tumor immunology: bacteria may be understood not merely as passive carriers of therapeutic payloads but as active participants in the remodeling of the tumor ecosystem. This review examines the conceptual and empirical foundations of this paradigm shift, tracing the evolution from bacteria as delivery vehicles to bacteria as "niche engineers" capable of metabolic reprogramming, immunological modulation, and structural reorganization of the tumor microenvironment. The discussion progresses through four interconnected dimensions-colonization, remodeling, orchestration, and adaptation-each of which redefines the bacterium's functional role in the therapeutic context. Critically, the review engages with unresolved mechanistic questions that complicate the therapeutic narrative, including the dual role of IL-10 in both sustaining bacterial persistence and suppressing antitumor immunity, the spatial heterogeneity of bacterial colonization and its implications for therapeutic efficacy, and the evolutionary pressures that may select for loss-of-function mutants. The clinical translation landscape is examined with attention to manufacturing challenges, regulatory uncertainties, and the potential failure modes of combination strategies. By situating engineered bacteria within the broader ecological dynamics of the tumor microenvironment, this review aims to provide a framework for the next generation of bacterial therapeutics that engage more fully with the complexity of cancer as a systemic disease.

articles.title: From Nature to Nanomedicine: Green Nanobased Innovations for Melanoma Therapy.
articles.abstract: Cutaneous melanoma is an aggressive malignancy for which conventional treatments are often limited by acquired resistance, systemic toxicity, and insufficient dermal penetration. To overcome these therapeutic limitations, green nanomedicine has emerged as a promising alternative, employing biological systems such as plant extracts to sustainably synthesize bioactive metal and metal oxide nanoparticles, including Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), Gold nanoparticles (AuNPs), Zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnONPs), Cerium oxide nanoparticles (CeO2NPs), and Copper nanoparticles (CuNPs). The phytochemical capping of these biogenic nanoplatforms enhances biocompatibility and enables multiple antineoplastic mechanisms, including targeted oxidative stress, metabolic disruption, and photothermal ablation. Translating these cellular-level effects into clinical efficacy requires overcoming significant physiological barriers, particularly the stratum corneum. As a result, research is increasingly focused on incorporating these bioactive metallic cores into advanced, stimuli-responsive delivery vehicles. Examples include polymeric scaffolds for enhanced payload retention and solid lipid nanoparticles for improved transdermal penetration. Although hierarchical bio-nanocomposites offer a promising approach to overcoming tumor resistance, successful clinical translation will require standardized large-scale synthesis and comprehensive in vivo evaluation to bridge the gap between preclinical studies and targeted precision therapy.

articles.title: Aztreonam-Avibactam (Emblaveo®) for Carbapenem-Resistant and Metallo-β-Lactamase-Producing Gram-Negative Infections: A Comprehensive Review.
articles.abstract: Metallo-β-lactamase (MBL)-producing Enterobacterales represent a major antimicrobial-resistance threat because MBLs hydrolyse most clinically used β-lactams and are not inhibited by currently approved serine β-lactamase inhibitors. Aztreonam-avibactam (ATM-AVI; Emblaveo®) addresses this therapeutic gap by combining aztreonam, a monobactam that is stable to MBL-mediated hydrolysis, with avibactam, which inhibits many co-produced class A, class C, and selected class D serine β-lactamases. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on ATM-AVI pharmacology, microbiological activity, pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, clinical efficacy, safety, resistance, and regulatory positioning. Large surveillance datasets show high in vitro activity against most MBL-producing Enterobacterales, including many co-producing β-lactamases from multiple Ambler classes. Population pharmacokinetic modelling supports a renal-function-adjusted fixed 3:1 dosing ratio and more reliable joint target attainment than separately administered ceftazidime-avibactam plus aztreonam. In the phase 3 REVISIT trial, clinical cure with ATM-AVI was comparable to meropenem in the overall population; however, few participants had confirmed MBL-positive infections. Direct clinical evidence therefore remains limited, supported by convergent microbiological, pharmacokinetic, and observational data. Regulatory indications differ substantially between the European Union and the United States. ATM-AVI is an important advance for selected MBL-producing and multi-class-co-producing Gram-negative infections, but its long-term value will depend on targeted use, reliable susceptibility testing, continued surveillance, and further trials in the intended target population.

articles.title: Recent Advances in Electrospun Nanofiber Membrane Based Biomimetic Tissue Barriers and Drug Screening Functions.
articles.abstract: The construction of highly biomimetic in vitro tissue barrier models is essential for new drug development, as it enables accurate evaluation of the permeability efficiency, safety, and pharmacokinetic properties of drug candidates. Animal models have long been regarded as the standard criterion for assessing drug efficacy; however, they pose increasingly severe ethical concerns. Moreover, substantial interspecies differences in transmembrane transporter expression and metabolic pathways contribute to the low rate of successful clinical translation. Traditional 2D cell culture models lack a 3D matrix microenvironment and physiological mechanical signals similar to those in vivo. Consequently, epithelial or endothelial cells are prone to phenotypic alteration. They struggle to assemble structurally intact and functionally mature tight barriers. As a result, drug permeability and toxicity results often deviate markedly from in vivo physiological conditions. In contrast, electrospinning technology offers a promising approach for constructing biomimetic barriers. Electrospun nanofiber membranes closely resemble the fibrous network structure of the natural extracellular matrix and provide several distinct advantages, including precisely controllable pore sizes, large specific surface areas, and readily modifiable functional surfaces. Furthermore, the arrangement and physicochemical properties of the fibers can be precisely tailored to provide cells with inductive cues that mimic the in vivo physiological microenvironment. This review summarizes the design strategies of electrospun nanofiber membranes for the construction of key tissue barriers, including the lung, blood-brain barrier, intestine, kidney, and skin. In addition, it discusses recent advances in the application of these membranes for drug screening. Finally, universal design principles for cross-barrier construction are proposed. Overall, this review aims to support the development of more efficient and reliable in vitro drug-screening platforms.

articles.title: Plant-Derived Bioactives in Ocular Drug Delivery: A Critical Evidence Map of Formulation Roles, Material Participation, and Therapeutic Attribution.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Better ocular delivery does not establish that a plant-derived bioactive functions as a material or adds a material-specific therapeutic benefit. Methods: A structured critical synthesis of seven databases mapped 327 eligible full-text records using parallel role, material-participation, bioactivity, comparison and interaction codes. Independent full-text reassessment and human adjudication were followed by sensitivity analysis in 313 report-family units. Results: External cargo accounted for 237 records (72.5%); delivery modulators, active/co-functional interfaces and structural/self-assembling participants accounted for 27 (8.3%), 29 (8.9%) and 34 (10.4%), respectively. Practical-formulation comparisons occurred in 234 records, whereas 35 included attribution-oriented comparisons. Three records reported model-based interaction analyses, with limitations that prevented unrestricted claims of ocular synergy. Family-sensitive analysis preserved the principal patterns. The synthesis distinguished released-drug exposure from retained-interface function and aligned dry-eye, infection and corneal-repair claims with their measured models, endpoints and controls. Conclusions: This corpus more often evaluates delivery performance than an isolated material-specific contribution. Added complexity should address a defined treatment limitation, demonstrate the claimed increment against a credible comparator and remain compatible with product use. The framework guides claim-matched experiments rather than ranking platforms or predicting clinical success.

articles.title: Targeting Inflammation and Vascular Dysfunction in Androgenetic Alopecia: Emerging Therapeutic Opportunities and Future Perspectives.
articles.abstract: Androgenetic alopecia (AGA) is mainly characterized by androgen-dependent follicular miniaturization. However, increasing evidence suggests that inflammation, fibrosis and vascular changes may also affect the follicular microenvironment. This review summarizes the normal vascular and cellular regulation of the hair follicle and discusses how these processes may be altered in AGA. Human studies have identified perifollicular inflammation, reduced perfusion and changes in angiogenesis-related genes, but their causal roles remain unclear. Experimental studies further show close communication among dermal papilla cells, endothelial cells, immune cells and hair follicle stem cells. Current treatments mainly reduce androgen signaling or stimulate hair growth and may not fully address these microenvironmental changes. Emerging approaches, including anti-inflammatory treatments, nitric oxide and VEGF-based systems, microneedles, hydrogels and nano-enabled delivery, may regulate several pathways at the same time. However, most of these strategies remain preclinical. Future studies should clarify whether inflammation and vascular dysfunction contribute to follicular miniaturization and whether targeting these pathways improves clinical outcomes in AGA. Key research priorities include longitudinal human studies, disease-relevant experimental models, biomarker validation and clinical trials.

articles.title: Bridging the Gap in Pediatric Tuberculosis Treatment: Challenges and Potential of Rifampicin Self-Emulsifying Drug Delivery Systems.
articles.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) persists as a devastating global health crisis, exacting a disproportionate burden on low-middle-income countries (LMICs), within which the burgeoning pediatric TB population is especially vulnerable to severe TB manifestations. Rifampicin, a cornerstone of the first-line TB regimen, is indispensable, yet its therapeutic potential is substantially constrained by intrinsic poor aqueous solubility, limited permeability, physicochemical instabilities, and deleterious drug-drug interactions with drugs such as isoniazid. Although current research focuses on formulating rifampicin into fixed-dose combinations-some reporting improved outcomes-the variable and often suboptimal rifampicin bioavailability in such formulations remains a critical concern. Consequently, the development of a stable, independent rifampicin oral formulation should be prioritized to ensure effective TB treatment. There are currently no commercially available rifampicin-only liquid preparations, despite the urgent need for palatable, flexible, age-appropriate formulations. This paucity constitutes a profound and persistent gap in pediatric TB, compromising accurate weight-based dosing, treatment adherence, and therapeutic outcomes while contributing to rifampicin resistance. This paper highlights the key characteristics and formulation challenges of rifampicin, with particular emphasis on pediatric TB. It further discusses liquid self-emulsifying drug delivery systems (SEDDSs) as a novel approach to enhance oral rifampicin delivery. These feasible lipid-based delivery systems offer notable promise, as they are capable of maintaining rifampicin in a solubilized and stable state throughout the gastrointestinal tract, which in turn will likely improve bioavailability. The possible development of a stable liquid rifampicin SEDDS represents a paradigm shift in addressing the longstanding neglect of pediatric TB treatment.

articles.title: Appraising Evidence for Hippocampal Synaptic Restoration by Traditional Chinese Medicine-Derived Antidepressant Interventions: Causality, Exposure, and Translation.
articles.abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)-derived interventions have been associated with antidepressant-like behavioral effects and changes in markers of hippocampal plasticity, but evidence of functional synaptic recovery remains limited. This critical narrative review evaluates 29 purposively selected preclinical reports using six qualitative appraisal domains: mechanistic causality, independent replication, anatomical resolution, methodological reporting, central target exposure, and clinical translation. The selected reports examined interventions including Yueju, Xiaoyaosan, ginsenoside Rb1, baicalin, and danshensu in stress-based models and behavioral screening paradigms. Behavioral effects and changes in AMPA receptor-associated signaling, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and its receptor tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), and synaptic proteins were frequently reported; however, these findings cannot substitute for direct measurements of synaptic physiology. Studies of repeated-dose Rb1 and baicalin reported hippocampal cornu ammonis area 1 (CA1) long-term potentiation (LTP). In the Rb1 study, miR-134 perturbation was tested against the LTP endpoint, whereas TrkB inhibition in the baicalin study was evaluated against behavioral outcomes in separate experiments. Zhi-Zi-Chi-Tang (ZZCT) was also associated with improved CA1 LTP, but 14-3-3ζ knockdown was not tested against that functional endpoint. Unclear animal-versus-slice denominators, limited data on unbound hippocampal exposure, and insufficient independent replication constrain causal inference. Overall, the selected evidence supports specific functional findings and mechanistic associations but does not establish a shared, causally validated pathway for hippocampal synaptic restoration.

articles.title: Gut Microbiota and Its Metabolites in Psoriasis: Therapeutic Potential of Natural Products and Traditional Chinese Medicine.
articles.abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease whose development and progression have been associated with disturbances in gut microbial composition and metabolic function. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on natural products and traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) in psoriasis, focusing on the relationships between intervention-associated microbial and metabolic changes and intestinal barrier function, immune and inflammatory responses, and oxidative stress. The principal metabolic processes examined include short-chain fatty acid production, bile acid biotransformation, and tryptophan metabolism. Metabolites involved in these pathways may influence intestinal epithelial barrier function and immune cell activity, thereby modulating inflammatory responses along the gut skin axis. Host responses reported across intervention studies include improved intestinal barrier integrity, T helper 17 (Th17)/regulatory T (Treg) balance, attenuation of interleukin-23 (IL-23)/interleukin-17 (IL-17)-associated inflammation, and suppression of oxidative stress, accompanied by improvements in psoriasiform skin lesions. These findings suggest that modulation of the gut microbiota and its metabolites may contribute to the antipsoriatic effects of natural products and TCM in experimental models. Future research should clarify the causal contributions of the gut microbiota and its metabolites to treatment responses and evaluate the efficacy and safety of these interventions through rigorous randomized controlled trials to support clinical translation.

articles.title: All-Inclusive: Personalized Drug Metabolism by Microbiota in Gut Organoids.
articles.abstract: The metabolism of drugs takes place for the most part in the liver. Next to the liver, however, microbiota in the gut also play an active role in the metabolism of drugs, either in generating active compounds or deactivating the drug. In vivo, the gastrointestinal tract is populated by a complex and highly individual microbiota. Gut organoids are powerful ex vivo tools for studying drug metabolism. Organoids also allow for studying the role of microbiota in drug metabolism. The technical challenges in co-culturing eukaryotic organoids with prokaryotic bacteria are considerable and have only partly been overcome. Next steps will include mimicking the complex composition of the gut microbiome and distinguishing between host and microbial metabolites. This manuscript provides a state-of-the-art overview of current concepts and of the most promising avenues for future research and applications in drug development.

articles.title: Lyophilized Mesenchymal Stromal Cell-Derived Products in Regenerative Medicine: A Systematic Review of Biological Activity, Stability, Safety, and Therapeutic Effects.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Lyophilization may facilitate storage and distribution of mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC)-derived products. This systematic review assessed biological activity, storage stability, safety, and therapeutic effects of lyophilized MSC-derived products in regenerative medicine.
