Methods: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection were searched through 28 August 2026. Eligible English-language original studies included in vivo animal or human therapeutic evaluations. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261426429) and reported following PRISMA 2020. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using SYRCLE, RoB 2, or ROBINS-I according to study design. Heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis; findings were synthesized narratively. Results: Thirty-nine studies were included from 884 records; only one contained a human interventional component. Products included conditioned medium, secretome, extracellular vesicles, and whole-cell or synthetic preparations. Sixteen studies evaluated biological activity or stability: 12 directly compared lyophilized and fresh or non-lyophilized products, whereas four assessed post-lyophilization activity without a fresh or non-lyophilized comparator. Retention depended on product formulation and processing conditions, and storage-stability evidence was limited. Twelve studies provided safety evidence; no major systemic toxicity signal emerged, although concentration-dependent cytotoxicity in vitro and transient local reactions occurred. Most studies reported improvement in at least one regenerative or functional outcome, with neutral or mixed findings in some applications. Incomplete reporting of randomization and blinding limited confidence in the evidence. Conclusions: Some lyophilized MSC-derived products retain biological properties and exhibit therapeutic activity, predominantly in preclinical models. Evidence is insufficient to establish clinical efficacy or long-term safety. Translation requires standardized manufacturing, validated potency and storage-stability testing, systematic safety assessment, and well-designed human studies.

articles.title: The Role of Psychostimulants in the Management of Refractory Catatonia: A Comprehensive Review of Case Reports.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome characterised by motor, behavioural, and affective abnormalities and is frequently associated with mood disorders, particularly major depressive and bipolar disorders. Although benzodiazepines and electroconvulsive therapy are considered first-line treatments, a substantial proportion of patients show partial or no response, especially in chronic, affective, or medically complex presentations. Contemporary neurobiological models implicate dysfunction across multiple neurotransmitter systems, including GABAergic, glutamatergic, and dopaminergic pathways, as well as disturbances in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits involved in psychomotor control and arousal regulation. Within this framework, psychostimulants may exert therapeutic effects by enhancing dopaminergic and noradrenergic transmission, thereby modulating frontal-striatal networks and facilitating behavioural activation and motor initiation. Evidence from conditions characterised by psychomotor slowing, apathy, and impaired behavioural initiation provides a neurophysiological rationale for their adjunctive use in selected cases of catatonia, particularly when associated with mood disorders. However, there is a dearth of empirical data, with the evidence largely confined to case reports, hence the need for comprehensive reviews of cases and controlled studies to clarify the role of psychostimulants and to explore drug combinations in the treatment of catatonia. Methods: We conducted a comprehensive review of case reports on 22 October 2026 on PubMed, Scopus, PsycInfo/PsycArticles, and Web of Science. Results: We included 9 studies. Psychostimulants were usually helpful in inducing rapid symptoms resolution of catatonia. Conclusions: Psychostimulants may be used in cases of catatonia and provide rapid improvement. Future longitudinal, double-blind designs are likely to allow reliably assessing the value of psychostimulants in catatonia.

articles.title: Nanostructured Natural Bioactives: A Promising Frontier for MASLD Therapy.
articles.abstract: Background: Natural bioactives derived from medicinal plants and dietary sources have long been used to manage metabolic and hepatic disorders. However, their application in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is restricted by poor solubility, instability, low bioavailability, rapid metabolism, and insufficient hepatic exposure. This review evaluates the pharmacological mechanisms and therapeutic potential of nanostructured natural bioactives for MASLD. Methods: Published preclinical and clinical evidence on natural bioactives and their nanostructured formulations for MASLD was narratively reviewed. Evidence was synthesized according to nanocarrier type, pharmacokinetic advantages, mechanisms of action, therapeutic outcomes, safety, and clinical translation. Results: The included studies primarily covered three categories: nanostructured natural small-molecule bioactives, bioactive fractions, and single-source therapeutics. Small-molecule bioactives constituted the largest group, encompassing flavonoids, polyphenols, terpenoids, alkaloids, and lignans. Liposomes, nanoemulsions, polymeric nanoparticles, and micelles were the principal delivery platforms used to improve effective exposure through encapsulation, protection, and controlled release. Mechanisms included modulation of AMPK, SREBP-1c/FAS-, and PPARα/CPT-1-related lipid metabolism, suppression of NF-κB-associated inflammation, and enhancement of Nrf2-related antioxidant defenses, collectively attenuating hepatic lipid accumulation and injury. Nanostructured bioactive fractions and single-source therapeutics additionally involved multicomponent interactions, intestinal barrier protection, and gut-liver axis modulation. Nanostructured small-molecule bioactives showed translational promise, with oral nano-curcumin providing preliminary clinical evidence, although its additional benefits on hepatic fat content were inconsistent. Naturally derived vesicle-like nanoparticles also showed potential, but their compositional standardization, in vivo behavior, and long-term safety require further investigation. Conclusions: Nanostructuring may improve the pharmacokinetic performance and pharmacological efficacy of natural bioactives against MASLD. Future studies should prioritize standardized formulation characterization, dose-exposure-response relationships, direct comparisons with free bioactives, long-term safety, and clinical trials.

articles.title: Phytochemical Modulation of NF-κB Signaling in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Preclinical Progress and Pharmacological Perspectives.
articles.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains characterized by aggressive progression, extensive stromal remodeling, early metastatic dissemination, and resistance to systemic therapy. Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) integrates oncogenic, inflammatory, survival, angiogenic, and treatment-induced signals and therefore represents a pharmacologically relevant regulatory node in pancreatic cancer. Phytochemicals including curcumin, xanthohumol, parthenolide, dimethylaminoparthenolide, triptolide, resveratrol, emodin, and related compounds have been investigated as modulators of NF-κB activity, although the strength of mechanistic evidence differs substantially among agents. This review evaluates canonical and noncanonical NF-κB biology in pancreatic cancer, interactions with KRAS, PI3K-AKT, STAT3, MAPK, and Nrf2 signaling, and the consequences of NF-κB modulation for apoptosis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, angiogenesis, tumor microenvironmental communication, and chemotherapy resistance. Particular emphasis is placed on separating direct pharmacodynamic evidence from downstream pathway association and computational prediction. Curcumin and xanthohumol have been evaluated using direct NF-κB measurements linked to defined antitumor phenotypes and in vivo validation, whereas parthenolide and dimethylaminoparthenolide support a mechanistic relationship between NF-κB activity and gemcitabine resistance. Clinical evidence remains limited and is dominated by early phase curcumin studies, which also illustrate major barriers involving bioavailability, tumor exposure, and target engagement. Future development requires exposure-response analysis, cell-type-specific pharmacodynamics, rational combination therapy, validated biomarkers, and formulations or derivatives with improved pharmacokinetic properties. An evidence-based pharmacological framework may clarify which phytochemical NF-κB modulators warrant further translational development and biomarker-guided evaluation in PDAC.

articles.title: From Glycan-CAZyme Compatibility to Personalized Medicinal Polysaccharide Interventions: Mechanistic Evidence, Response Variability, and Predictive Opportunities.
articles.abstract: Individuals given the same medicinal polysaccharide can differ in substrate utilization, metabolite production and host response. Accessible glycan structure, effective colonic exposure and the recipient's carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZyme) systems help explain these differences. This review examines compatibility from microbial substrate acquisition to host effects and separates substrate utilization, microbial products and host outcomes. Medicinal-glycan studies identify selective utilization, substrate-induced polysaccharide utilization loci and catalytic reactions, with genetic evidence for selected systems. Utilization specificity and prevalence of compatible functions jointly influence community responses, while enzyme induction, competition, metabolic exchange, absorption, direct glycan recognition and preparation composition shape conversion and host exposure. We propose selecting candidate predictors from these response processes and testing them against prespecified endpoints. Human dietary-fiber studies provide complementary evidence for taxonomic prediction, functional biomarkers and fermentation-guided choice. The available evidence supports a proof-of-concept rationale, not a clinically validated rule for selecting medicinal polysaccharides, and the reviewed studies do not establish improved host outcomes from a matching rule. The key test is whether explicit glycan-utilization matching improves prediction beyond taxonomy and the separate effects of structure and function. Paired comparisons under common validation conditions can isolate that contribution, while baseline fermentation can add information when screening and validation endpoints are measured independently. Predicting response to one preparation and choosing the best preparation require different evidence. The practical value of matching depends on improving host outcomes over a common preparation or usual selection practice.

articles.title: From Supportive Care to Precision Medicine: Emerging Therapies for Inherited Epidermolysis Bullosa.
articles.abstract: Background: Inherited epidermolysis bullosa (EB) comprises monogenic disorders characterised by tissue fragility, recurrent blistering, chronic wounds and multisystem complications. Although multidisciplinary supportive care remains fundamental, it cannot correct the molecular defect or prevent cumulative tissue damage. This narrative review examines emerging disease-modifying therapies for inherited EB, emphasising their application in clinical practice. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE was searched using terms relating to EB subtypes and pharmacological, gene-, RNA-, protein-, cell- and genome-editing therapies. Reference lists, clinical guidelines, consensus statements and regulatory documents were also examined. Clinical studies and preclinical investigations were synthesised qualitatively; no meta-analysis was performed. Results: Recent advances have expanded treatment beyond conventional wound care. Oleogel-S10 enhances endogenous wound healing independently of genotype, whereas beremagene geperpavec delivers functional COL7A1 copies directly to dystrophic EB wounds. Prademagene zamikeracel combines ex vivo correction of autologous keratinocytes with epidermal grafting, offering potentially sustained closure of selected chronic wounds. Nevertheless, these treatments remain predominantly local and do not fully address generalised skin fragility or extracutaneous disease. Mesenchymal stromal cells, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, recombinant type VII collagen, RNA-based treatments and genome editing may provide broader or more durable benefits, but evidence remains limited, and concerns regarding delivery, safety, durability and accessibility persist. Conclusions: Precision and regenerative therapies are transforming EB management but remain complementary to multidisciplinary supportive care. Clinical evaluation should extend beyond wound closure to include pain, function, growth, quality of life and caregiver burden. Long-term surveillance and personalised combination strategies are essential to determine whether early treatment can safely alter the natural history of EB.

articles.title: Integrated Strategies for Enhanced Cordycepin Production from Cordyceps militaris: Biosynthetic Regulation to Translational Applications.
articles.abstract: Cordyceps militaris offers a cultivable source of cordycepin, a pharmaceutically relevant nucleoside. This review integrates evidence on cultivation, cordycepin biosynthesis and regulation, artificial intelligence and omics applications, recovery, and biological activities, with emphasis on reproducible production and pharmaceutical development. Solid-state and submerged cultivation serve different production targets; however, cordycepin yield and product quality vary with strain, substrate, developmental stage, and process conditions. Cordycepin production depends on biosynthetic activity and protection against deamination associated with the cns1-cns4 cluster, precursor supply, and environmental regulation rather than on gene expression alone. Genetic engineering, metabolic modelling, multi-omics, machine learning, and process monitoring have supported production improvement, pathway analysis or prediction, but these approaches remain poorly integrated. The reviewed studies do not demonstrate validated online cordycepin estimation or autonomous control. Recovery methods involve trade-offs among yield, purity, cost, and throughput, highlighting the need for consistent product specifications. Cordycepin shows anticancer, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant activities, although evidence remains preclinical and limited by variable experimental exposures, incomplete mechanistic validation, and insufficient pharmacokinetic and clinical data. Future progress requires standardized strains and cultivation protocols, causal metabolic validation, externally validated predictive models, integrated process control, scalable recovery, and translational evaluation.

articles.title: Pharmacological Disruption of the BRCA2-RAD51 Interface: Inducing BRCAness to Exploit Synthetic Lethality in Homologous-Recombination-Proficient Cancer.
articles.abstract: Homologous recombination is a high-fidelity DNA repair pathway that preserves genome integrity during replication stress and double-strand break repair. Central to it is the BRCA2-RAD51 axis, in which BRCA2 coordinates RAD51 recruitment, nucleoprotein filament assembly and protection of recombination intermediates. PARP inhibitors have validated synthetic lethality in BRCA-deficient cancers, but their benefit requires pre-existing homologous-recombination deficiency and is limited by acquired resistance. Pharmacological disruption of the BRCA2-RAD51 interface offers a route to a reversible "BRCAness" state in homologous-recombination-proficient tumors. This review examines the structural basis of BRCA2-mediated RAD51 control, the small-molecule disruptors reported to date-triazoles, dihydroquinolone pyrazolines, CAM833, N-acylhydrazones, fragment-derived compounds and quinoline-based analogs-and the peptide, D-amino-acid and aptamer modalities targeting the same axis, together with combination evidence, pancreatic cancer as the dominant disease model, pharmacodynamic biomarkers, selectivity and resistance. Because reported potencies derive from heterogeneous protein constructs and assay formats, the construct used is stated for every value and biochemical and cellular potencies are tabulated separately, and each agent is classified explicitly as a mechanistic probe or an early lead. We emphasize three limitations that the field has not yet addressed: no interface disruptor of any modality has completed in vivo pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic characterization, unbound tissue exposure and the reversibility of homologous-recombination inhibition are unmeasured, and peptide and oligonucleotide agents face unresolved barriers of nuclear delivery, proteolytic or nucleolytic degradation, biodistribution and innate immune activation. BRCA2-RAD51 interface disruption is therefore a mechanistically rational but strictly preclinical strategy whose feasibility will be decided by in vivo exposure-response and tolerability data that do not yet exist.

articles.title: From Sequence to Spatial Pharmacology: A Translational Evidence Framework for Peptide Systems in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
articles.abstract: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the problem is access, not merely affinity. Yet recent reviews emphasize discovery platforms, theranostic probes or clinical translation; to our knowledge, none appraises, across peptide roles, what the evidence shows about access, exposure and benefit by disease stage, including negative randomized results. This structured critical review introduces a spatial-pharmacology framework that asks of every peptide what job it performs (drug, targeting or penetration ligand, trigger, antigen or reporter), where it must act, which clinical state can reveal benefit, and which unresolved experiment most threatens translation. By classifying evidence maturity (tiers T0-T5) separately from outcome direction and profiling five translational domains, it compares heterogeneous systems without pooling and prevents evidence transfer between roles. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, publisher records and citation chains through 13 August 2026 and purposively charted decision-informative programs in a source-linked atlas. Three cross-system conclusions emerge. First, early human evidence differs in kind by role (for example, target access for reporters, immunogenicity for vaccines) and is not interchangeable, while many direct, stromal and immune-enabling peptides remain preclinical. Second, evidence maturity and benefit often diverge: randomized evidence is limited, partly conference- or developer-reported, and largely negative or non-confirmatory, whereas supportive signals come mostly from lower evidence tiers. Third, the decisive missing evidence is role-specific: site-of-action exposure for direct, stromal and penetration peptides, setting-appropriate endpoints for vaccines, and effect on clinical decisions for reporters. We propose six minimum development standards; the framework is a planning heuristic, not a validated predictor of benefit.

articles.title: Opportunities and Challenges for Rescuing the Diabetic Microvasculature: Repurposing Anti-Inflammatory Drugs to Target the HO-1 Axis via Advanced Delivery Systems.
articles.abstract: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are characterized by severe microvascular impairment, where unresolved chronic inflammation and persistent oxidative stress disrupt endothelial function and arrest angiogenesis. The collapse of the vascular niche underscores the clinical need to shift the microenvironment from inflammation to active resolution. The heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) signaling pathway is a critical endogenous defense mechanism that mitigates reactive oxygen species (ROS) and generates vasoprotective metabolites, making it an optimal target for vascular rescue. This review explores the potential strategic repurposing of classic anti-inflammatory agents, such as locally administered glucocorticoids, aspirin-triggered pro-resolving mediators, and macrolides such as azithromycin as upstream modulators of HO-1 to reprogram the hostile DFU microenvironment. While systemic administration of these drugs often delays wound healing and risks immunosuppression, their localized therapeutic potential is immense. Consequently, we highlight the pivotal role of advanced pharmaceutical engineering, specifically macrophage-targeted nanocarriers and stimuli-responsive hydrogels, designed to localize anti-inflammatory delivery directly within the ischemic tissue. By bridging immunopharmacology and advanced drug delivery, targeting the HO-1 axis provides a potential translational framework to modulate chronic inflammation and support microvascular regeneration, while acknowledging the current challenges for clinical implementation.

articles.title: From Model Explanations to Drug Discovery Evidence: A Critical Review.
articles.abstract: Explanations can inform which molecular analog is synthesized, which protein contact is investigated, and which repurposing hypothesis is tested. This structured critical narrative review examines the evidence supporting such uses across drug-discovery tasks. A literature-derived evidence-oriented explainability framework (EOEF) provides a conceptual guide for assessing specified explanation claims, connecting established evaluation concepts to explanation objects, reference provenance, comparison conditions, retained coverage, and intended use. Seven scoped records from six selected studies illustrate these relationships. Published comparisons show that contact supervision improves structural recovery under tested novelty conditions, whereas measured structure-activity relationships, structural calculations, and external prediction support different scientific questions. Counterfactual uncertainty filtering increases agreement with a computational property oracle on a retained subset; gain and remaining coverage must be read together. Predictive feature sets can remain useful despite variable individual rankings. Human-evaluation findings likewise depend on the information supplied by the tested interfaces. These comparisons distinguish evidence for model investigation, domain hypotheses, and candidate prioritization. A recommended claim-evidence-scope record makes the relevant conditions traceable, helping connect an explanatory claim to the observation and comparison needed for a discovery choice.

articles.title: Weed-Derived Secondary Metabolites in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: Target Engagement, Exposure Plausibility and a Safety-Gated Framework for Candidate Prioritization.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Existing PCOS reviews largely catalogue natural products and reported molecular pathways. This structured critical review asks a different translational question: which constituents from weed, ruderal and invasive taxa remain credible candidates when target engagement, pharmacological direction, realistic exposure and safety are considered together. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection and CAB Abstracts were searched from inception to 2 September 2026, with CABI resources used to verify weed status. Eligible pharmacological, pharmacokinetic and toxicological evidence was critically appraised using a T1-T4 mechanistic evidence hierarchy and evaluated for exposure plausibility, methodological quality and citation integrity. Results: No positive mechanistic claim reached T3 or T4. Urtica dioica L. lignans demonstrably displace dihydrotestosterone from SHBG in vitro, but the predicted consequence for free androgen exposure in vivo remains untested; flavonoid aromatase effects are assay- and context-dependent; and several widely cited systemic mechanisms are not supported by current exposure data. Silybin exposure supports a narrower liver-directed hypothesis, whereas non-absorbed inulin-type fructans provide a luminal gut-axis case in which systemic exposure is not required. Mentha spicata L. provides a reproducible human endocrine signal but no defined active constituent or molecular target. Conclusions: The principal barrier to clinical translation is not a shortage of activity signals but the absence of demonstrated in vivo target engagement, target-site pharmacokinetics and reproductive-safety qualification. No candidate currently clears all five gates. Silybum marianum flavonolignans and Cichorium intybus inulin-type fructans are therefore only provisionally prioritized for node-specific nonclinical development, while M. spicata is a mechanism-resolution research signal rather than a pharmacological lead. The framework prioritizes the experiments needed to establish development readiness; it does not infer PCOS-specific efficacy from the existing evidence.

articles.title: The Evolutionary Trajectory of Marine-Derived Polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN): A Bibliometric Mapping from Pharmacology to Advanced Biomaterials.
articles.abstract: Polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN), a bioactive marine macromolecule extracted from Salmonidae sperm, has garnered substantial attention in regenerative medicine, dermatology, and orthopedic repair. However, a comprehensive bibliometric mapping synthesizing its intellectual evolution, research frontiers, and interdisciplinary knowledge flows remains lacking. Based on bibliographic data retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and PubMed databases covering 1992 to 2025, this study systematically deconstructed 439 core publications using R-bibliometrix (version 5. 0), VOSviewer 1.6.20, and CiteSpace 7.0.1. Global publication outputs, institutional collaboration topologies, intellectual bases, thematic clusters, citation bursts, and strategic coordinate arrays were thoroughly analyzed. The results demonstrate that global PDRN research has exhibited an exponential growth trajectory (R2 = 0.8628), albeit accompanied by a low international co-authorship rate (14.81%) and prominent regional clustering. The research paradigm has decisively transitioned from classical single-target purinergic pharmacology (adenosine A2A receptor agonism) toward an advanced "Extracellular Niche Remodeler" model integrating smart biopolymeric delivery systems for wound healing, skin barrier restoration, and osteoarthritis management. Current frontiers prioritize fabricating bio-composite hydrogels combining PDRN with hyaluronic acid or chitosan. Despite these promising advancements, clinical translation remains hindered by three critical gaps, namely the absence of standardized international extraction protocols, a deficit of high-quality multi-center randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and insufficient mechanistic insights into non-receptor-mediated metabolic flux reprogramming. Ultimately, this study provides robust theoretical insights and strategic foresight for advancing marine-derived nucleic acid therapeutics into precision regenerative medicine.

articles.title: Seaweed-Derived Bioactive Compounds Modulating MMP-2 and MMP-9 in Cancer: Redox Mechanisms and Therapeutic Limitations.
articles.abstract: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are zinc-dependent endopeptidases which play essential roles in extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. Among them, MMP-2 and MMP-9 are mainly associated with tumor invasion, angiogenesis, metastasis, and other pathological processes such as fibrosis and inflammation, making them attractive therapeutic targets for cancer treatment. Marine natural products, particularly seaweed-derived bioactive compounds, have attracted increasing attention because of their structural diversity, broad pharmacological activities, and generally favorable biocompatibility. Seaweeds are a rich source of polysaccharides, phenolic compounds, fatty acids, pigments, vitamins, and other metabolites with anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidant, and anti-cancer properties. Growing evidence indicates that several of these compounds could suppress cancer cell proliferation, invasion, migration, and metastasis by regulating the activity and/or expression of MMP-2 and MMP-9 and their associated signaling pathways, including MAPK signaling pathways. This review comprehensively summarizes current evidence on seaweed-derived bioactive compounds as modulators of MMP 2 and MMP-9 with particular emphasis on their effects on enzymatic activity, expression, and MMP-associated signaling pathways. In addition, current limitations, translational challenges, and future perspectives for developing seaweed-derived compounds as potential MMP-targeted strategies for cancer prevention and therapy are discussed.

articles.title: Shilajit Extract: Examining Biomedical Applications-A Systematic Review Protocol.
articles.abstract: Background: Shilajit, a natural mineral exudate utilized for centuries in traditional Ayurvedic and Eastern European medicine, is regarded as a traditional adaptogenic substance and rejuvenator. This systematic review synthesizes contemporary scientific evidence regarding the biomedical applications of Shilajit extract, critically evaluating its pharmacological properties and therapeutic potential. Methods: A systematic search was performed across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for peer-reviewed literature published between 1951 and 2026. Studies were screened against rigorous eligibility criteria, and methodological quality was appraised using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 and SYRCLE tools. Results: Studies were included in the final analysis. Characterized by high concentrations of fulvic acid and dibenzo-α-pyrones, Shilajit exhibits antioxidant activity, anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective, and adaptogenic activities. Preclinical data demonstrate dose-dependent cytotoxicity against multiple cancer cell lines via apoptosis induction. Furthermore, evidence suggests its efficacy in enhancing muscular strength, improving reproductive function, and mitigating protein aggregation in neurodegenerative contexts. Conclusions: Shilajit possesses significant biomedical potential that aligns with its traditional applications. However, clinical integration requires addressing standardization challenges, implementing stringent quality control to mitigate heavy metal risks, and conducting large-scale human trials to definitively establish safety and efficacy profiles.

articles.title: Double-Edged Phytochemicals in Endometrial Receptivity: Dietary Exposure, Context Dependence, and the Limits of Directional Claims.
articles.abstract: Dietary and supplemental phytochemicals are investigated as modulators of endometrial receptivity, yet studies of the same compounds report favorable and unfavorable effects. This critical narrative review examines five compound classes through the lens of pharmacologically relevant exposure. For compounds with paired pharmacokinetic and in vitro data, nominal experimental concentrations exceed plasma concentrations reported after dietary intake, conventional supplementation or a 12 g curcumin probe dose; the comparisons are indirect, and no ratio can be established for some classes. Neither nominal nor plasma concentration indexes the concentration reached in endometrial tissue, which has not been reported for any class; the circulating species may also differ from the molecule tested in culture. We propose five contextual dimensions: receptor context, achieved exposure, exposure window, tissue and cell state, and the measured endpoint. The literature largely evaluates recovery from induced impairment rather than enhancement of normal receptivity. Within the screened records no study directly quantified endometrial perfusion after a defined-compound exposure, and the available endpoints are surrogates of receptivity, not pregnancy outcomes. Because the evidence is heterogeneous and the search was not systematic, the framework is a set of testable propositions, not an established model. We provide an evidence map and a reporting checklist for studies measuring exposure, context and implantation-related outcomes.

articles.title: Clitoria ternatea L.: Ethnopharmacology, Phytochemistry, Pharmacological Activities and Toxicological Evaluation.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Clitoria ternatea L. is a medicinal plant widely used in traditional medicine and is increasingly studied for its phytochemical and pharmacological properties. This review summarises current knowledge on its traditional uses, phytochemical constituents, pharmacological activities and toxicological profile. Methods: The relevant literature was identified through searches of major scientific databases, with emphasis on studies reporting the phytochemistry, pharmacological activities and toxicological evaluation of C. ternatea. Results:C. ternatea contains a diverse range of bioactive compounds, including flavonoids (including anthocyanins), peptides (including cyclotides), terpenoids and other phenolic constituents. Experimental studies have reported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, antidiabetic, anticancer, neuroprotective, hepatoprotective and other pharmacological activities. Several of these effects have been associated with oxidative stress, inflammatory pathways and cholinergic function, although the compounds responsible for many of the reported effects remain unclear. Available toxicological studies indicate relatively low acute toxicity under the experimental conditions tested, but information on repeated-dose and long-term exposure remains limited. Conclusions: Overall, the available evidence supports the pharmacological potential of C. ternatea, although most studies remain preclinical. Further studies using chemically characterised extracts and isolated compounds, together with more comprehensive toxicological and clinical evaluation, are needed to better establish its efficacy and safety.

articles.title: Atractylodes macrocephala in Ulcerative Colitis: Bioactive Constituents, Microbiota, and Translational Gaps.
articles.abstract: Atractylodes macrocephala Koidz. rhizome (Atractylodis Macrocephalae Rhizoma, AMR; Bai-Zhu) is a widely used medicinal plant, and its specialized metabolites are now being mapped onto defined molecular targets. Existing reviews of this material are genus-wide, formula-level, or restricted to a single constituent class, and none grades the ulcerative-colitis (UC) evidence constituent by constituent while separating what has been demonstrated in colitis models from what is extrapolated from other disease contexts; that gap is the rationale for the present review. Here we review, constituent by constituent, how AMR acts in UC. The sesquiterpenoid lactones account for much of the activity: atractylenolide I protects the epithelial barrier (RhoA/ROCK/MLC; S100A9/AMPK/mTOR), reshapes intestinal metabolism and the microbiota (SPHK1/B4GALT2) and limits carbonic anhydrase IX-mediated ferroptosis, whereas atractylenolide II drives Nrf2-dependent antioxidant responses (in non-colitis models), and interleukin-17 receptor A is nominated as a candidate direct target of atractylenolide III-awaiting independent replication-through which it may curb macrophage M1 polarization. The polysaccharides rebalance Th17/Treg immunity and remodel the gut microbiota and its tryptophan metabolites with pregnane X receptor-associated signaling, while the volatile oil and vesicle-like particles are likewise protective. We grade each mechanism by the strength of the underlying colitis-model evidence and stay explicit about what remains extrapolation. Controlled human trials are still lacking, with only very preliminary clinical observation to date. Finally, we single out endothelial-leukocyte adhesion-already exploited by anti-adhesion biologics-as a promising but still untested hypothesis for translating these constituents toward the clinic.

articles.title: Advancing Cancer Immunotherapy Through Advanced Drug Delivery Platforms: Microneedles, Oral Dissolving Films, and Exosomes.
articles.abstract: Recent advances in drug delivery have shifted the focus toward improving specificity, reducing toxicity, and developing novel platforms that are suitable for diverse routes of administration, including injections and oral therapies. Conventional cancer therapies often suffer from poor pharmacokinetics and off-target side effects, limiting their clinical utility and effectiveness in cancer treatment. Cancer immunotherapy, a treatment strategy that utilizes the body's immune system to recognize and eliminate tumors, has emerged as an alternative to traditional therapies, but is limited by inefficient and non-specific delivery of immunomodulatory agents. Therefore, strategies such as microneedles (MNs), exosomes, and orally dissolving films (ODFs) have gained attention for their ability to target treatment specificity and improve patient response. Microneedles offer a minimally invasive, localized delivery strategy that bypasses the skin barrier and directly targets areas with high immune cell activity, making them promising for cancer immunotherapy and vaccine delivery. As naturally derived nanocarriers, exosomes provide a biocompatible, low-immune-response platform for delivering proteins, nucleic acids, and immunomodulatory agents, with the added advantage of naturally targeting specific cells. The flexibility of engineered exosome-based delivery systems is underscored by the wide range of cellular sources from which exosomes can be derived and their capacity for customization potential to improve targeting. Meanwhile, ODFs offer a patient-friendly alternative that enables rapid mucosal absorption and partial metabolic avoidance, supporting both small-molecule and immunotherapy-based applications. These strategies pave the way for a more personalized and efficient therapeutic delivery system. Each approach offers clear benefits, but challenges such as drug-loading capacity and regulatory hurdles persist. Continued development and integration of these technologies may significantly improve treatment outcomes, particularly in cancer, by enabling more targeted, controlled, and patient-accessible drug delivery.

articles.title: Extracellular Vesicles as a Delivery and Therapeutic Platform for RNA- and Protein-Based Cardiovascular Therapeutics: A Multi-Omics, Ancestry-Aware Roadmap.
articles.abstract: RNA- and protein-based medicines are expanding cardiovascular therapeutic options, but efficient delivery to cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, vascular cells, and lesional immune cells remains difficult. Target selection also relies disproportionately on European-ancestry datasets, limiting causal resolution and portability. This narrative review evaluates extracellular vesicles (EVs) as carriers and active biological products for cardiovascular RNA and protein therapeutics. We distinguish EVs carrying a defined active ingredient, intrinsically bioactive EV preparations, and EV-inspired synthetic systems. We link delivery design to human multi-omics by integrating diverse-ancestry genome-wide association studies, fine-mapping, molecular quantitative trait loci, colocalization, Mendelian randomization, and single-cell or spatial transcriptomics. Hepatic targets such as PCSK9, LPA, APOC3, ANGPTL3, AGT, and TTR provide benchmarks against which EV platforms can be assessed. The strongest rationale for EVs lies in extrahepatic programs where tissue access limits otherwise compelling myocardial, fibrotic, vascular, or regenerative targets. We propose a stage-gated roadmap connecting causal evidence and cell-state specificity to modality selection, cargo loading, targeting, endosomal escape, biodistribution, human cardiac models, manufacturing, potency, and safety. We then apply the framework to worked examples (LPA, CAMK2D, COL6A3-derived endotrophin, AGER/RAGE, and VEGFA), in which fine-mapping, colocalization, Mendelian randomization, ancestry-specific evidence, and cell-state localization jointly determine the modality and the carrier, including targets for which an EV is not the appropriate choice. Cited delivery studies are graded on a four-level evidence ladder spanning tissue association, intact-cargo delivery, cytosolic release, and pharmacodynamic activity, because most cardiovascular EV reports establish only the lower levels. The cardiovascular EV studies reviewed do not establish clinical benefit or an advantage over optimized lipid nanoparticles at matched active-cargo dose in a cardiovascular disease model. Clinical translation depends on reproducible functional delivery, a defined mechanism, consistent product quality, and meaningful benefit relative to established treatments.

articles.title: Comparative Adverse-Event Risk in Placebo-Controlled Phase I Trials: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis in Healthy Korean Participants.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Adverse events in phase I trials may reflect treatment, background symptoms, or study procedures. We compared investigational treatment with placebo in healthy Korean participants. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, the Korea Citation Index, the Research Information Sharing Service, and Google Scholar through 30 April 2026 (PROSPERO: CRD420261426647). Outcomes were any treatment-emergent adverse event or adverse event (any TEAE/AE) and adverse drug reaction or treatment-related AE (ADR/related AE). The prespecified inverse-variance random-effects analysis used 0.5 continuity correction, Paule-Mandel variance estimation, and modified Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals (CIs). Post hoc analyses used treatment-arm correction, Mantel-Haenszel pooling without correction, and a Poisson mixed model. Results: Forty-one studies were included. Any TEAE/AE was reported in 323/929 active-treatment and 66/267 placebo recipients; ADRs/related AEs occurred in 230/960 and 53/282. Prespecified risk ratios were 1.108 (95% CI 0.885-1.388) and 0.971 (0.764-1.234). Continuity-corrected inverse-variance analyses showed no significant difference. Mantel-Haenszel and Poisson estimates for any TEAE/AE were 1.393 (1.122-1.728) and 1.396 (1.070-1.820); ADR/related AE results were borderline and method-dependent. A highly imprecise gastrointestinal signal rested on one placebo event. Most risk-of-bias assessments raised some concerns. Conclusions: This was not an equivalence or non-inferiority analysis. Comparative estimates were sensitive to sparse-data methods, and clinically important increases in risk cannot be excluded. Concurrent controls and complete arm-specific reporting remain essential for interpreting early safety signals.

articles.title: Decoding the Multi-Target Anticancer Pharmacology of Alpinia galanga: Integrating Redox Vulnerability, Apoptotic Signaling, and Translational Barriers.
articles.abstract: Cancer remains one of the main causes of death worldwide. The development of drug resistance, systemic toxicity, and poor therapeutic selectivity continues to limit the efficacy of conventional treatments. Multi-target therapeutic agents that can modulate complex oncogenic networks are gaining increasing interest among natural products. Alpinia galanga (L.) Willd. is a medicinal plant that is a promising source of bioactive compounds with high anticancer potential. This review summarizes the current evidence on the anticancer activities of A. galanga extracts and its major phytochemicals, including 1'-acetoxychavicol acetate (ACA), 1'-acetoxyeugenol acetate (AEA), galangin, chrysin, pinocembrin, and related flavonoids. Mechanistically, these compounds modulate various hallmarks of cancer by modulating oxidative stress, apoptosis, autophagy, cell-cycle arrest, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory signaling, and metastatic pathways, particularly NF-κB, PI3K/Akt, MAPK, and p53-associated networks. Recent findings have shed light on the emerging roles of A. galanga compounds in overcoming resistance to targeted therapy, suppressing immune evasion through efferocytosis, remodeling the tumor microenvironment, and augmenting chemosensitivity and immunotherapeutic responses. Importantly, advances in nanotechnology-based formulations, such as lipid nanocarriers, exosome-mediated delivery systems, and biomimetic nanovaccines, have greatly improved the translational potential of galangin and other phytochemicals by improving their bioavailability, tumor targeting, and immune activation. This review also provides a critical discussion of the current pharmacokinetic limitations, translational challenges, and future opportunities for integrating A. galanga-derived compounds in precision oncology and combination-based cancer therapies. Collectively, the available evidence suggests that A. galanga is a platform with mechanistic versatility and clinical promise for next-generation anticancer therapeutics.

articles.title: Anticancer Activities and Molecular Mechanisms of 2-Methoxy-1,4-Naphthoquinone: A Systematic Review of Preclinical Evidence.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: 2-Methoxy-1,4-naphthoquinone (MNQ) is a naturally occurring, redox-active compound with reported anticancer activity, but its preclinical evidence has not been systematically reviewed. This review evaluated the anticancer-related activities and associated molecular mechanisms of MNQ across preclinical cancer models. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Web of Science were systematically searched, with the final search performed on 26 October 2026. Original English-language studies evaluating the anticancer effects or cancer-related biological activities of MNQ were included. Findings were narratively synthesised and mapped to the Hallmarks of Cancer framework. Risk of bias was assessed using adapted OHAT and SYRCLE tools for in vitro and in vivo evidence, respectively. Results: Fourteen studies were included, all involving in vitro experiments, with one also reporting an in vivo hepatoma xenograft study. MNQ showed cytotoxic and antiproliferative activities, alongside apoptosis, necrosis, cell-cycle alterations, oxidative stress, DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and suppression of glycolysis, migration, and invasion. Alterations in autophagy-related markers, inflammatory and cellular stress responses, inhibition of EBV early antigen activation, and alterations in MAPK, PI3K/Akt, NF-κB, and PKC-related signalling were also reported. The in vivo study reported reduced tumour growth. Risk-of-bias assessments identified methodological reporting limitations in in vitro studies and predominantly unclear risk-of-bias judgements for the in vivo study. Conclusions: Current preclinical evidence suggests that MNQ affects biological processes associated with six Hallmarks of Cancer, highlighting its potential for further anticancer investigation. Nevertheless, the evidence remains predominantly in vitro, while experimental heterogeneity and methodological limitations emphasise the need for further mechanistic and in vivo validation.

articles.title: Mesoamerican Codices: Prospects for Anxiolytic and Antidepressant Drug Discovery.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Anxiety and depression are leading causes of disability worldwide. Although current pharmaceuticals are effective, adverse effects reduce adherence, driving the search for alternatives in traditional plant-based medicine. This article analyzes ancient Mesoamerican codices and documents to identify candidate plants, establishing a baseline for pharmacological validation and potential treatment development. Methods: This narrative review analyzes and synthesizes data from specialized databases and physical libraries in Spanish and English. Results: Plants described in Mesoamerican codices demonstrate anxiolytic- and antidepressant-like effects in preclinical models, linked to phytochemicals such as sterols, flavonoids, alkaloids, and terpenes. Mechanisms appear to involve oxytocinergic cells; the GABAergic, serotonergic, noradrenergic, and dopaminergic systems; BDNF activation; and monoamine oxidase regulation. Although translation is complicated by uncertainties in historical interpretation, botanical identification, and reproducibility, these studies remain essential for identifying natural products to inform future drug discovery. Conclusions: Analyzing ancient Mesoamerican medical records helps identify plants with anxiolytic and antidepressant potential. However, characterizing their pharmacokinetic, toxicological, and neurochemical profiles is required before proposing clinical trials to ensure patient safety.

articles.title: MicroRNAs in Alzheimer's Disease: From Molecular Pathogenesis to Biomarkers and Therapeutic Strategies.
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline due to accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques outside neurons and neurofibrillary tangles inside neurons. The polygenic, multifactorial nature of the disease has limited the efficacy of single-target therapeutics and has shifted interest towards agents that act on several pathological pathways. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are well suited to this purpose: they are small non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally, and a single miRNA can regulate many transcripts within a common pathway. Since their first identification, appreciation of their regulatory capacity in the healthy and diseased brain has grown substantially and altered miRNA expression is now linked to a range of neurodegenerative diseases. In AD, selected miRNAs have been associated with amyloidogenic APP processing, BACE1 expression, tau phosphorylation, apolipoprotein E lipidation and neuroinflammation. Circulating miRNA signatures in blood and cerebrospinal fluid are being explored as minimally invasive diagnostic biomarkers alongside established plasma phosphorylated tau and Aβ42/40 measures. More recently, attention has turned to the therapeutic potential of these molecules, with crossing the blood-brain barrier remaining the major hurdle. This review summarizes the biogenesis and mechanism of action of miRNAs and critically assesses their emerging value as biomarkers and therapeutic candidates.

articles.title: New Drugs in the Treatment of Uncontrolled or Resistant Hypertension.
articles.abstract: Arterial hypertension remains one of the leading modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular and renal morbidity and mortality worldwide, while resistant hypertension continues to represent a major therapeutic challenge despite the widespread use of conventional antihypertensive agents. Recent advances in the understanding of hypertension pathophysiology have enabled the development of novel pharmacological strategies targeting previously unexplored mechanisms. This review summarizes recently approved and emerging drugs for hypertension, with particular emphasis on agents acting on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), endothelin pathway, aldosterone synthesis, and RNA interference technology. Novel approaches include modulation of the ACE2/angiotensin-(1-7)/Mas receptor axis, inhibition of aminopeptidase A, and targeting tissue-specific RAAS activity, aiming to counteract the deleterious effects of classical RAAS activation. Dual endothelin receptor antagonists, particularly aprocitentan, have demonstrated significant and sustained blood pressure reduction in resistant hypertension with improved tolerability compared with earlier endothelin receptor antagonists. Highly selective aldosterone synthase inhibitors, including baxdrostat, lorundrostat, vicadrostat, and dexfadrostat, provide effective blood pressure lowering while minimizing cortisol suppression associated with previous agents, although hyperkalemia remains an important adverse effect. Small interfering RNA (siRNA)-based therapies represent an innovative therapeutic class, with zilebesiran producing prolonged suppression of angiotensinogen synthesis and sustained antihypertensive effects after infrequent subcutaneous administration. Collectively, these therapies offer promising alternatives for patients with uncontrolled or resistant hypertension and may provide additional cardiovascular and renal protection beyond blood pressure reduction. Nevertheless, many of these agents remain under clinical investigation, and further large-scale, long-term studies are required to establish their safety, cost-effectiveness, and impact on cardiovascular outcomes before their routine incorporation into clinical practice.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence and Biotechnology in the Sustainable Design of Polymeric Biomaterials and Hybrid Drug Delivery Systems.
articles.abstract: The integration of circular bioeconomy principles, biotechnology, and artificial intelligence (AI) offers new opportunities for the rational design of sustainable polymeric biomaterials and hybrid drug delivery systems. Rather than reviewing these fields independently, this review examines how they can be connected within a feedstock-to-therapy framework, linking the selection and characterization of bio-derived resources with polymer production, material formulation, performance prediction, and biomedical application. Particular attention is given to the challenge of translating variable biological feedstocks, including plant biomass and microbial resources, into materials with reproducible physicochemical and biological properties. The review discusses natural polymers, microbial and enzymatically produced biopolymers, and biomass-derived functional compounds as building blocks for hydrogels, nanocomposites, scaffolds, and controlled drug delivery platforms. It further considers how biotechnology, including metabolic engineering and synthetic biology, can expand the range and improve the consistency of available material components. Within this framework, machine learning, materials informatics, and hybrid mechanistic-data-driven models are evaluated in terms of their potential to support feedstock characterization, formulation optimization, and prediction of material properties and drug-release behavior. The review identifies key barriers to integrating these approaches, including heterogeneous data, limited dataset sizes, feedstock variability, and insufficient experimental validation across different stages of material development.

articles.title: Targeting Autophagy with Puerarin: From a Natural Isoflavone to Therapeutic Applications.
articles.abstract: Autophagy is an evolutionarily conserved lysosomal degradation process that eliminates damaged organelles and misfolded proteins to maintain cellular homeostasis. Its dysfunction drives cancer, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular, hepatic, renal and skeletal muscle disorders, making autophagy a promising therapeutic target. Puerarin, a characteristic isoflavone from the leguminous medicinal plant Pueraria lobata, exerts broad pharmacological functions via autophagy modulation, yet no systematic review summarizes its tissue-specific regulatory patterns. This narrative review collects and categorizes recent cellular and animal studies on puerarin-autophagy crosstalk from mainstream databases. It organizes puerarin's bidirectional autophagy effects across multiple organs and summarizes core signaling pathways, including AMPK/mTOR and PI3K/Akt/mTOR. Puerarin exhibits context-dependent dual regulation of autophagy: it induces protective autophagy to relieve metabolic and degenerative organ injuries, while inhibiting excessive autophagy to alleviate fibrosis and tumor progression. Its regulatory roles depend on Nrf2, JNK/Beclin1 and mitophagy-related axes in cardiac, hepatic, pulmonary, renal, bone, muscle and nervous tissues, as well as various tumor models. These mechanistic insights may support the development of natural isoflavone-based therapeutic strategies targeting autophagy and broaden the value-added utilization of Pueraria lobata as a medicinal and agricultural resource.

articles.title: Hydroxyurea Pharmacokinetics and Precision Dosing in Sickle Cell Disease: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract: Background: Hydroxyurea is the cornerstone disease-modifying therapy for sickle cell disease (SCD), but interindividual pharmacokinetic (PK) variability contributes to differences in drug exposure and treatment response. This scoping review synthesised evidence on hydroxyurea PK, pharmacodynamic (PD) relationships, determinants of exposure, pharmacometric modelling, and precision dosing approaches in SCD. Methods: A scoping review was conducted according to PRISMA-ScR guidance. Studies involving paediatric or adult patients with SCD that evaluated hydroxyurea PK, PK-PD relationships, exposure determinants, pharmacometric modelling, or PK-guided dosing were included. Study characteristics, PK parameters, covariates, modelling approaches, and key findings were charted and synthesised descriptively. Results: Twenty-seven studies published between 2005 and 2026 were included. Hydroxyurea demonstrated rapid oral absorption (Tmax 0.73-1.7 h), a short elimination half-life (1.7-2.9 h), and variability in systemic exposure across individuals (coefficient of variation approximately 40-45%). Body weight and renal function were the most consistently identified determinants of disposition, with renal impairment associated with reduced clearance and increased exposure. PK of hydroxyurea were well described by population PK and physiologically based PK models. PK-guided dosing showed potential to shorten the time to maximum tolerated dose and improve haematological responses. However, exposure-response and exposure-toxicity relationships remain insufficiently characterised, and evidence directly linking hydroxyurea exposure to patient-centred clinical outcomes was limited. Conclusions: Pharmacometric modelling and model-informed precision dosing (MIPD) have potential to support individualised hydroxyurea therapy, particularly in paediatric patients and those with altered renal function. Prospective external validation across diverse paediatric and adult populations, together with validated exposure-response and exposure-toxicity targets and clinically meaningful efficacy and safety outcomes, is required before routine clinical application can be recommended.

articles.title: Mitochondria-Related Protein Abundance Changes Following Tianeptine Treatment in Rats Exposed to Chronic Social Isolation: A Focused Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Chronic psychosocial stress contributes to depression and has been associated with changes in mitochondrial function and cellular energy metabolism. Tianeptine (Tian), an atypical antidepressant, has been shown to modulate stress-related behavioral and molecular adaptations, but its effects on hippocampal mitochondrial proteins remain insufficiently characterized. This focused narrative review summarizes findings from two previously published proteomic datasets obtained using the same rat model of chronic social isolation (CSIS) stress, an animal model of depression. The datasets examined Tian-associated changes in hippocampal protein abundance in nonsynaptic mitochondria (NSM) and mitochondria-related proteins detected in the synaptosome-enriched fraction. Increased abundance was reported for proteins associated with oxidative phosphorylation, ATP synthesis, and mitochondrial transport across the two fractions, although voltage-dependent anion channel 1 was the only protein showing increased abundance in both. Changes in the abundance of proteins associated with pyruvate oxidation differed between the fractions, with decreases reported in NSM and increases among the mitochondria-related proteins detected in the synaptosome-enriched fraction. Glutamate dehydrogenase abundance decreased in NSM but increased in the synaptosome-enriched fraction. Other changes in NSM involved proteins associated with amino acid transport, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, redox homeostasis, fatty acid metabolism, and mitochondrial gene expression. In the synaptosome-enriched fraction, additional changes involved mitochondria-related proteins associated with protein quality control/proteostasis and antioxidant defense, as well as proteins involved in synaptic membrane trafficking. Overall, comparison of the two datasets revealed overlapping and divergent patterns of protein-abundance changes, suggesting that the proteomic alterations associated with chronic Tian treatment in CSIS rats vary across hippocampal subcellular fractions.

articles.title: Plant-Derived Compounds in Monogenic Epilepsies: Mechanistic Evidence, Genotype-Relevant Models, and Translational Considerations.
articles.abstract: Monogenic epilepsies and developmental and epileptic encephalopathies are biologically heterogeneous, and evidence for plant-derived interventions ranges from ethnopharmacology to randomized clinical trials. This review critically maps that evidence using a four-level genotype-relevance framework while separating antiseizure, neuroprotective, mechanistic, and clinical endpoints. Highly purified cannabidiol (CBD) has the strongest evidence chain: antiseizure activity in Scn1a-based Dravet models is complemented by randomized clinical efficacy at the syndrome level. However, current trial evidence does not establish an SCN1A-genotype-specific treatment response. β-Caryophyllene has direct preclinical evidence in a genetically relevant Dravet model. Luteolin has direct CDKL5-model evidence for reducing microglial overactivation and improving neuronal and neurodevelopmental outcomes, but seizure-frequency or video-EEG efficacy in CDKL5 deficiency disorder has not been demonstrated. Curcumin, resveratrol, epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), quercetin, and sulforaphane are supported mainly by non-genetic seizure models and therefore remain mechanistically plausible candidates rather than validated treatments for monogenic epilepsy. Medicinal plants, crude extracts, standardized preparations, and isolated compounds are considered separately. Translational prioritization should require a reproducible genotype-associated secondary phenotype, clinically meaningful functional outcomes, achievable systemic and brain exposure, acceptable safety and drug-interaction profiles, and reproducible formulation. Plant-derived compounds should therefore be viewed as potential adjuncts to established antiseizure, syndrome-specific, and gene-directed therapies rather than substitutes.

articles.title: A Digital Twin Framework for Multitarget Antibacterial Discovery in Chronic Wound Infections.
articles.abstract: Chronic wound infections are difficult to treat because they involve polymicrobial communities, biofilm-associated tolerance, impaired healing and repeated antimicrobial exposure. These factors promote persistence and antimicrobial resistance, while the development of new antibacterial agents remains costly and prone to failure. This review discusses a Digital Twin framework for supporting multitarget antibacterial discovery and formulation design in chronic wound infections. The proposed concept integrates microbiological and epidemiological data, bacterial target networks, structure-based screening of plant-derived metabolites, and formulation-dependent release prediction. Natural compounds are particularly relevant because many phytochemicals affect several bacterial processes, including membrane integrity, cell wall biosynthesis, DNA-related targets, quorum sensing, and biofilm formation. However, their use is often limited by poor solubility, low stability, and insufficient local exposure. Therefore, the framework also includes delivery-system engineering, such as electrospun fibres, polymeric nanoparticles, lipid-based carriers and controlled-release platforms. Machine learning models may then be used to link formulation descriptors with predicted release profiles and local antibacterial exposure. The practical output of the framework is a prioritised set of compound-target-carrier combinations. The proposed Digital Twin framework is conceptual and has not yet been experimentally validated; however, it may reduce empirical screening and support more rational selection of such combinations for chronic wound management.

articles.title: From Generative Biology to Evidence-Centric Drug Discovery.
articles.abstract: Generative and predictive artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly increasing the number of molecular, structural, cellular, and therapeutic hypotheses that can be explored computationally. Experimental capacity, however, has not expanded at a comparable rate. The result is an evidence bottleneck, in which biological hypotheses are generated faster than they can be experimentally tested, reproduced, and translated. This mismatch is particularly consequential for pharmaceutical discovery, where computational predictions alone cannot establish biological function, mechanism, or therapeutic value. As the number of computationally generated hypotheses grows, the central challenge shifts from candidate generation to the prioritization of hypotheses for experimental validation. This evidence bottleneck represents a defining constraint of AI-enabled biological discovery. We examine how different biological claims, including structural, interaction, functional, mechanistic, and therapeutic claims, require distinct types and levels of evidence. We also address the cost and context-dependence of experimental validation. Furthermore, we discuss how information-guided experimental design and iterative model-experiment feedback can improve the allocation of limited experimental capacity. We propose an evidence-centric framework for drug discovery that extends the evaluation of generative models beyond their ability to generate or rank hypotheses. The framework emphasizes experimental testability, mechanistic understanding, reproducibility, and translation into actionable biological and therapeutic knowledge.

articles.title: Therapeutic Repositioning of Antidiabetic Drugs in Dermatology: Biguanides, Incretin-Based Therapies, and PPARγ Agonists in Cutaneous Disease Processes.
articles.abstract: Metabolic regulation has emerged as a central determinant of skin homeostasis, connecting inflammation, barrier function, tissue repair, aging, fibrosis, and tumorigenesis through altered cellular bioenergetics and stress signaling. Three antidiabetic drug classes have consequently attracted interest as metabolic-targeting strategies in dermatology: biguanides, incretin-based therapies, and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) agonists. This review synthesizes the preclinical and emerging clinical literature for each class. We propose an evidence-informed, unvalidated framework that relates these classes to overlapping processes in skin pathology. Biguanides, chiefly metformin, act broadly on inflammatory and proliferative signaling, oxidative stress, and cutaneous tumor biology; their reported effects vary across experimental settings that differ in exposure and delivery. Incretin-based therapies, comprising glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, have been investigated in regenerative repair, particularly diabetic wound healing, angiogenesis, epithelialization, and, through DPP-4 (CD26) inhibition, antifibrotic dermal remodeling. PPARγ agonists are most closely tied to epidermal differentiation, barrier and lipid homeostasis, and suppression of fibroblast activation, with additional signals in inflammatory dermatoses, pigmentary disorders, and malignancy. In all three classes, local and topical delivery may influence efficacy, making formulation an important variable for translational evaluation. Because the evidence remains largely preclinical, heterogeneous, and rarely comparative, we propose that metabolic therapies be positioned according to the dominant biologic defect of each dermatologic condition (inflammatory or proliferative dysregulation, regenerative failure, or differentiation and fibrotic remodeling) rather than applied uniformly across skin disease.

articles.title: Beyond Conventional ALA-PDT: Strategies for Deeper, Faster, and More Efficient Treatment of Non-Melanoma Skin Cancer.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) using 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and its derivatives is an established non-surgical approach for non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC), particularly basal cell carcinoma (BCC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in situ, and premalignant lesions such as actinic keratosis. Despite favorable cosmetic outcomes and its ability to treat field cancerization, conventional topical ALA-PDT is better suited to superficial lesions because of limited precursor penetration, heterogeneous protoporphyrin IX (PpIX) accumulation, and insufficient light delivery to deeper tissue layers. This review critically examines the biological and physical barriers that limit ALA-based PDT efficacy in NMSC and discusses emerging multimodal strategies to address these challenges. Methods: This review examines the biological and physical factors that limit topical ALA-based PDT, drawing on current knowledge of heme biosynthesis, mitochondrial regulation of PpIX accumulation, skin optical properties, and oxygen dependence. It also highlights near-infrared photobiomodulation (PBM) and microneedle-assisted ALA delivery as complementary strategies that may help overcome these barriers. Results: Near-infrared PBM is a promising adjunct: in cell culture and exploratory human skin studies, it modulates endogenous PpIX production. Whether this translates into greater photosensitizer availability at depth, shorter incubation, or reduced treatment-related pain in NMSC remains hypothetical and untested clinically. Concurrently, dissolving microneedle arrays (MAs) have shown enhanced intradermal ALA delivery and increased PpIX accumulation and distribution in preclinical studies. These are independent strategies that address distinct barriers within the PDT pathway and may be combined to maximize therapeutic response. Conclusions: Overcoming the depth and delivery limitations of conventional ALA-PDT may be approached by improving precursor delivery, photosensitizer generation, and efficient irradiation. Near-infrared PBM and microneedle-assisted drug delivery are separate, mechanistically grounded strategies that could extend PDT efficacy to thicker, more challenging NMSC lesions; whether they also improve patient tolerability remains to be established. Future translational and clinical studies should prioritize optimizing these protocols and validating their impact on long-term PDT response, recurrence rates, and patient-reported outcomes.

articles.title: Formulation optimization and in vitro/vivo evaluation of dexmedetomidine hydrochloride sublingual films prepared by hot-melt extrusion technology.
articles.abstract: Dexmedetomidine hydrochloride (DEX) is a highly selective α2-adrenergic receptor agonist used for sedation, anxiolysis, and analgesia. Its oral use is limited by extensive first-pass metabolism and low bioavailability. This study developed a hot-melt extruded dexmedetomidine hydrochloride sublingual film (DEX-SF) and optimized its formulation using design of experiments (DoE). Hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC), polyoxyethylene (PEO), tocopheryl polyethylene glycol succinate (TPGS), and neotame were screened to balance mechanical strength, rapid release, wettability, and taste-masking performance. The optimized film contained 0.6%DEX, 59.3% PEO, 35% HPC, 5% TPGS, and 0.1% neotame. It showed a uniform semi-transparent appearance, consistent drug content, suitable mechanical properties, and rapid in vitro release, with approximately 89% DEX released within 15 min. In male Beagle dogs, DEX-SF achieved a mean absolute bioavailability of 65.37 ± 24.46%, compared with 40.45 ± 12.73% for the marketed sublingual film Igalmi®. This difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.092), but DEX-SF showed a shorter and less variable Tmax (0.71 ± 0.10 h). Repeated sublingual administration for 14 days caused no visible ulceration or marked histological injury in male guinea pig oral mucosa. These findings support the feasibility of HME as a scalable manufacturing approach for DEX sublingual films and provide a preclinical basis for further formulation optimization and clinical evaluation.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence for pharmacokinetic drug-drug interaction assessment: from promise to practice.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI) is highly prominent in computational drug-drug interaction (DDI) research, yet adoption in real development and regulatory workflows lags publication volume. This gap reflects a mismatch between benchmark-driven method development and the decisions that DDI assessment supports. AREAS COVERED: We synthesize the AI methodology landscape - from shallow learning to large language models - and integrate it with physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling, static models, and regulatory guidance (ICH M12); the literature was identified via structured PubMed/MEDLINE searches (2012-2026, prioritizing 2018-2026). We propose a task-, stage-, and mechanism-specific framework in which pharmacokinetic (PK) change is an upstream surrogate whose clinical relevance is set by downstream pharmacodynamic and adverse-event outcomes. EXPERT OPINION: AI's practical strengths now lie in triage, parameter priors, and workflow acceleration rather than replacing mechanistic reasoning. Two caveats merit emphasis: large language models must not serve as standalone DDI prediction engines, and retrospective benchmark accuracy is no substitute for prospective, decision-oriented validation. The field should move from model novelty to fit-for-purpose, non-leaky benchmarks; interaction-strength-dependent, calibration-based evaluation; decomposed uncertainty; and prospective workflow-embedded validation.

articles.title: The future of stroke care in Egypt: a recovery-oriented perspective from acute reperfusion to long-term rehabilitation.
articles.abstract: Stroke remains a major cause of mortality and long-term disability in Egypt. Over the past decade, Egypt has made important progress through the expansion of stroke units, intravenous thrombolysis, and endovascular thrombectomy services. However, many patients still arrive outside therapeutic windows, lack access to comprehensive stroke pathways, or experience persistent neurological, cognitive, language, and psychosocial disability after the acute phase. This Perspective argues that the next stage of stroke-care development in Egypt should be recovery-oriented rather than reperfusion-limited. Key priorities include equitable hub-and-spoke stroke networks, workforce development, emergency medical services pre-notification, streamlined imaging pathways, expanded multidisciplinary rehabilitation, digital follow-up, and national quality-monitoring systems. Because ischemic stroke involves excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, inflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, impaired neuroplasticity, and network-level reorganization, adjunctive multimodal pharmacological strategies may complement reperfusion and rehabilitation in selected patients. Cerebrolysin is discussed as one example of an adjunctive neurorecovery therapy. A coordinated national strategy that integrates acute treatment, rehabilitation, quality improvement, and evidence-based recovery support may help reduce post-stroke disability and improve long-term outcomes for stroke survivors in Egypt.

articles.title: A reproducibility-audited, gate-based framework for early translational pharmacology: native-scale evidence, identifiability, and a 12-domain reporting checklist.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Early translational pharmacology often combines docking scores, machine-learning structure predictions, and physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations as if they formed a single evidentiary scale. This can create precise-looking but uncalibrated biological and clinical claims. METHODS: We applied a four-class provenance framework to the deposited erinacine A package. Vina records were re-executed where complete inputs existed; DiffDock-L and Boltz-2 outputs were audited on their native scales; PBPK project identity, executable content, and exported profiles were inspected; and conditional free-CNS calculations were recomputed over joint fu × Kp,uu,brain assumptions. A prospective G0-G8 gate-based decision architecture was then specified, separating identity control, decoy topology, docking, replicated MD, direct biophysical binding to purified molecular targets under assay conditions, optional mechanistic QM/MM analysis, unbound exposure, and pharmacodynamics. Erinacine A serves as a worked example and stress test of the framework rather than as evidence of validated molecular efficacy. RESULTS: The archived 8TKL value of -3.221 was compatible with more than one scoring/receptor footing and therefore had no unique recoverable origin. The direct 31-heavy-atom RMSD between archived and re-executed poses was 3.974 Å. All three complete Vina re-executions failed the prespecified protocol-specific 5 Å geometric adequacy rule. DiffDock top poses retained steric conflicts, and Vina versus Boltz-2 showed no global rank concordance (ρ = 0.00, exact p = 1.00). The deposited PK-Sim files encoded a human individual, not porcine physiology, and lacked the observed calibration dataset and a populated compound-reaction block; their numerical exports were internally reproducible but were not qualified as a pig PBPK reconstruction. Conditional CNS-band attainment ranged from 0% to 80.2%, whereas lower-bound attainment ranged from 0% to 100% across versioned sensitivity anchors. CONCLUSION: The transferable result is a gate-based governance protocol for translational computational evidence, combining provenance classification, native-scale constraints, structural-identifiability controls, and prespecified resource-allocation decisions. It preserves negative findings and missing provenance. The deposited outputs support prioritization and falsification tests, not proof of affinity, target engagement, porcine or human exposure, efficacy, formulation viability or clinical dosing. Progression through the prospective decision architecture requires a distinct evidentiary pass at each gate.
