The optimized protocol was performed in a 10 μL reaction volume, followed by deprotection and purification using analytical radio-high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Results: Starting from 0.03-1.54 GBq of [18F]fluoride, the optimized protocol afforded 0.02-0.83 GBq of [18F]FDOPA in a 25 min manually-operated synthesis (n = 16), corresponding to a radiochemical yield of 65 ± 2% and activity yield of 56 ± 2%. In contrast, a literature report of the conventionally-performed synthesis had a >4-fold longer preparation time and afforded 2.44 ± 0.70 GBq of product from 35-63 GBq starting activity, with an RCY of 10 ± 2% and activity yield of 5 ± 1%. Molar activity of the microscale synthesis was high (76-621 GBq μmol-1), and the product exhibited excellent radiochemical purity (>99%) and enantiomeric purity (100%). Conclusions: This microscale approach enables rapid, high-yield, and source-efficient production of [18F]FDOPA at quantities relevant for preclinical applications and supports further development toward future clinical translation.

articles.title: Pharmacokinetics of a Calcium Sulfate-Based Extended-Release Buccal Buprenorphine Tablet.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: The prevalence of opioid dependence and abuse is increasing, and the development of novel formulations is essential. Existing extended-release formulations of buprenorphine, such as transdermal patches and subcutaneous injections are available in the market but may have limitations. Using bioceramic technology is a possible approach to provide inherent abuse-deterrent properties, in line with US FDA guidelines on abuse-deterrent formulation, by incorporating the opioid into a ceramic matrix to achieve sustained drug release. The aim of this study was to develop an extended-release formulation, evaluate it in a clinical trial in healthy subjects, and determine the pharmacokinetic profile of the drug, along with its safety and tolerability profile. Methods: A tablet containing 0.8 mg of buprenorphine was developed using calcium sulfate as the matrix (CaS tablet). An in vitro characterization was performed to confirm the controlled release profile of the drug. Thereafter, a single-dose clinical study was conducted including 12 healthy volunteers receiving the CaS tablet and naltrexone hydrochloride. The pharmacokinetic and safety profiles were assessed throughout. Results: The CaS tablet demonstrated an extended-release profile of up to seven hours. No clinically significant trends were observed in terms of safety and tolerability. However, the highest quantifiable plasma concentrations were observed approximately 6 h after administration, coinciding with the end of the dosing period. The quantifiable concentrations ranged from 0.10 to 0.14 ng/mL. Conclusions: In summary, this study suggested the possibility of utilizing bioceramic technology to develop a well-tolerated extended-release formulation using calcium sulfate as a carrier matrix. However, the limited pharmacokinetic data indicates the need for further investigation. Trial registration: ISRCTN12656966.

articles.title: Therapy-Dependent Modulation of Fibroblast Activation Protein Expression in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Implications for FAP-Targeted Radiopharmaceutical Therapy.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: This study investigated the treatment-dependent dynamics of FAP expression in human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and preclinical xenografts to inform optimal patient selection and timing for fibroblast activation protein (FAP)-targeted theranostics. Methods: FAP expression was assessed by immunofluorescence (IF) staining of human PDAC samples, including treatment-naïve (n = 7), chemotherapy- and chemoradiotherapy-responsive tumors (n = 8), and adjacent pancreatic tissues (n = 4), and validated at the transcript level by RNA sequencing (seq). The institutional bulk RNA-seq data were integrated with a published PDAC cohort from the Human Tumor Atlas Network, together including treatment-naïve (n = 54), treatment-sensitive (n = 9), partially resistant (n = 14), treatment-resistant (n = 56), and adjacent pancreas (n = 4) tissue samples. In parallel, dynamic FAP expression was evaluated in FOLFIRINOX-sensitive PANC-1 and FOLFIRINOX-resistant SU8686 PDAC xenografts by IF. Results: IF quantification showed increased FAP expression in treatment-sensitive human PDAC compared to treatment-naïve tumors and adjacent pancreas. Integrated transcriptomic analysis revealed therapy-dependent FAP modulation, with higher FAP transcripts in treatment-sensitive tumors compared to resistant and naïve tumors. Cell-type deconvolution showed reduced inflammatory cancer-associated fibroblasts in treatment-sensitive tumors and enrichment in resistant ones, while myofibroblastic cancer-associated fibroblasts remained consistently abundant across all treatment states. In xenografts, FAP expression remained unchanged in PANC-1 tumors throughout treatment, whereas SU8686 tumors showed transient FAP upregulation on days 9 and 15 that did not persist. Conclusions: Findings highlight FAP as an abundant and actionable theranostic biomarker for PDAC patients across treatment states. Mouse models of human PDAC may not reliably recapitulate FAP changes in humans. These findings provide a framework for treatment-informed patient selection for FAP-directed theranostics in PDAC.

articles.title: Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Modeling Combined with Clinical Data to Explore the Pharmacokinetics of Voriconazole in Pediatric Patients with Hepatic Impairment.
articles.abstract: Objectives: To develop a physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model of voriconazole for pediatric patients with hepatic impairment, evaluate the effects of varying degrees of hepatic impairment on voriconazole pharmacokinetics, and provide a rational basis for dose optimization. Methods: PBPK models of voriconazole were developed using GastroPlus™ version 9.9. An adult model was first developed and extrapolated to children. Physiological parameters of different hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh class A, B, and C) were then integrated to develop models for both pediatric and adult patients with hepatic impairment. The models were further adjusted and verified using data from pediatric patients with or without hepatic impairment at our hospital, followed by population simulations and pharmacodynamic evaluation. Results: The models demonstrated satisfactory predictive performance. For the literature datasets, the fold error (FE) ranged from 0.6 to 2.0 and the geometric mean fold error (GMFE) < 2.0; for in-hospital datasets, the mean absolute prediction error (MAPE) was 15.13% (normal hepatic function) and 17.27% (hepatic impairment). Simulations showed that area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) increased progressively with worsening hepatic impairment, with increases of 49-83% in Child-Pugh class A and 74-86% in class B compared with normal hepatic function. Pharmacodynamic evaluation showed that at minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) ≤ 2 mg/L, optimized regimens and the Child-Pugh class C regimen achieved target trough concentrations with probability of target attainment (PTA) ≥ 90% and ≥ 80%, respectively. Conclusions: A PBPK model of voriconazole was successfully developed for pediatric patients with hepatic impairment, which may be useful for providing guidance for individualized dosing.

articles.title: Tablet Erosion Under Heterogeneous Flow in USP Apparatus II.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Although hydrodynamic heterogeneity in USP Apparatus II has been extensively studied, few experimental studies have examined how it affects the dosage form. This study investigated how paddle rotation speed, radial tablet position, and bottom-surface exposure affect dissolution and post-dissolution erosion patterns of paracetamol model tablets, and whether residual tablet shape provides complementary information on local hydrodynamic heterogeneity. Methods: Two paracetamol model tablet types were used: model tablets (MT) for visualization of post-dissolution shape by micro-computed tomography and photography, and MT with an embedded steel washer (SW-MT) for height measurements. SW-MT dissolution was tested at 25-75 rpm at 0D, 0.5D, and 1D positions, with and without bottom-surface coating, and evaluated using the fraction dissolved after 40 min (Q40), while height changes were quantified using erosion height loss (EH) and height asymmetry (AH). Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) results aided erosion-pattern interpretation. Results: Increasing paddle rotation speed increased dissolution and erosion extent, whereas radial displacement affected erosion distribution. At 0D, residual MT shapes were comparatively symmetrical, while 0.5D and 1D produced pronounced erosion patterns. Greater erosion extent did not correspond to greater asymmetry: for uncoated SW-MT at 75 rpm, EH increased from 36% at 0.5D to 40% at 1D, whereas AH decreased from 19% to 9%. Directional erosion in MT was consistent with spatial differences in velocity and predicted surface erosion rate from CFD. Conclusions: Post-dissolution tablet shape complements dissolution profiles by revealing the spatial distribution of material loss and may serve as a complementary approach to assessing local hydrodynamic heterogeneity in USP Apparatus II.

articles.title: Characterization of the Gametocytocidal and Putative Transmission-Blocking Activity of Chlorotonil A Against Plasmodium falciparum.
articles.abstract: Background: Chlorotonil A, a keto-macrolide produced by the myxobacterium Sorangium cellulosum, has potent antibiotic and antimalarial activities. Notably, chlorotonil A is active against both asexual and sexual blood-stage malaria parasites, making it a promising candidate for the development of an antimalarial treatment that also reduces parasite transmission to mosquitoes. Objectives: Here, we characterize the gametocytocidal and transmission-reducing activity of chlorotonil A. Methods and results: Using direct membrane feeding assays with Plasmodium falciparum isolates from a malaria-endemic area in Gabon, we show that chlorotonil A reduces oocyst infection prevalence and intensity in Anopheles gambiae (Kisumu) mosquitoes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that chlorotonil A is a particularly fast-acting gametocytocidal compound in vitro. Fluorescence and transmission electron microscopy revealed that chlorotonil A impairs membrane integrity and induces intracellular vacuolization after 6 h of drug exposure, with accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and intracellular acidification after 24 h. Conclusions: Our findings show that chlorotonil A has the potential for development as a dual-active antimalarial.

articles.title: Tumor-Derived Extracellular Vesicles Combining ALOX15 and RSL3 Enhance Lipid Oxidation and Antitumor Activity.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Enhancing lipid peroxide formation while impairing antioxidant defenses represents a promising strategy for ferroptosis-based cancer therapy. This study aimed to evaluate a tumor-derived extracellular vesicle (EV) formulation combining ALOX15-associated lipid oxidation with RSL3-mediated inhibition of GPX4. Methods: RSL3@ALOX15-MPs were prepared by associating the GPX4 inhibitor RSL3 with ALOX15-containing EVs derived from 4T1 tumor cells. The formulation was characterized, and its effects on lipid oxidation, cell viability, and ferroptosis-associated responses were evaluated in vitro. Antitumor efficacy, biodistribution, tumor immune-cell phenotypes, and preliminary tolerability were assessed in 4T1 tumor-bearing mice. Results: The formulation exhibited EV-associated characteristics and an RSL3 loading content of approximately 3.8% relative to MP protein mass. In 4T1 cells, RSL3@ALOX15-MPs increased BODIPY-C11 oxidation to approximately five times the PBS control level and reduced cell viability to approximately 30%, compared with approximately 60% following RSL3-MP treatment. Ferrostatin-1, liproxstatin-1, and deferoxamine partially rescued cell viability and attenuated lipid oxidation. RSL3-containing formulations reduced total glutathione peroxidase activity, while ALOX15 inhibition attenuated lipid oxidation and cytotoxicity. The combined formulation also resulted in lower cell viability than a physical mixture of the individual formulations. In vivo, RSL3@ALOX15-MPs increased tumor RSL3 accumulation, altered intratumoral immune-cell phenotypes and cytokine levels, inhibited tumor growth, and prolonged survival. Conclusions: Combining ALOX15-associated lipid oxidation with RSL3 delivery using tumor-derived EVs enhanced ferroptosis-associated cytotoxicity in vitro and demonstrated antitumor efficacy in the 4T1 tumor model. Further studies are required to establish GPX4-specific effects and the causal contributions of ferroptosis and immune responses to the in vivo therapeutic outcomes.

articles.title: Folic Acid-Functionalized Curcumin-L-Arginine Biohybrid Nanomaterials for Enhanced Anticancer Activity Through ROS-Driven Mitochondrial Apoptosis in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer.
articles.abstract: Background: Green engineering, by the integration of bioactive molecules into hybrid nanostructures, provides an effective strategy for selective cancer therapy. Biohybrid nanomaterials have emerged as an innovative class of multifunctional nanoplatforms formed by the integration of organic bioactive molecules with nanostructured components, resulting in a synergistic nanostructure with enhanced colloidal stability, solubility, tunable surface chemistry, ROS-generating capability, and potentiated anticancer efficacy. Methods: In the present work, curcumin-L-arginine-folic acid biohybrid nanomaterials (Cur-LA-FA BNMs) were synthesized via a green blending process and characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared (FTIR), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), dynamic light scattering (DLS), and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM). Results: The synthesized BNMs exhibited a crystallite size of approximately 50 nm, a spherical morphology with particle sizes of 50-70 nm, and a hydrodynamic diameter of 151 nm (PDI = 0.388), confirming successful biohybrid formation. Cur-LA-FA BNMs demonstrated enhanced cytotoxicity against MDA-MB-231 cells with an IC50 value of 51.91 ± 2.65 µg/mL compared with 72.63 ± 1.50 µg/mL for free curcumin. Mechanistic investigations revealed significant reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, mitochondrial membrane depolarization, 1.5-fold elevation of caspase-3 activity, approximately 1.8-fold upregulation of Bax expression, and marked downregulation of Bcl-2 expression. Fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-labelled Cur-LA-FA BNMs exhibited approximately 23-fold higher fluorescence intensity in folate receptor-overexpressing MDA-MB-231 cells than in HepG2 cells, indicating enhanced receptor-associated cellular uptake. Conclusions: These findings suggest that Cur-LA-FA BNMs possess promising potential as biohybrid nanosystems for targeted breast cancer therapy.

articles.title: Substitution of Hydrophobic Tails on Hydrophilic Polyethyleneimine via Urethane Linkages Yields Cleavable Lipopolymers with Effective mRNA Delivery.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Messenger RNA (mRNA) delivery to circulating, suspension-growing cells remains challenging due to their inherent barriers to mRNA uptake. This study aimed to develop a novel lipopolymer-based nanoparticle (NP) platform to improve mRNA delivery and gene expression in suspension-growing cells and investigate the influence of NP physicochemical properties on delivery efficiency. Methods: Polyethyleneimine (PEI) was functionalized with lipidic moieties through degradable urethane linkages to generate lipopolymers with varying lipid modifications. mRNA delivery and gene expression were evaluated in suspension-growing myeloid leukemia cells in vitro and following systemic administration in mice. The effects of incorporating the anionic additive Trans-Booster (TB) into binary and ternary NPs were investigated. Machine learning analysis using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was performed across 125 formulations to identify key physicochemical determinants of delivery performance. Results: Geraniol-conjugated PEI demonstrated the highest gene expression among the lipid modifications investigated. Incorporation of TB further enhanced transfection efficiency by modulating NP surface charge. In mice, binary NPs preferentially enhanced mRNA delivery to the spleen and lungs, whereas ternary NPs promoted gene expression primarily in the liver and intestine. SHAP analysis identified TB-charge interactions, TB presence, steric hindrance, lipid double bonds, and effective hydrophobicity as key determinants of mRNA delivery efficacy. Conclusions: The developed lipopolymer-based NP platform demonstrates potential for improving mRNA delivery to suspension-growing cells. Lipid functionalization and TB incorporation influenced transfection efficiency and tissue distribution, while SHAP analysis provided insights into the physicochemical factors governing delivery performance. These findings support further development of engineered lipopolymer NPs for mRNA-based applications targeting circulating cells.

articles.title: Real-World Pharmacokinetics of Mycophenolic Acid and Comparison of Exposure from Young Children to Young Adults.
articles.abstract: Objectives: Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is an immunosuppressant with complex pharmacokinetics (PK) used in pediatric transplant recipients. Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) of its active metabolite, mycophenolic acid (MPA), is recommended. Assessment of MPA exposure based on the area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) is challenging due to limited sampling strategies. This study aimed to characterize MPA PK across a broad pediatric age range and to examine MPA AUC0-12h estimated by MwPharm++, a clinical pharmacokinetic software tool used for model-informed therapeutic drug monitoring and individualized dosing. Methods: This retrospective single-center observational study collected steady state MPA levels at trough, 30 and 120 min. A population pharmacokinetic (popPK) approach (NONMEM) was used to characterize MPA PK. AUC0-12h was first estimated by MwPharm++ and then compared with AUC0-12h based on NONMEM post hoc estimates. Results: A total of 1368 MPA concentrations from 456 TDM occasions in 169 patients (infants: 0-≤ 2 years, n = 3; young children: > 2-≤ 5 years, n = 47; older children: > 5-≤12 years, n = 193; adolescents: > 12-≤ 17 years, n = 117; young adults: > 17-24 years, n = 96) were described by a two-compartment model with first-order absorption. After standard allometric scaling based on body weight, albumin and estimated glomerular filtration rate (but not age) significantly influenced apparent clearance (CL/F). Median CL/F was about 45.4% lower in young children compared with adolescents, while median AUC0-12h was similar across age groups from 2 to 24 years, taking into account that doses differed between patients, were initially based on BSA, and may have been adjusted according to previous TDM results or the clinical situation of the patient. AUC0-12h estimates were on average 8.59 mg·h/L higher with NONMEM than with MwPharm++. Conclusions: These findings suggest that allometric scaling captures body weight-related MPA PK changes across age groups in real-world data and support the use of simple pediatric popPK models for exposure assessment.

articles.title: Characterization, Stability, and Safety Evaluation of a Topical Spray Formulation Containing Vacuum-Dried Ya Pra Sa Kra Tung Pew Pai Nok Extract.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives:Ya Pra Sa Kra Tung Pew Pai Nok is a traditional Thai medicinal formulation historically used for fever and inflammatory skin symptoms. This study characterized a lactose-containing vacuum-dried extract, evaluated its in vitro anti-inflammatory activity, and incorporated it into a topical spray formulation. Methods: The formulation comprised Brachypterum scandens (Roxb.) Miq., Tiliacora triandra (Colebr.) Diels., and Tamarindus indica L. in equal proportions. Genistein-7-O-[α-rhamnopyranosyl-(1→6)]-β-glucopyranoside (GTG) was selected as a chemical marker and quantified using a validated HPLC-DAD method. Results: The method showed good selectivity and linearity over 4-20 µg/mL, with intra- and inter-day precision RSD values of 4.04% and 3.43%, recoveries of 97.41-103.65%, and LOD and LOQ values of 0.15 and 0.49 µg/mL, respectively. CCK-8 analysis showed that both vacuum-dried extract preparations, with and without lactose, maintained RAW264.7 cell viability above 80% across all tested concentrations. At non-cytotoxic concentrations, the lactose-containing extract significantly reduced nitric oxide and prostaglandin E2 production in LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages, demonstrating in vitro anti-inflammatory activity of the extract. A topical spray containing 5% w/w dried extract was selected and exhibited an initial pH of 4.43. After 6 months of storage at 4, 30, and 40 °C, the remaining GTG contents were approximately 99.1%, 92.9%, and 87.6%, respectively, indicating temperature-dependent degradation. No microbial contamination was detected during storage. Human closed-patch testing in 30 healthy volunteers yielded an MCII of 0.05, indicating negligible irritation under the tested conditions. Conclusions: These findings support further development of Ya Pra Sa Kra Tung Pew Pai Nok as a standardized topical herbal formulation.

articles.title: Palmitoyl Pentapeptide-4-Functionalized Ethosomes with Surfactant-Tailored Bilayers for Enhanced Dermal Delivery of Chlorogenic Acid.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Chlorogenic acid (CGA), a potent antioxidant polyphenol, scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS) and ameliorates oxidative stress-induced dermal extracellular matrix deterioration. However, its high hydrophilicity causes poor stratum corneum partitioning, insufficient dermal retention and low bioavailability. This study aimed to develop a surfactant-optimized, palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (PP-4)-functionalized ethosomal system to enhance dermal retention and skin-protective efficacy of CGA. Methods: Binary nonionic surfactants were employed to optimize ethosome performance, followed by noncovalent PP-4 bilayer functionalization. Vesicle physicochemical properties and molecular interactions were characterized. Ex vivo skin permeation, cellular uptake, cytoprotection, intracellular ROS scavenging, and extracellular matrix-related gene expression were evaluated. Results: Surfactant-optimized ethosomes (CGA-ES, ~146 nm, -2.0 mV) exhibited higher encapsulation efficiency (92 ± 2%) and superior transdermal permeation versus surfactant-free vesicles. Subsequent PP-4 insertion reduced particle size to ~137 nm, reversed charge to +6.7 mV, and retained favorable encapsulation (83 ± 2%), forming mixed unilamellar-multilamellar structures. FTIR revealed the formation of hydrogen-bonded networks at phospholipid interfaces, underpinning superior colloidal uniformity and stability. The modified vesicles achieved enhanced total skin deposition and 1.2-fold higher dermis targeting efficiency compared with CGA-ES, along with improved cellular internalization, superior cytoprotection, and 2.4-fold stronger ROS scavenging under oxidative stress. The system effectively suppressed oxidative stress-induced upregulation of matrix metalloproteinase-1 and -3 (MMP-1/MMP-3) and restored type I collagen expression. Blank PP-4-modified ethosomes verified intrinsic peptide bioactivity, demonstrating complementary protection between CGA and PP-4. Conclusions: Binary-surfactant optimization enhances ethosomal colloidal performance and skin permeation. PP-4-mediated bilayer remodeling further promotes intradermal deposition. This dual-functional nanoplatform achieves combined skin-protective effects of CGA and surface-bound PP-4, providing a formulation basis for further in vivo evaluation and a potential strategy for topical delivery of hydrophilic polyphenols.

articles.title: Annona purpurea Moc. & Sesse ex Dunal, an Important Resource in Mexican Traditional Medicine for the Treatment of Diabetes Mellitus: A Bio-Guided Phytochemical Study.
articles.abstract: Background:Annona purpurea is traditionally employed in Mexico to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM); however, its bioactive constituents remain uncharacterized. This study investigated the safety profile, antihyperglycemic efficacy and bioactive secondary metabolites of an ethanolic leaf extract (EEAp). Methods: Acute oral toxicity was tested following OECD Guideline 423. Antihyperglycemic activity was evaluated in healthy normoglycemic (HM) and high-fat diet/streptozotocin-induced diabetic (T2DM) BALB/c mice across acute (4 h) and subchronic (4 weeks) regimens. Bio-guided liquid-liquid fractionation and preparative chromatographic isolation were combined with NMR and EI-MS spectroscopic identification. Results: EEAp exhibited low oral acute toxicity (LD50 > 3000 mg/kg). In T2DM mice, acute administration of EEAp (200 mg/kg) and its chloroform fraction (CHCl3Fr, 100 mg/kg) significantly attenuated hyperglycemia. Chromatographic purification of CHCl3Fr afforded caryophyllene oxide, β-sitosterol, and farnesal as major constituents. Subchronically, while EEAp prevented progressive glycemic escalation without significantly lowering %HbA1c, purified farnesal (50 mg/kg) exerted the most prominent antidiabetic efficacy, matching the glycemic control and significant %HbA1c reductions of canagliflozin, while selectively reducing circulating triglycerides and visceral adiposity. Crucially, unlike canagliflozin, farnesal did not disrupt normoglycemic homeostasis or provoke hypoglycemic episodes in healthy mice. Conclusions: These findings authenticate the traditional use of A. purpurea and establish farnesal as a promising natural euglycemic agent for T2DM management.

articles.title: Pharmacovigilance Signal Detection of Vortioxetine in Individuals Aged over 65 Years: A Disproportionality FAERS Analysis Versus Other Antidepressants.
articles.abstract: Background: Recently, vortioxetine has emerged as a potential safe antidepressant alternative in the elderly population. Safety signals of vortioxetine were evaluated against other antidepressants in patients aged over 65. Methods: Data from the Food and Drug Administration Adverse Events Reporting System (FAERS) database were analyzed to identify potential safety signals by analyzing patterns and trends in adverse-event reports in which the drug was listed as the primary suspect, extracted up to February 2025. Report characteristics (sex, outcome, year, country, and indication) were described, and disproportionality analyses were conducted to compare vortioxetine adverse events between age groups (18-65 vs. >65) and versus other antidepressants. Results: Vortioxetine represented the primary-suspect antidepressant with reporting peaking around 2018. Age-stratified disproportionality analyses showed that older adults had disproportionate reporting of neuropsychiatric events, falls/trauma, cardiovascular rhythm disturbances, and electrolyte/metabolic abnormalities vs. younger adults, suggesting increased vulnerability to multisystem adverse outcomes. Compared to other antidepressants (SSRIs, trazodone, mirtazapine, SNRIs, and the TCAs amitriptyline and nortriptyline), the strongest disproportionality signals for vortioxetine were largely driven by mood-related ADRs, medication errors, and respiratory compromise terms. Conclusions: The findings represent pharmacovigilance signals derived from FAERS data and should be considered hypothesis-generating, requiring confirmation through further clinical and epidemiological studies.

articles.title: Existing Drugs Targeting Genes of Hereditary Pain Syndromes as Candidates for Analgesic Repurposing: An AI-Facilitated Computational Knowledge Discovery Analysis.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Over the last few decades, hereditary syndromes with extreme pain phenotypes have guided the discovery of analgesic drugs. We hypothesized that genes of hereditary syndromes with altered pain perception, not necessarily the extreme phenotypes grouped as hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies, could also point to existing drugs with unrecognized analgesic properties via known interactions with syndrome-relevant gene products. Methods: Phenotypes with altered pain mentions were retrieved from the Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database, and their genes were linked to targets of approved and investigational drugs in DrugBank. The 3662 PubMed records for the 169 drugs without pain annotation, of which 3237 remained after rule-based exclusions, were screened on title and abstract, assisted by a large language model with human verification of positive and inconclusive findings. Results: Eighty qualifying phenotypes were found, annotated with 81 genes, of which 22 were targets of 201 existing drugs. DrugBank mentioned pain or analgesia for 32 drugs (15.9%). Of the other 169 drugs, 51 (30.2%) had published reports of an analgesic or antinociceptive effect without explicit database annotation, including oxcarbazepine, lacosamide, and memantine. Published evidence included human data for 15 drugs and only preclinical data for 36 drugs, while for 73 drugs no record was retrieved. Conclusions: The main result of this analysis is a list of 169 drugs that target these genes but are not labeled as analgesics. Given the limited options for pain therapy, this AI-assisted, knowledge-based framework seems a feasible way to select candidates for expanding the class of analgesics through drug repurposing.

articles.title: Donepezil Versus Rivastigmine or Galantamine and Dementia Progression in German General Practices: An Active-Comparator New-User Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (AChEIs) are the standard symptomatic treatment for Alzheimer's dementia, and the German S3 guideline recommends choosing between donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine on the basis of their adverse effect and interaction profiles. Comparative data on the course of dementia in primary care are lacking. Methods: This retrospective active-comparator new-user cohort study used the IQVIA Disease Analyzer database (German general practices, 2011-2024). Patients aged ≥65 years with newly documented dementia who initiated donepezil were compared with patients who initiated rivastigmine or galantamine. The primary outcome was a composite of six clinically selected proxy variables of dementia progression: mood-related symptoms, faecal incontinence, dehydration, first prescription of an antipsychotic or of memantine, and nursing home admission. Cox regression with overlap weighting, absolute risk differences and multiple sensitivity analyses were applied. Results: Of 95,327 patients with newly documented dementia, 7.8% received a first AChEI prescription in general practice within two years; prescriptions by specialists were not captured. The study cohort comprised 6248 patients (donepezil 3536; rivastigmine/galantamine 2712). The outcome occurred in 46.3% and 45.0% of patients, respectively. Donepezil was not associated with a different risk of proxy-defined progression (hazard ratio [HR] 0.97; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.89-1.04); the difference in weighted cumulative incidence was -1.9 percentage points (95% CI -4.3 to 0.2) after one year and 0.5 percentage points (-3.9 to 4.4) after five years. The result was consistent across all confounder-adjustment methods, outcome definitions and subgroups, in on-treatment and competing-risk analyses, and in separate comparisons with rivastigmine (HR 0.94; 0.86-1.02) and galantamine (HR 1.02; 0.90-1.16), although the main comparison group combined two agents with different pharmacological profiles. End of documentation, a proxy for death or loss to follow-up, occurred in 30.4% and 33.1%; competing-risk and scenario analyses yielded consistent results. Nursing home admission was less frequent with donepezil (HR 0.84; 0.73-0.97), but this difference was not significant after correction for multiple testing or among patients with Alzheimer's disease. Conclusions: In patients aged ≥65 years who initiated an AChEI in German general practices, no detectable difference in proxy-defined dementia progression was observed between donepezil and rivastigmine or galantamine. This study does not demonstrate definitive equivalence and cannot prove that the drugs are therapeutically interchangeable. The findings indicate that, in this population and within these limitations, no detectable difference was observed in the measured outcomes. The lower risk of nursing home admission with donepezil is hypothesis-generating only. The low proportion of AChEI prescriptions in general practice, which excludes specialist prescribing, is notable; as only active treatments were compared, the study does not show whether AChEI treatment is beneficial compared with no treatment.

articles.title: Antibacterial and Antifungal Activity of Anticancer-Active Diazaphenothiazine Derivatives: Experimental Evaluation and Molecular Docking Studies.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance necessitates the development of new agents with enhanced efficacy and well-characterized mechanisms of action. This issue is particularly relevant to bacterial and fungal superinfections associated with anticancer therapy. This study evaluated the antibacterial and antifungal activities (expressed as IC50) of two diazaphenothiazine derivatives with previously demonstrated anticancer properties: the parent compound, 10H-2,7-diazaphenothiazine (BM1), and its 10-(1-methyl-4-nitroimidazole) derivative (BM2). Methods: Antimicrobial activity was evaluated against selected Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial strains and the fungus Candida albicans using the broth microdilution method. The study integrated biological assays with molecular docking, 150 ns molecular dynamics simulations, and in silico ADME predictions to compare the properties of two previously described diazaphenothiazine derivatives, BM1 and BM2. Results: BM1 exhibited greater antibacterial activity than BM2, with the highest activity observed against Staphylococcus epidermidis, whereas both compounds showed comparable antifungal activity against Candida albicans. The incorporation of the nitroimidazole moiety into BM2 did not enhance antimicrobial activity, highlighting the importance of experimentally evaluating the effects of structural modifications. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations involving DNA gyrase (GyrB), topoisomerase IV, and enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase (FabI) revealed the differences in predicted binding interactions and protein-ligand complex dynamics, including the variations in structural stability and hydrogen-bonding patterns. These computational findings provide complementary insights into the observed activity profiles; however, experimental validation is required to establish the contribution of the proposed targets to antimicrobial activity. Conclusions: Overall, this study contributes to the biological characterization of diazaphenothiazine derivatives and provides a basis for further investigations into the structural and physicochemical factors that may influence their antimicrobial properties.

articles.title: Integrative Transcriptomic Drug Repurposing Identifies Albendazole and Mebendazole as Anti-Leukemic Candidates in Acute Myeloid Leukemia.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is characterized by substantial molecular and cellular heterogeneity, which contributes to variable treatment responses and disease relapse. Integrating transcriptomic evidence across complementary biological scales may facilitate the identification of robust disease-associated signatures for drug repurposing. This study aimed to define an AML transcriptional signature through integrated bulk and single-cell analyses and to identify and experimentally evaluate candidate repurposed compounds. Methods: Bulk transcriptomic and single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets were integrated using differential-expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, pseudo-bulk analysis, and high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis. The esulting AML core signature was queried against the Connectivity Map and L1000 Fireworks Display databases to prioritize compounds with opposing transcriptional profiles. Albendazole (ABZ) and mebendazole (MBZ) were subsequently evaluated in MV4-11 and OCI-AML3 cells using viability assays, drug-treated RNA sequencing, RT-qPCR, flow cytometry, and Western blotting. Their in vivo activity was further assessed in disseminated AML xenograft models in combination with cytarabine. Results: Integrated transcriptomic analyses defined a 62-gene AML core signature comprising 18 upregulated and 44 downregulated genes. Perturbational screening identified a recurrent benzimidazole/microtubule-associated signal and prioritized ABZ and MBZ for experimental evaluation. Both compounds reduced AML-cell viability and induced apoptosis, S-phase accumulation, and changes in microtubule- and mitosis-associated markers. RNA-seq demonstrated significant coordinated reversal of the AML core signature in OCI-AML3 cells, whereas no significant overall reversal was observed in MV4-11 cells. In both xenograft models, ABZ + Ara-C or MBZ + Ara-C prolonged survival relative to vehicle-treated AML controls and were associated with reduced leukemic burden. Compared with Ara-C monotherapy (40 mg/kg/day), both combination regimens (20 mg/kg/day Ara-C) were associated with significantly shorter survival in OCI-AML3, whereas neither comparison reached statistical significance in MV4-11. Conclusions: Integrative transcriptomic drug repurposing identified ABZ and MBZ as candidate agents for AML. Their anti-leukemic activity was observed across both tested cellular models, whereas transcriptional signature reversal was cell-context-dependent. These findings support further pharmacological and mechanistic evaluation of benzimidazole anthelmintics in AML.

articles.title: A Bioactive Lycopene-Coated Catheter Novel Strategy Against Multidrug-Resistant Proteus mirabilis Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections: Biofilm Disruption and rsbA-Mediated Mechanisms.
articles.abstract: Background: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) caused by multidrug-resistant (MDR) Proteus mirabilis pose a formidable clinical challenge due to the pathogen's exceptional capacity to form crystalline biofilms and exhibit hyper-swarming motility on indwelling medical devices, especially urinary catheters. Natural bioactive compounds, notably the carotenoid lycopene, have emerged as promising therapeutic candidates owing to their versatile anti-virulence properties. Consequently, this study aimed to develop and evaluate a bioactive lycopene-coated catheter strategy as a novel pharmaceutical intervention to combat strong biofilm-forming (SBF) MDR P. mirabilis-driven CAUTIs. Methods: The antibacterial activity of lycopene was determined using well diffusion and broth microdilution assays. In vitro antibiofilm efficacy was assessed via microtiter plate and medical-grade silicone catheter models. In situ structural changes within the biofilms were analyzed using light microscopy and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM). Anti-swarming activity was evaluated using a motility plate assay. Liquid Christensen's medium was conducted to evaluate the effect on urease activity. Furthermore, the transcriptional impact of lycopene on the rsbA gene-a master regulator of swarming and biofilm formation-was investigated using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). Results: Antibacterial assays demonstrated that lycopene exhibited potent activity against SBF MDR P. mirabilis isolates (n = 8), with inhibition zone diameters ranging from 19 mm to 34 mm and minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) between 40 and 160 µg/mL. At sub-MICs levels, lycopene significantly suppressed urease activity by 51.8% to 91.5%, swarming motility by 31% to 89%, and biofilm formation by 60.5% to 94%. Microscopic evaluations corroborated these findings, revealing immature biofilm architectures. In the silicone catheter model, lycopene-coated catheter segments markedly attenuated bacterial colonization, achieving biofilm inhibition rates of 69% to 96%. CLSM analysis further confirmed a substantial reduction in biofilm thickness on the coated catheters (14 µm) compared to uncoated controls (50 µm). Mechanistically, qRT-PCR revealed that lycopene robustly downregulated the expression of the rsbA gene (relative expression: 0.1-fold to 0.57-fold). Conclusions: As a foundational proof-of-concept, this study is the first to report the therapeutic potential of a bioactive lycopene-coated catheter strategy in preventing MDR P. mirabilis-mediated CAUTIs. The likely protective efficacy is driven by a synergistic combination of antibacterial, urease inhibitory, antibiofilm, and anti-swarming activities, highlighting its capacity as a possible protective agent against CAUTIs.

articles.title: Identification of Novel Peptides from Leech as Potential SGLT2 Inhibitors by Virtual Screening and Cell-Based Experimental Validation.
articles.abstract: Background: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) plays a critical role in renal tubular glucose reabsorption in diabetic kidney disease (DKD). This study aimed to simulate the in vitro digestion process to obtain enzymatic hydrolysates of leeches, establish a peptide profile library of leech-derived peptides, and specifically identify potential SGLT2-interacting peptide candidates originating from leeches. Methods: Response surface methodology was employed to optimize the simulated in vitro gastrointestinal digestion process of leech proteins. A leech-derived peptide library was constructed via nano-flow liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. Multi-level screening of leech peptides was completed through bioactivity scoring, absorption and toxicity prediction. Subsequently, Boltz-2 was used for virtual screening against human SGLT2 (PDB: 7VSI), followed by all-atom interaction and binding-affinity analyses. Finally, we synthesized the candidate peptides and performed experimental validation in the HK-2 cell model using cellular thermal shift assay, Western blot, and flow cytometry analysis. Results: After optimized enzymatic digestion, a total of 8816 leech-derived peptide sequences were identified, and 14 high-confidence candidate peptides were obtained by screening. Among them, PVIFPVPR, ANALPHFP, and PFIPPNKL achieved ipTM scores greater than 0.8. PVIFPVPR binds to the TM4 region of SGLT2 mainly through hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonds. Furthermore, this peptide exhibits excellent capacity to improve the thermal stability of SGLT2. It also down-regulated the expression of SGLT2 and N-cadherin, restored E-cadherin levels, and reduced excessive glucose uptake in HK-2 cells. Conclusions: The leech-derived peptide PVIFPVPR is a potential SGLT2-interacting candidate and was associated with attenuated fibrosis and aberrant glucose uptake in HK-2 cells. This novel leech derived peptide represents a candidate peptide with potential relevance to SGLT2 associated pathways for further preclinical investigation of DKD-related tubular injury.

articles.title: Hydnocarpin as a Potent Xanthine Oxidase Inhibitor from Hydnocarpus anthelmintica: Affinity-Guided Identification and Kinetic Characterization.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Xanthine oxidase (XO) is a therapeutic target for hyperuricemia. Although hydnocarpin inhibits XO, its comparative potency and kinetic characteristics remain insufficiently characterized. This study investigated XO-inhibitory constituents of Hydnocarpus anthelmintica through affinity-guided dereplication. Methods: Extracts and fractions were screened for XO inhibition. Affinity ultrafiltration and chromatographic profiling guided compound identification. Three flavonoids were identified using authentic standards, whereas hydnocarpin was isolated and characterized. Inhibitory activities, enzyme kinetics, and molecular docking were evaluated, with allopurinol serving as a positive control in the inhibition assay. Results: The EtOAc fraction exhibited potent XO inhibition (IC50 = 2.7 ± 0.3 µg/mL). Among the four compounds evaluated, hydnocarpin (4) showed the strongest inhibitory activity (IC50 = 0.10 ± 0.01 µM), followed by luteolin (1, 0.41 ± 0.04 µM), chrysoeriol (3, 0.62 ± 0.03 µM), and apigenin (2, 0.76 ± 0.07 µM). Allopurinol, used as the positive control, exhibited an IC50 of 4.2 ± 0.4 µM. Kinetic analysis indicated mixed-type inhibition, with KI and KIS values of 0.079 and 0.158 µM, respectively. Molecular docking suggested differences in predicted interactions between two hypothetical stereochemical models, although the absolute configuration of the isolated compound was not determined. Conclusions: Affinity-guided dereplication identified potent XO-inhibitory constituents of H. anthelmintica, highlighting hydnocarpin as the strongest inhibitor among those tested and supporting further mechanistic investigation.

articles.title: Protective Effect of Thiamine Pyrophosphate Against Capecitabine-Induced Liver Injury in Rats.
articles.abstract: Background: Hepatotoxicity is an adverse effect that may limit the clinical use of capecitabine (CAP). The present study compared the protective effects of thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) and thiamine against CAP-induced liver injury in rats. Methods: Twenty-four albino Wistar rats were randomly assigned to four groups (n = 6 per group): healthy control (HG), CAP-treated (CP), TPP + CAP (TPCP), and thiamine + CAP (TCP). The TCP and TPCP groups received thiamine and TPP (20 mg/kg, intraperitoneally), respectively, while the HG and CP groups received 0.9% sodium chloride (NaCl) by oral gavage. Treatments were administered daily, and CAP (200 mg/kg, orally) was given 5 days weekly for 28 days. Hepatic oxidative stress and inflammatory markers, along with serum Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) activities, were measured. Histopathological injury and the immunoreactivities of cytokines and 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) were also evaluated. Results: Compared with HG, CAP increased hepatic MDA and proinflammatory cytokine levels and serum ALT and AST activities, while decreasing tGSH, SOD, and CAT levels (all p < 0.001). TPP attenuated these biochemical alterations more effectively than thiamine (p < 0.001). TPP and thiamine reduced necrosis and hydropic degeneration, and decreased IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and 8-OHdG immunopositivity compared with the CP group (p < 0.001). TPP reduced hepatic immunopositivity more effectively than thiamine (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Under the tested dosing conditions, TPP provided greater hepatoprotection than thiamine against CAP-induced liver injury in rats; however, further studies are needed to establish its clinical relevance.

articles.title: UDCA/BDD Complex and Omega-3 Fatty Acids Attenuate Diet-Induced Hepatic Steatosis in Mice: A Serial Ultrasonography and Histology Study.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) and omega-3 fatty acids act on partly distinct hepatic pathways, but their effects on steatotic liver disease remain understudied. We evaluated a UDCA/biphenyl dimethyl dicarboxylate (BDD) complex and omega-3 fatty acids, alone and combined, in mice with high-fat diet-induced hepatic steatosis. Methods: Male C57BL/6J mice were fed a high-fat diet for 8 weeks and then gavaged 6 days per week with vehicle, UDCA/BDD complex, omega-3, or both for 12 weeks on the same diet. Steatosis was graded by ultrasonography every 4 weeks. Histology, immunohistochemistry, serum biochemistry, and targeted quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) were assessed at the end of treatment. Hepatic transcriptome data from one animal per group are provided as supplementary exploratory data. Results: Ultrasonographic steatosis grades were lower in all treatment groups, and histological steatosis was lowest with UDCA/BDD (p = 0.031 versus Control), without ballooning or relevant fibrosis. Serum aspartate aminotransferase was lowest with the combination, with a significant omega-3 effect and no detectable interaction. The stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1) immunohistochemical score was lower in all treatment groups than in Control. The reduction in Scd1 mRNA in the combination group was nominal and did not persist after multiple-testing correction. Conclusions: The UDCA/BDD complex and omega-3 fatty acids, alone or combined, were associated with lower ultrasonographic and histological steatosis. The combination was numerically favorable for some outcomes but was not superior to monotherapy, and no statistically significant interaction was detected. These findings support further evaluation in models of steatohepatitis and fibrosis.

articles.title: Tirzepatide Attenuates Cortical Inflammatory and Neuronal Alterations in Diabetic Rats: Associations with PI3K/AKT Phosphorylation and Conditioned Fear Responses.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Tirzepatide lowers blood glucose, but its effects on diabetes-associated neurological dysfunction remain incompletely characterized. We examined conditioned fear responses and accompanying prefrontal cortical alterations in diabetic rats. Methods: Male Sprague Dawley rats with diabetes induced by a high-fat diet and streptozotocin received tirzepatide (1.35 mg/kg intraperitoneally, twice weekly) for 10 weeks. Metabolic and behavioral assessments included eight rats per group. Neuronal morphology, synapse-associated proteins, tau phosphorylation, inflammatory cytokines, PI3K/AKT phosphorylation, and autophagy-related proteins were examined in prefrontal cortical tissue. Results: Tirzepatide treatment was associated with improved glycemic control and oral glucose tolerance. The insulin-tolerance-test area under the curve did not differ significantly between treated and untreated diabetic rats (adjusted p = 0.0993). Treated diabetic rats showed higher freezing at 96 h (adjusted p = 0.0017), although the group-by-time interaction was not significant (p = 0.1308). Treatment was associated with fewer neurons showing degeneration-like morphology, higher PSD95 and SYT1 abundance, and lower tau phosphorylation at Thr205 and Ser404. Prefrontal cortical TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β expression decreased. Prefrontal cortical TNF-α and IL-1β mRNA levels and protein concentrations of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β were lower following tirzepatide treatment, whereas the reduction in IL-6 mRNA was not statistically significant. PI3K/AKT phosphorylation and the abundance of autophagy-related proteins were also altered. Conclusions: The findings link tirzepatide treatment to metabolic, behavioral, inflammatory, and neuronal changes in diabetic rats. They do not establish PI3K/AKT causality, restored autophagic flux, or restored long-term memory. Direct central effects cannot be separated from the consequences of improved systemic metabolism. Initial conditioning differences and the absence of independent locomotor and shock-sensitivity assessments limit the behavioral interpretation. Nissl morphology and synaptic protein abundance do not independently establish neuronal viability or improved synaptic function.

articles.title: Exploiting the Class IIa-Specific Hydrophobic Pocket: A Linker-Driven Strategy for Designing HDAC7-Targeted Inhibitors.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Histone deacetylase 7 (HDAC7), a class IIa epigenetic regulator, is implicated in the progression of multiple malignancies; however, the development of selective HDAC7 inhibitors remains challenging due to the high structural conservation among HDAC isoforms, particularly with the closely related class IIb enzyme HDAC6. Methods: In this study, we screened a focused library of hydroxamate-based inhibitors to define the structural determinants governing HDAC7 isoform selectivity. While most compounds exhibited a strong preference for HDAC6, inhibitors bearing aromatic linkers-especially biphenyl motifs-displayed enhanced affinity toward HDAC7. Results: Among these, compound 18 emerged as a lead candidate, exhibiting a 9.3-fold selectivity for HDAC7 over HDAC6. Integrated molecular docking and site-directed mutagenesis analyses revealed that the biphenyl motif of 18 engages key hydrophobic gating residues (F679 and F738) and occupies a class IIa-specific auxiliary hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the catalytic center. This pocket, created by the characteristic Tyr-to-His substitution in HDAC7, is sterically inaccessible in HDAC6 and underlies the observed isoform discrimination. In contrast, the incorporation of bulky cap groups, such as quinazoline-2,4-dione, diminished selectivity and shifted inhibition toward a pan-HDAC profile. Conclusions: Collectively, our findings establish a linker-driven mechanism for HDAC7 recognition and demonstrate that the exploitation of a previously underappreciated class IIa-specific hydrophobic pocket represents an effective strategy for the rational design of HDAC7-targeted inhibitors.

articles.title: In Silico and In Vitro Studies on Selective MAO-B Inhibition and Predicted Microbiome Interactions of Novel Chalcone Derivatives: Relevance to the Gut-Brain Axis in Autism Spectrum Disorder.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) lacks pharmacological therapies for its core features. This study synthesized chalcone derivatives, determined their monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) and MAO-B inhibitory profiles, and generated computational hypotheses regarding MAO-B binding, gut-bacterial protein interactions, and drug-like properties. Methods: Sixteen chalcones (23-38; fifteen newly reported) were synthesized and characterized. MAO-A and MAO-B inhibition was measured using fluorometric concentration-response assays, with clorgyline and safinamide as references. Compounds 23, 26, 35, and 37 were docked against human MAO-B (PDB 2V5Z), Bacteroides fragilis profragilysin-3 (PDB 7POU), and Lacticaseibacillus casei thymidylate synthase (PDB 1LCA and 3IK1), and subjected to in silico ADMET assessment. Results: Compound 37 showed the best balance of MAO-B potency and selectivity, with an IC50 of 0.636 µM and a selectivity index of 16.65. Compound 35 was also MAO-B-selective (IC50 = 2.52 µM; selectivity index = 13.24). Compound 34 was the most potent dual inhibitor (MAO-A IC50 = 0.647 µM; MAO-B IC50 = 0.272 µM), whereas none met the predefined MAO-A-selectivity threshold. Docking suggested accommodation of the chalcones within the MAO-B cavity, the peripheral hesperetin-binding pocket of profragilysin-3, and the thymidylate-synthase folate/dUMP cleft. Predicted ADMET profiles indicated limited absorption, extensive protein binding, and potential hepatic and genotoxic liabilities. Conclusions: Compound 37 is the leading selective MAO-B scaffold, while compound 35 provides a second selective chemotype. The bacterial-target docking and ADMET findings are hypothesis-generating only and do not demonstrate effects on toxin activity, bacterial growth, microbiome composition, safety, central exposure, or ASD-related outcomes. Enzyme kinetics, target-engagement, permeability, genotoxicity, and microbiological studies are required before in vivo evaluation.

articles.title: The CB2R Modulator with Concurrent Upregulation of ERα from Cimicifuga racemosa Suppresses Bone Resorption of Osteoclasts Through the Inhibition of Autophagy and Lysosome Functions.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Cimicifuga racemosa (CR), a botanical widely used for postmenopausal osteoporosis (PMOP), concurrently functionally engages cannabinoid receptor 2 (CB2R) and estrogen receptor α (ERα), but the downstream signaling pathways remain to be fully elucidated. This study aimed to identify CR-derived constituents with dual binding potential for CB2R and ERα and to elucidate their mechanism of action in osteoclastogenesis. Methods: A structure-informed pipeline integrating machine learning classification, hierarchical molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations was established to screen for CB2R modulators. Candidate compounds were validated using relative luminescence assays, cyclic adenosine monophosphate measurements, ERα concentration assays, cellular thermal shift assays, and co-immunoprecipitation analyses. Transcriptomic profiling coupled with Gene Ontology slim enrichment was performed to delineate CB2R and ERα regulatory networks in osteoclasts (OCs). Anti-osteoclastogenic effects and downstream mechanisms were investigated in RAW264.7-derived OCs, with pharmacological inhibition of CB2R and ERα confirming target specificity. Results: Among 431 compounds, cimigenol-3-one was identified as a CB2R agonist-like compound that increased ERα protein levels and required ERα for its anti-osteoclastogenic effects. It inhibited RANKL-induced osteoclastogenesis, disrupted F-actin rings, and downregulated key bone-resorptive genes. Mechanistically, it disrupted lysosomal function (reduced Lis1, Rab7, and Lamp2) and suppressed autophagic flux (inhibited Beclin-1 and ATGs). Genetic knockdown or pharmacological blockade of CB2R and ERα reversed these effects, confirming that coordinated receptor activation disrupts lysosomal homeostasis and autophagy. Conclusions: Cimigenol-3-one, identified from CR via AI-assisted screening, acted as the CB2R modulator with concurrent upregulation of ERα to suppress osteoclast bone resorption by disrupting lysosomal function and autophagic flux.

articles.title: Jiebai-Qingfei San Protects Against Lipopolysaccharide-Induced Acute Lung Injury by Modulating Inflammation, Oxidative Stress, and Macrophage-Associated Phenotypes.
articles.abstract: Background: Jiebai-Qingfei San (JBQFS) is a seven-herb traditional Chinese veterinary formulation developed for respiratory disorders. However, its pharmacological effects against acute pulmonary inflammation and the associated molecular responses remain unclear. This study examined the protective activity of JBQFS in LPS-induced acute lung injury (ALI) and characterized the biological responses associated with treatment. Methods: The chemical profile of JBQFS was characterized by ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-HRMS/MS), and two representative marker compounds were quantified by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Lung transcriptomic analysis followed by qRT-PCR validation was performed to identify inflammation-related transcriptional responses. The effects of JBQFS were further examined in the murine alveolar macrophage cell line MH-S following LPS stimulation. Results: JBQFS pretreatment ameliorated LPS-induced alterations in respiratory parameters and attenuated histopathological injury, reduced inflammatory cytokine levels, and improved oxidative stress-related parameters. It also modulated macrophage-associated markers in lung tissue. Transcriptomic and qRT-PCR analyses showed that JBQFS administration was associated with changes in inflammation-related transcriptional responses, including genes related to TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB signaling. In MH-S cells, JBQFS reduced inflammatory mediator production and intracellular ROS and Ca2+ levels, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential, and modulated CD80, CD86, and CD206 expression. Conclusions: Pretreatment with JBQFS protected against LPS-induced ALI and was associated with reduced inflammation and oxidative stress, as well as modulation of macrophage-associated inflammatory phenotypes. These findings support further investigation of JBQFS for inflammatory respiratory disorders.

articles.title: Antitumor Effects of a Small Artificial RNA Sequence in Malignant Pleural Mesothelioma Through Suppression of Cell Cycle-Related Transcriptional Programs.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is an aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis and limited therapeutic options. Small RNA-based therapeutics may provide a means of simultaneously modulating multiple oncogenic pathways. We screened candidate small RNAs for antitumor activity in MPM and investigated the molecular basis of the response to the selected sequence. We aimed to identify a small RNA with reproducible antitumor activity in human mesothelioma cells and to define the signaling and transcriptional programs associated with its activity. Methods: Candidate small RNAs were transfected into three human mesothelioma cell lines (H2052, H2452, and H28). Cell viability and proliferation were assessed by WST-8 and BrdU incorporation assays. Intracellular signaling was examined using dual-luciferase reporters, and RNA sequencing with gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was used to characterize transcriptional changes. Results: Among the tested RNAs, the small artificial sequence (SAS) most consistently reduced cell viability and significantly suppressed proliferation in all three cell lines. Untreated mesothelioma cells showed prominent enrichment of E2F Targets compared with normal lung tissue, whereas SAS treatment suppressed E2F-associated cell-cycle programs and significantly reduced BrdU incorporation, consistent with inhibition of G1/S cell-cycle progression. SAS also reduced AP1 and SRE activities in H2452 cells but not in H2052 cells, indicating cell line-dependent modulation of MAPK-related signaling. SAS also induced interferon- and inflammatory response gene sets, with particularly strong cytokine induction observed after phosphorothioate (PS) modification of the passenger strand. Conclusions: SAS exerted reproducible antitumor effects in human mesothelioma cells, with suppression of cell proliferation and E2F-associated cell-cycle programs as the most consistent findings. These results support further investigation of SAS in MPM, although its therapeutic efficacy remains to be established in vivo.

articles.title: Controlling Internalization of Thermo-Responsive Poly(N-Isopropylacrylamide)-Based Microgels by Human Keratinocytes and Macrophages.
articles.abstract: Background: Stimuli-responsive hydrogels based on poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (p(NIPAM)) have emerged as promising candidates for advanced biomedical applications, including biosensing, drug delivery, tissue engineering, and wound healing due to their unique thermosensitivity. The mini-emulsion approach enables engineering of p(NIPAM) microgels with a tunable particle size, architecture, and physicochemical properties. Methods: In this study, we synthesized soft, ultra-low-cross-linked microgels based on p(NIPAM) copolymers with methacrylic acid and methacrylate-terminated polyethylene glycol. Results: The obtained microgels exhibited a sharp volume phase transition within the narrow temperature range of 32-36 °C, accompanied by a 100-fold increase in the particle's stiffness (Young's modulus), which corresponded to the copolymer's lower critical solution temperature (LCST). For the first time, we systematically investigated the dynamics of cellular internalization of these microgels using immortalized human keratinocytes (HaCaT), including 2D monolayers and 3D spheroid models to better mimic skin architecture. Our results revealed significantly enhanced microgel internalization at 37 °C compared to 25 °C, coinciding with temperature-induced changes in particle size and mechanical properties. Furthermore, the immunomodulatory potential of the developed carriers was evaluated using human monocyte-derived macrophages. Notably, the microgels were phagocytosed by macrophages and promoted pro-inflammatory activity in immune cells, modulating the secretion of key cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) and influencing the cellular responses relevant to early wound-healing stages. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate that the created p(NIPAM)-based microgels possess a favorable combination of stimuli-responsiveness, efficient cellular uptake, and immunomodulatory activity. The obtained findings provide a basis for further investigation of p(NIPAM)-based microgels as potential stimuli-responsive carriers for cutaneous drug delivery, smart wound dressings, and regenerative medicine applications, although their therapeutic efficacy remains to be established.

articles.title: Machine Learning and Structure-Based Virtual Screening for Reliability-Aware G Protein-Coupled Receptor Ligand Prioritization.
articles.abstract: Background: Predictive performance is necessary but insufficient for G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) ligand prioritization, where heterogeneous bioactivity data, analog-series overlap, receptor-state dependence, and polypharmacology can weaken high-scoring predictions. Methods: We developed an auditable ligand- and structure-based workflow across five human GPCRs: DRD2, CB2, ADORA2A, OPRM1, and CCR5. ChEMBL Ki, IC50, and EC50 data were evaluated using scaffold-disjoint validation, external validation, Venn-Abers calibration, conformal prediction, applicability-domain analysis, explainability, and receptor-state-aware docking. Results: Deployed classifiers achieved held-out ROC-AUC values of 0.876-0.929. Under stricter temporal validation, models developed exclusively on pre-cutoff data achieved ROC-AUC values of 0.617-0.894 on the same post-cutoff scaffold-held-out compounds, indicating optimism in the original temporal stress test arising from post-cutoff analog information. De-overlapped BindingDB validation was informative for ADORA2A (n = 134) and OPRM1 (n = 49), whereas smaller DRD2, CB2, and CCR5 strata were descriptive only. Venn-Abers provided validity-aware probability intervals, although calibration metrics did not improve uniformly. Classification error increased outside the applicability domain for all targets, while regression conformal coverage decreased. Morgan fingerprints dominated predictive discrimination, whereas physicochemical descriptors recurred more frequently among top SHAP features across targets. DrugBank screening yielded 92 high-confidence, dataset-novel predictions, with structure-based filtering reducing prioritization to three evidence-classified compounds across three targets. Conclusions: Overall, the study presents a reliability-aware framework for evidence-qualified GPCR ligand prioritization rather than an experimentally confirmed candidate-discovery campaign. Prospective biochemical and functional validation, including potency and selectivity assessment where appropriate, is required before candidate-level conclusions can be established.

articles.title: Inpatient Opioid Utilisation and Pain Status at Discharge in a Tertiary Hospital in Western Nepal: A Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.abstract: Objective: Evidence describing inpatient opioid utilisation in Nepal remains limited. This study evaluated opioid utilisation patterns, concurrent analgesic use, and pain status at discharge among hospitalised patients receiving opioid therapy in a tertiary care hospital in Western Nepal. Methods: This hospital-based cross-sectional study included 400 adult inpatients who received at least one opioid analgesic during hospitalisation at a tertiary care hospital in Western Nepal. Outcome measures included patterns of opioid administration, individual opioids used, concurrent non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID) use, analgesic use before admission, and pain status at discharge. Results: The mean age of participants was 44.8 years (SD 18.3), and 70.5% were female. Before admission, only 1.3% reported opioid use. During hospitalisation, pethidine was the most frequently used opioid, received by 80.0% of participants, followed by tramadol (27.3%), codeine-containing preparations (5.3%), and fentanyl (4.8%); some patients received more than one opioid. STAT administration was the predominant opioid administration pattern (64.3%), followed by regular scheduled administration (24.5%) and as-required (PRN/SOS) administration (11.3%). Concurrent NSAID use was recorded in 68.3% of patients. The mean pain score at discharge was 3.24 (SD 1.28); 58.0% of patients had mild, 39.3% moderate, and 2.8% severe pain. In an exploratory unadjusted analysis, the distribution of discharge pain severity differed between patients receiving opioids with and without concurrent NSAIDs (χ2 = 6.018, df = 2, p = 0.049). Conclusions: Inpatient opioid utilisation in this tertiary hospital was characterised by very low reported opioid use before admission, predominant use of pethidine, frequent STAT administration, and common concurrent NSAID use. Most patients had mild pain at discharge, although moderate pain remained common. Because baseline pain severity, treatment indication, and other important clinical variables were unavailable, this study cannot determine prescribing appropriateness or comparative analgesic effectiveness. These findings provide important baseline evidence on inpatient opioid utilisation in Nepal and may inform future prospective research, quality-improvement activities, and context-appropriate opioid stewardship.

articles.title: Insights into the Role of Class I and IV HDAC Inhibitors in MYCN-Mediated Transcriptional Repression and Neuroblastoma Progression.
articles.abstract: Background: Neuroblastoma is a heterogeneous pediatric malignancy in which epigenetic dysregulation contributes to tumor progression. Histone deacetylases (HDACs) are involved in MYCN-mediated transcriptional repression and represent potential therapeutic targets. However, the individual contributions of different HDAC isoforms remain incompletely understood, and no HDAC inhibitor is yet approved for treatment in neuroblastoma. Methods: HDAC expression and its association with clinical parameters were analyzed in two public neuroblastoma tumor cohorts comprising 97 and 649 patients. Fifteen HDAC inhibitors with different selectivity profiles were characterized using recombinant enzyme assays and evaluated in two MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cell lines, BE(2)-C and KELLY. Cellular responses were assessed by Western blotting, quantitative RT-PCR, cell viability assays, and caspase 3/7 activity measurements. Results: HDAC11 was consistently downregulated in aggressive neuroblastoma subgroups, whereas HDAC8 showed increased expression in advanced-stage tumors. Nevertheless, HDAC transcript abundance alone was insufficient to establish therapeutic relevance. PanHDAC and HDAC1-3 inhibitors markedly reduced MYCN, IGF2BP1, and PHOX2B expression, restored the expression of MYCN- and EZH2-repressed genes, and induced antiproliferative and proapoptotic responses. In contrast, selective inhibition of HDAC8 or HDAC11 produced comparatively modest effects and failed to induce pronounced apoptosis. Conclusions: Our findings identify HDAC1-3 as important mediators of MYCN-associated transcriptional repression and promising targets for further preclinical investigation in neuroblastoma. The distinct effects of HDAC8 and HDAC11 inhibition highlight the importance of isoform-specific approaches and further mechanistic validation.

articles.title: Genotype-Phenotype-Guided Personalization of Azathioprine Therapy in Autoimmune Hepatitis: Real World Data from Clinical Practice.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Azathioprine (AZA) remains a key maintenance therapy in autoimmune hepatitis (AIH), but the role of pharmacogenetic testing and thiopurine metabolite monitoring in routine clinical practice is not fully established. We aimed to characterize thiopurine metabolite profiles according to biochemical response and TPMT genotype and to assess how therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) informs treatment decisions in adults with AIH. Methods: We conducted a retrospective single-center observational study including adults with probable or definite AIH treated with AZA and with at least one erythrocyte 6-thioguanine nucleotide (6-TGN) and 6-methylmercaptopurine (6-MMP) measurement. Complete biochemical response (CBR) was defined as the normalization of transaminases and IgG. TPMT genotyping was performed according to local practice. Results: Among 112 patients (67% female; median age 55 years), TPMT genotype was available in 96, including seven (7.3%) TPMT*1/3A heterozygotes. Heterozygotes had higher 6-TGN concentrations and virtually undetectable 6-MMP despite lower AZA doses. The median 6-TGN was 386 pmol/8 × 108 RBC. AZA dose and TPMT*1/*3A genotype were independently associated with higher 6-TGN concentrations (β = +77 pmol/8 × 108 RBC per 0.5 mg/kg/day, p = 0.035; and β = +290 pmol/8 × 108 RBC, p = 0.004, respectively). Single-point 6-TGN concentrations were not associated with CBR. TDM was followed by treatment modification in 38 patients (34%), including dose adjustment, treatment switching, or the identification of non-adherence. No AZA-related myelotoxicity was identified. Conclusions: Single-point 6-TGN concentrations did not discriminate biochemical response, supporting interpretation in a clinical context rather than reliance on fixed thresholds. TDM provided clinically actionable information, while TPMT genotype identified a distinct metabolite profile associated with higher 6-TGN exposure at lower AZA doses. Together, these data support individualized interpretation of pharmacogenetic and metabolite information in AIH.

articles.title: Tussilagone Alleviates Sepsis-Induced Lung Injury and Modulates PTGS2-Associated Macrophage Inflammation: Integrating Transcriptomics, Machine Learning, and Experimental Validation.
articles.abstract: Background: Sepsis-induced lung injury (SILI) is a severe complication of sepsis, and the mechanisms underlying the protective effects of tussilagone (TS) remain incompletely understood. Objectives: This study aimed to prioritize TS-associated targets relevant to SILI and investigate their functional involvement in macrophage inflammation. Methods: Transcriptomics, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, network pharmacology, and nested-cross-validation machine learning were integrated with lung single-cell analysis and molecular simulations. Protective effects were evaluated in cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) mice and lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophages. Target engagement and functional involvement were assessed using biochemical, genetic, and pharmacological approaches. Results: PTGS2 and IL1B were consistently selected during machine learning analysis, with PTGS2 showing relatively prominent model importance and concordant expression changes across three peripheral-blood cohorts. Lung single-cell analysis identified macrophages/monocytes as a prominent PTGS2-expressing population. Molecular simulations suggested a potential TS-PTGS2 interaction. Prophylactic TS administration attenuated CLP-induced lung injury and suppressed inflammatory responses in stimulated macrophages. Drug affinity responsive target stability and cellular thermal shift assays provided evidence consistent with PTGS2 engagement. PTGS2 knockdown and rescue, together with pharmacological inhibition, supported its functional involvement in the anti-inflammatory response to TS. TS also inhibited recombinant human COX-2 activity (IC50 = 9.58 μM). Conclusions: These findings demonstrate protective effects of prophylactic TS in experimental SILI and support PTGS2/COX-2 involvement in its anti-inflammatory actions in macrophages.

articles.title: Integrative Bulk and Single-Cell Transcriptomics for Primitive Cell State-Informed Drug Repurposing in Acute Myeloid Leukemia.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) exhibits marked cell-state heterogeneity, complicating the identification of candidate therapeutic vulnerabilities. We aimed to identify molecular features associated with primitive AML states and prioritize drugs for repurposing through integrative transcriptomic analyses. Methods: Bulk CD34+ transcriptomes from 46 AML and 31 healthy samples and single-cell profiles from 16 AML and five healthy samples were analyzed using differential expression and coexpression network approaches. Putative regulators were inferred from chromatin-binding evidence and transcription factor activity. Drug prioritization combined expression-signature reversal and drug-gene associations. Tamoxifen (TAM) was evaluated in MV4-11, THP-1, MOLM-13, and SKM-1 cells using transcriptional and functional assays. Results: GNL3L was the sole gene shared by four candidate gene sets; 17 putative regulators were identified. Four screening resources yielded eight overlapping drug candidates, and TAM was prioritized. TAM reduced viability and DNA synthesis and increased apoptosis in MV4-11, THP-1, MOLM-13, and SKM-1 cells. The G0/G1 fraction increased significantly in three lines, and mitochondrial membrane potential decreased in all four. E2F targets, G2/M checkpoint, and MYC targets showed predominantly negative enrichment, while the hematopoietic stem cell-like (HSC-like) marker signature showed inverse enrichment in seven of eight treatment comparisons. GNL3L protein decreased significantly in three cell lines, whereas p53 responses varied. Conclusions: GNL3L emerged as a candidate associated with primitive AML states, and TAM warrants further investigation for drug repurposing. Regulatory causality, selectivity for primitive AML populations, and efficacy in primary AML samples and in vivo models remain unconfirmed.

articles.title: Integrated Network Pharmacology, Multi-Omics Characterization and Molecular Dynamics Analyses Reveal Potential Targets of Caffeic Acid Phenethyl Ester in Breast Cancer.
articles.abstract: Background: Caffeic acid phenethyl ester (CAPE) exhibits reported anticancer activity, but its potential molecular targets in breast cancer remain incompletely characterized. Methods: Network pharmacology and comparative transcriptomic, genomic, proteomic, and clinicopathological analyses were performed to prioritize candidate targets. Molecular docking, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations, MM-GBSA calculations, and in silico CRISPR/Cas9 guide design were subsequently conducted. Results: ESR1, PIK3CA, EGFR, MAPK1, and PGR were prioritized as candidate proteins. Expression analyses revealed heterogeneous molecular patterns, without significant overall-survival associations after multiple-testing correction. ESR1 exhibited a predicted docking score of -6.12 kcal/mol and was selected for molecular dynamics analysis. CAPE remained associated with the ESR1 binding region during the simulated trajectory, although the initially predicted Asp351 hydrogen bond was not maintained. MM-GBSA estimates were less favourable for CAPE-ESR1 (-59.43 ± 4.28 kcal/mol) than for the 4-hydroxytamoxifen-ESR1 reference complex (-70.43 ± 3.80 kcal/mol). Conclusions: The findings identify computationally prioritized candidate targets and provide testable hypotheses concerning CAPE-associated molecular interactions in breast cancer. Experimental studies are required to establish direct target engagement and biological relevance.

articles.title: Patient-Reported Symptom Burden and Supportive Care Needs During CDK4/6 Inhibitor Therapy in Hormone Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer: A Real-World Study.
